THE APOLOGY.
Think me not unkind end rude

That I walk alone in grove and glen: I go to the god of the wood To fetch his word to men. Tax not my sloth that I Fold my arms beside the brook; Each cloud that floated in the sky Writes a letter in my book. • Chide me not, laborious band, For the idle flowers I brought; Every aster In my hand Goes home loaded with a thought. There was never mystery ,But 'tis figured in the :lowers.; Was never secret history • But birds tell it in the bowers. One harvest from thy field Homeward brought the axes strong; A second crop thine acres yield, Which I gather in a song. E3IERSOV,

A Masuistosata Lonser.—A tmsseller in the United State.s gives a curious account of a matrimonial lottery, which was founded there with beneficial effects, how- sever singular it may sewn. "I was passing," says he, ••• through the State of South Carolina, and in the even- ing arrived in the stfourbs of the town of —, where I had an acquaintance, on whom I called. I was quickly informed that the fatally was invited to a wedding in a neighbouring house ; and on being requested I changed say clothes and went srith them. As soon as the young couple were married, the company was seated, and a sprofound silence ensued. A young lawyer then arose, snd addressed the company very eloquently; and in finishing his discourse, begged leave to offer a new scheme of matrisiony, avhich, he believed, would be ibenehcial; and, on obtaining leave, he proposed That one roan in the company should be selected as president; that this president should be duly sworn te keep en- tirely secret all communications that should be for- warded to his° in his official department that night ; and that each unmarried gentleman andllady should write his or her name on a piece of ,paper, 'and glades it the name of the ?person. they wished to marry, then hand ft the president for Inspection, and if any gentleman and lady had reeiproesfly chwsen eaeb other, the presi- dent was Ito inform each the of- result, and those who i had not been reeiprocal n their choice, kept entirely secret.' After the appointment of the president,,e‘rn- atunieation.s were accordingly handed sip to the chair, and it was found that twelve young ladies and gentle- men had made reciprocal choices, but whom they had chosen remained a seeret to all but themselves and the president. The conversation changed, andiale comPartY respectfully retired. Now hear the conclusion. I was passing through The same place on the 16th March fol- lowing, and was informed that eleven of the twelve snatches had been solemnised, and that the young gentle- men of eight couples of the eleven had declared that their diffidence was so great, that they certainly should not have addressed their respective wives if thf above scheme had not been Introduced." A certain Irishman Pursued the occupation of "knocker-up" in a thriving Yorkshire town, and one day as he was going his round he arrived at the resi- dence of one of his customers, and was just going to open the garden gate leading to the house door, when he saw a dog sitting on the doorstep. Being afraid to proceed further, he cried, " Hallo, mister, git up an' sind this dog away, so as I can cum an' wakin' ye:" WOMEN IN THE FatriammaND.—Women In German farmhouses are occupied in driving waggons, cutting the hay, spreading the dressing on the land, planting and digging the potatoes, barefooted and bareheaded, carry- ing on their heads or their backs the farming tools and sweepings of the road, harnessed to a cart with a dog! She must also telid her babies, cook her food, and bear sons to be compelled to do military servicse when most she needs them to rest her weary hands. No wonder she cannot tidy her house, clean her children, or make her own person womanly or smart. She merely exists to labour, and to labour till age has bent her double; yet in every little farming village in Germany, in all its filth and bad odours, grows on each window-ledge a box of blossoming plants, carefully tended. It seems to be the one outlet of that feminine love el grace and beauty which every woman has. THE Fran' REFORM BILL.—hI a recently published work on "The Life and 'limes 'Of William 1V.," the reader will find a good resyme of the private history of the passing of the first Reform lffl, including the famous letter of Lord Grey, regarding the creation of Peers with a direct view to carry the bill, of all which, if it is not exactly new, it is interesting to be reminded at this time. The King, as will be remembered, suggests a compro- mise that should be satisfactory to the Peers, with a stray hint that his Ministry must comply or be dis- missed, adding: "An arrangement to this effect would relieve the King from t 1 embarrassment under which he has been placed by the proposal to make so extensive a creation of Peers for the purpose of passing the Re- form Bill, and would be highly satisfactory to his Majesty." Earl Grey, however, stuck to his point. "It is" (he replies) most painful to Earl Grey to press upon your Majesty anything to which he has reason-to believe that your Majesty's opinions are adverse; but he is under the necessity of adding, with the unanimous con- currence of his colleagues, that it-appears indispensable, if it should be your Majesty's pleasure to continue them in their offices, that they should have your Majesty's consent to a creation of Peers, if it should be required, td give additional strength to your Majesty's Govern- ment in the House of Lords." Complete surrender fol- lowed upon this bold but especially Oonstitutional kand in the shape of the memorable note, "The King grants permission to .Earl they and to his Chancellor Lord Brougham, to create such a number of Peers as will be sufficient to ensure the passing of the Reform Bill—first calling Peers' eldest sons.—Windsor, May 17, 1832.— WILLIAM R.." CITRIODS PAYMENTS Fon LAN-D.—The term pepper- corn rent' is a familiar one to us all, and instances of such a rent having been fixed are neither few nor far between. Thus, Bermeton, in Durham, was held by the service of three grains of pepper yearly; Plnchley, in Middlesex, spy the annual rent of a pound of pepper; Highgate, in Denbigh, was leased for a term of 500 years at the annual rental of one peppercorn; and for a fortieth part of one knight's fee in the manner of Ley- I ham, in Su.ffolk,'Philippa Ross rendered "one capon and the third part ef one capon, and the third part of one pound of pepper," A similar custom was that of Pokerly, in Durham, which lands were held by " one clove on St Cuthbert's Day, in September, for all other services." All theloregoing examples of services may be regarded as to some extent reasonable, though inadequate as pay- ment far the landteld, but many of the gervrces rendered appear 'to be purely arbitrary and capricious, as when a farm at Brook House, in 'Yorkshire, was held by the paymentrof a "snowball at Midsummer, and a red rose at Christmas." Roses often appear its these services. Laadsin Crendon, in Buckinghamshire, were held by the "service of one chaplet of roses at Christmas." For the manor of Fulmer, in the same county, Sir Marma- duke Darel rendered one red rose yearly; as did Ralph de Balvoir for lands in Mickelharn, Surrey; and Sir Tides for the manor of Steno and H' inton, in North• - ampton. Lastly, certain lands at Haine, in Surrey, " were held of the men of 'Kingston upon condition of renfleainglo the said men three clove gilliflowers at the king's coronation; and perhaps the single dove referred to'above is if it were a spice, should rather be regarded as a-Similar flower.

EXCELLENT CRMCS.—An Englishwoman in Japan writes :—At the country house of a Daimo, where we obtained lodging and entertainment, I was a cause of muth amusement. A number of ladies were invited to meet me at afternoon nice (the name for dinner). 'They sat on their heels around the little table which fused as a chair. My feet were stretched out before me. The hostess, with, as I took it, many apologies, began to inspect my boots. As her curiosity was keen, I drew them off. All the ladies pounced upon them, and some of them asked leave to fit them on. Before doing this, they caused bowls of hot water to be fetched, washed their feet carefully, and dried them • by fanning them, which made the wet evaporate , quickly. As they had all lehildren's feet, my boots -were awfully_ big and more ridiculous than I can-say. The ladies next handled my skirt and corsage, and to oblige them I took them off. The petticoats had their turn, then my stockings, which they did not laugh at; after them my buckled elastic garters, and last my stays. 'Japanese pdlitness here broke down. Everyone shook and cried with laughter in looking at • my stays. One of the ladies had picked up some French iztOsoka (a-treaty port) and explained to me that the others wished to know whether the stays had been in- vented to servo as a cuirass to protect fair Europeans from rude men, or was it worn as a penitential garment to expiate sins? I said : "No but to beautify the figure." This answer convulsed them. A stayed-up woman•affected their impressionable and well-educated nes as something monstrously ugly and absurd. Japanese dress is beautiful and so easy. There was yet another question to be answered. There are, so far as I know, neither cows nor goats in Japan. Children are not,!therefore, weaned until they are big enough to go to sehool. I had noticed that poor little Miss Mite was an gobject of general commiseration. I did not know why. The -reason came out when ray stays were being ex- amined. They were a barrier between the mother and The child, which were cut off ley them from its lacteal rights. I told them that We delegated the nursing duties to poor women and cows. lam afraid that I was imperfectly translated, for I saw that for a moment I wassn object of horror. 'Nicks OF BEGGARS.—From a conversation at the Philosophers' Club, New York, on the subject of beggars, we extract the following That Confederate soldier business isa comparatively new deal, though it has been wofked before," remarked the cynical philosopher. "I'd like to wager that he was not in this country during the war." "I believe in that fellow," replied the sympathetic philosopher. 't He must be honest or he wouldn't come up befordNorthern men and adroit that he was in the Southern army." "That's just Where you make-a mis- take," retorted the other. "This is an era of recon- ciliation, and he's sharp enough to take advantage of it. The stippled Union soldier is played out, and doesn't command attention on the streets any more. The Con- federate soldier racket appeals to the brotherhood, re- stored feeling between the North and South, which is just at 'present at its flood tide. Besides, its novelty at- tracts attention, and every beggar knows that when he induces -the average man to listen to him half the battle is won. That's why they talk so fast. When a beggar steps up betide a man in the street he knows that he's got to glit'hia entire argument before his victim in some- thing like 'lO seconds or else he'll &et out of hearing. Therefore he must arrest his curiosity, or pity, or in- terest by something striking or startling. The ten-centsfor-a-drink racket was one of these. A beggar would step up before a man and say:—' Please, mister, give me 10c. to get a drink. I'm dying for a glass o' whisky.' Ah,' the charitable man would say to himself, at last I have found a 'beggar who is honest, who will not stoop to lie, pauper though he is. I will reward his frank- ness,' and out would come a dime. I—" "You're right," interrupted the sad philosopher. "I had that played on me 'in Park-row only the other night. A tattered rascal came up to me in front of thapost-office and said with 'winning frankness :—'Mister, l'know by your appearance that you can appreciate my condition. I haven't had a drink for a week. Please, Oh please, sir, give me a dime to get just one good drink, and then I can die happy.' Well, I gave the fellow 10e., and ten minutes later I saw rthe wretched impostor, Through Hitchcock's window, buying a plate of beef asd 'beans' with the money." "The base hypocrite !" ejaculated the fat philosopher. "That man would be'capable of pasturing a goat on his grandmother's grave. But I had a new trick sprung on me about seven o'clock one night this week. A fellow came up to me in East Twenty-first-street, or rather he called after me, 'Young gentleman! Young gentleman!' As he was so flattering to my personal appearance, I stopped until be

, came up. Then' he said, in gruff. desPerate tonef "Look here. I've been to every single house on both sides of the street in this block to ask for something to eat, and been insulted everywhere. At one place a woman told me to go out by the back yard and the dog would give me a bite, and in two or three places the servants sassed me. Then I made up my mind to one thing—(here his tones were horribly itysterious)—l said 'l'll ask one man more for assistance, and,if he don't help me I'll steal something.' Now, I ask you, sir, if you'll keep a desperate man from crime by giving him a couple o cents. I mean just what I say. If you don't help me I'll rob somebtody." "'ls that all?' I in- quired. Go ahead, then. I don't care if you carry off ' the whole block.' I have yet to hear that he has com- mitted any crime, but his threat would have taken in anyone but a sophisticated man of the world Ilk my- self.'" "That reminds me," said the thin philosopher, "of the olci story about "Don't tell it," wailed the other four philosophers in unison. 40 —the citizen who wag 'braced' by a tramp," proceeded the thin philosopher, unruffled, "who told him that if he did not give him a dollar he should be driyen to a deed his soul abhorred. The citizen plunged into his clothes and forked out the money, and then ventured to ask what the deed was that the soul of the beneficiary abhorred. Work; repued the tramp.

The number of horses exported from Ireland to Great Britain during the week ending the 11th inst. was 701; in the corresponding week of last year, 1,028. Fattening cattle not quite ready for the butcher should have cake or corn on the grass now, or they will waste. Those who have stalls, sheds, or boxes had better house their cattle as the weather becomes cold and unsettled. Warm shelter is a great enconomise of food.

It is calculated that on the average 14-ilbs. of cheese are consumed per annum by each Englishinan. It is surprising that this wholesome food is not more generally used in Ireland, it would be an advantageous addition to the diet of labourers, and would cause a developraent of the dairy industry.' School Girl, a pony belonging to Messrs. Smallwood and Carr, Whitby, has just completed its season's per- formances as a leapor. During the last three months it has engaged in twenty-two competitions for prizes for leapers, and succeeded in winning no less than sixteen first, four seconds, and one third. The amount of the prizes is £94 13s. 4d. If a horsekeeper were to take a feed of oats from the bin and throw half of it into the Inanure heap, he would be considered fit for a lunatic asylum. That is just what more than half the worldare doing, as half the oats given to horses uncrushed are not assimilated in the stomach,but pass away whole and untouched. Hence, half the quantity of oats, if crushed,,will do the animal just as much good. At a recent meeting of the Carse of Vowrie Farmers' Club, Mr. Smith, of Balruddy,advocated the increase of dairying on arable land, pointing out that dairy farmers had stood the bad times better than other farmers,. He also urged, as a means of raising more stock at home, . the rearing of calves more,extensively. With the aid of , artificials he had reared 70 dalves on the milk of four , cows, and got from £9 to £lo.a head for the animals at the age of 11 mouths. ORIGIN Olir WHEAT IN AMERICA.—The first wheat raised in the new world was sown by 'the Spaniards on the Island of Isabella, in January, 1494, and March 30 the ears were gathered. The foundation of the wheat harvest of Mexico is said to have been three or four

grains carefully cultivated in 1530, and preserved by a slave of Cortes. The first crop of Quito was raised by a Franciscan monk in front of the convent. •Garcilazo de la Vega affirms that in ;Peru, up to 1658, wheaten bread had not been sold in Cusco. In the famous butter district of France the aim is to have the dairy not luxurious, but clean and sweet. Many prefer. having the dairy underground in a cellar, .as in Normandy and Flanders; this secures more uni- formity of temperature. In Denmark the dairies are as lofty as 201 t. The dairy, like a wine cellar, ought +to be exempt from shakingby the passage of carts, &c., and, above all, away from the neighbourhood of bad smells. In the milk districts of Jura, Switzerland, North ,Flan- ders, Holland, and Holstein cleanliness, shade, and tran- quillity characterise dairy sites. KEEPING Burrsit.—An exchange recommends a pickle made of table salt, and strong enough to bear an egg, to .be put into a stone jar, in summer, for the purpose of preserving odd pieces of butter. The butter for this purpose should be worked over, . and a little more salt added. It is most convenient for use if put into two- pound TORS, and wrapped in very thin• muslin before putting it into the pickle. The butter will' keep from September until May, and be perfectly sweet. Stone or glass jars alone should be used for pickles. The glazing of red earthenware contains red lead, which is .eaten into by the acid of the vinegar, and becomes poisonous. VALVE OF GOOD Her.—Some experiments have been made to show the comparative value of good hay for stock. It is estimated that 1001bs. of hay equals g73lbs. of green maize, 4001bs. of green clover, 1751b5. of raw potatoes, 3001bs. of carrots, 5041b5. of. turnips, 541bs. of rye, 401bs. of wheat, 591bs. of oats, 571bs. of maize, 641bs. of buckwheat, 451bs. of beans, 681bs. of acorns, 1671b5. of chaff, 591bs. of linseed, 1051bs. of wheat bran, and 3391b5. of mangel wurtzel. This shows that for conve- nience and use hay should always hold its own against roots and green crops. In times when grain is abnor- nudly cheap the advantages of feeding it largely to stock are clearly seen from the chemist's figures. WORKING THE CORN MARKETS.—" A County 14iller," writing in Dornbvscles List, wants to know who is, responsible for the "official" reports on the market at Mark Lane telegraphed all over the country. He says:— A speculative movement takes place some day in America, say one or two cents per bushel—next Mark Lane official report says : "Market. firmer, in conse- quence of American advance." This is followed 'up by a cable from the other side of the Atlantic: "Market stiffer, in consequence of better feeling in Mark Lane." And so it goes on for a week or two, each market raising and being raised by the other, until the thing is found to'be hollow and buyers won't work. In ten days or so letters from Chicago say (date 29th Sept.): "Our market has advanced about 4 cents from the lowest point touched. There has bop a strong effort by local opera-. tors to bull the market, in the hope that your markets would turn in sympathy." 'OXFORD Dowsrs.—Oxford Downs are comparatively of very recent origin, brought about within the past fifty years. From the blending of the blood and type of the pure Hampshire Down, with the equally pure Cotswold, we have the Oxford Down result. Ana a brilliant suc- cess the continuing process of breeding from the result has proved. For some years these sheep were looked upon as a good class of cross-breds but who now can point out anymarked variation in their prevailing type? No variation exists worthy of notice, and we have in them a pure hreed of noble sheep, " made " well within the recollection, Of .many living though veteran flock- masters. As farmers' sheep there are no better than Oxferd Downs;. many sorts are not half so good, none are more profitable. The Oxford is good all round, and this in the end wins. They make large weights, of very excellent Down mutton of a quality which sells rela- tively well. In the flock, however, they show to still greater advantage. The ewes twin remarkably, and this valuable property places the flockmaster in a position which the owner Of other breeds seldom or ever enjoys. A breed of sheep that is singularly prolific in reproduc2 tion, hardy, and early to mature, is certain to occupy a front position in popular favour.

RENTS IN NORTH YORKSHIRE.—A letter appears in the Mark Lane Express from a North Riding farmer, com- plaining that rents in the North and East of Yorkshire are at .least as high as they were sixteen years ago, and protesting against the assertions of the Yorkshire Post that landlords have already made all the sacrifices that can be expected of them, and that Protection is the true remedy for agricultural depression. Protectionists have a right to declare their opinions, of course; but if they wait till they get a duty on foreign corn before they see any relief. of agricultural depression, they will die and turn to dust before they catch a glimmer of comfort. In the meantime, are they prepared to see the present race of tenants ruined outright? It has often been pointed in these columns that landlords have the alternative of reducing rents to sitting tenants, and so saving them from ruin, or allowing them to be ruined first, and then gnarling to new tenants greater reductions than would serve now. As a matter of self-interest it would be better to keep the men they know and trust on their faims, at an immediate sacrifice, than to take those they know-nothing of not long hereafterat a greater sacrifice. RESITS MUST COME DOWN.—A LANDLORD'S VIEW.— Lord Adlington, speaking at the Dorchester Agricultural Show, on Wednesday, said there was a much more serious question for agriculturists than the extension of the franchise; it was the state of agriculture. (Hear, hear.) He Wished that Mr. Gladstone and Lord Salis- bury Would meet together and see If they could not do something that would make the farmer get a fair profit for what the soil produced. (Applause.) He had lived in the county of Dorset all his life, and had been con- nected with Parliament all his life, and what he wanted to see the farmers do was to combine and ask for some- thing that they could get and were entitled to, and not to ask for 'what • they could not get, and had no chance of getting. Hemould tell them what they could get and what they could not get. What they could get was re- lief of some of the local taxes and burdens. And that was what they were entitled to. (Applause.) They were, to use a 'sporting expression, handicapped 71b. extra. (Laughter.) They had to compete with the whole world and were unfairly handicapped, and if they were half the fellows he thought they were they would not stop asking until they had got what they wanted in this matter. (Applause.) 'lf these times centinue rents must come down. (Applause.) He looked upon the sub- ject in a mercantile manner. Land was not worth so much now as It was formerly, and they must adapt themselves to' the circumstances of the day, (Applause.) Land- lords must suffer. 'He thought that farmers throughout the country had 'had a very .bad time. They had lost their capital. Many and many a farmer had paid his rent out of Ids capital and had nothing left. That was the real state of things. He did not think they would ever see a duty put on corn. He had told them the truth on this matter. In conclusion, his lordship con- gratulated the society on the splendid show. A MODERN CORN MILL.—Upon an upper floor 0110 Messrs. Leicester's huge premises, in Scotland-road, Liverpool, whither the visitor is chaperoned in an im- provised miller's dress, the grains of corn are introduced and broken down between rapidly rotating steel rollers, the first stage in the reduction of the wheat into the finest and whitest of flour. In the same process the grain is cleansed of accumulated dirt, separated into different sizes, and whilst the impurities are carried away in one direction the broken wheat is carried away in another, and between smaller and•firker sets of rollers reduced again and again. Finally the grain emerges from the process in form of semolina, a substance better known to thrifty housewives, who make puddings of it, than to printers. In the next stage the semolina is puri- fied and made to part with its woody fibre, and then upon smooth rollers, and, having got rid of its dirt and offal, it is ground down into flour. The grain is carried un from the lower floor to the higher by means of ele- vators, working automatically, and t onstrueted with ' spiral screws and buckets. Very delicate machinery is required and used in the purifying process. Under the old system flour, bran, and dirt were ground to- gether; the separation of the flour and the bran and the dirt was imperfect The firm keeps running what are technically known as thirty rollers, three pairs of stones for reducing fine semolina, thirty-five dressing reels, ,eight purifiers with fiat sieves, and SiXteell wind purl-
Jtj auff

fiers with 5,000 feet of spiral screws and 5,000 feet ol elevator. The machinery is driven with a 200t‘hor- power engine, and in power alone a saving of‘3o cent is effected-upon the old system. [Messrs. Leicest, take in their gram almost without the touch of a humitl. hand. The corn is shot into bins, and very little morels seen of it until, having passed through the maqhineryl it is emptied as finished flour into new sacks, renioed weighed, and booked; no hand touches the flo`ur from the beginning to the end of the mechanical processes. Their average output is 2,700 sacks of flour per week.— Liverpool Post. SALE OF STOCK ur WEicurr.--Sir I. B. Lawes writes to The Times-1n your article on crop and stock pres-' pects published in The Timesof September 221 was much pleased to notice a paragraph stating that It "system of selling cattle, novel in Britain, though not so in th& United States, 'was introduced at the auction sale at Um. berslade, near Birmingham, the live weight of each animal being stated in the catalogue." This, although not actually selling by live weight at so muchper pound, is a step in the right direction. I have already on many occasions called attention to the uncertainty connected with one of the most important branches of a farmer's business in consequence of the neglect of the use of Ike scales in the purchase and gale of stock, and I am san- guine enough to hope that in time the great body of agriculturists maY 130 induced to insist upon the weigh- ing of stock being substituted for the present most un- certain and unbusinesslike process of guessing which prevails :between buyegs and sellers. .The act of pur- ahltsing by Weight ,go finiversal in all'ordinary trans- actions that we can hardly realise how iimmense is the saving of time affected by this process quite apart from ' its affording the certain information Of the actual value of any bargain as soon as the price per pound or per ton is settled.• At this sale 'we are told that some of the itock was sold at the rate of 4s. 9d. per /41b., or about 4d. per pound. It is quite probable that if a number of farmers were asked how many pounds an ox of 15 cwt. or 18 cwt. would IWeigh there would be differences of 501 b., 601 b, or perhaps, even - more bet Ween their esti- mates. At 4d. per pound the difference of 301 b. in the weight of an ox As equal to 10s. on the animal. Farmers ' will often spend half a day at a fair bargaining for a few shillings over the price of a bullock; and yet a value greatly in excess of the amount under discussion would certainly be shown in favour of either one side or the other if the animal was placed on the weighbridge. In I common with other agriculturists, I myself suffer from this loose manner of doing business. Last autumn I purchased 40 head of cattle in Ireland, and though I could implicitly trust the judgment of the friend who selected them for me in regard to the quality of the stogli, it was not until the animals had reached my farm and had been placed upon the weighbridge that I had an opportunity of judging whether my purchase was a good one, or whether I could have done better elsewhere. Why should I not be able to say I will only give so much per pound for live weight? I protest in the strongest way I can against a system which prevents me from knowing the value of my purchases until after the trans- action is completed.

STABLE INIOTES.—BROKEN-WINDED HORSES. In the peculiar state of the lungs of a broken-winded horse, the great labour of the abdominal muscles is ab- solutely necessary to bring about the proper arterialisa- tion of the blood; hence, under certain states of atmo- sphere, when there is less oxygen in a given space, or from, perhaps, some other peculiar changes in its elec- trical condition which we cannot fathom, the difficulty of effecting the oxygenising of the blood is greatly. In- creased. If we urge a badly broken-winded horse into exertion he will drop; he is thrown into a state of asphyxia, in which, if he should die, his blood will be found quite bladk. Indeed, in bad eases, as the disease advances to a fatal termination, we find the lining mem- brane of the nose and mouth turning purple, evincing the condition of his system. According to our present knowledge, nothing can be done to effect a cure, though happily it is in our power greatly to alleviate the dis- tressing symptoms. If we suppose the difficulty of breathing to arise from a gorged condition of lung (which is generally the case in any presumed cause of disease), it is evident that any pressure against the diaphragm will increase the difficulty of breathing. Although the morbid appearance of emphysema of the lungs has not been found practically such a constant attendant cause of the complaint as is often supposed, yet the carrying out of certain principles has proved correct in the treat- ment; indeed, the practice of regulating the giving of food and water so that the horse is not obliged to work on a full stomach has its advantages in preventing broken wind. The palliative treatment of this disease' con- sists principally in a proper systetn of dieting. The stomach must always be kept unloaded prior to work. Hay, which appears to have exerted a baneful influence • in producing the disease, is to be given sparingly, and little at a time; and always of the best quality. Give the greatest supply at night, damping it; for a middle-sized 'horse, 7 lbs. are quite sufficient It may be asked, "Why give hay at all?" to which we can only answer, "Neces- sity obliges us to do so." It is a fact, we believe, well known in physiology, that concentrated food will not alone support life. The stomach must have It certain quantity or bulk to act on; and were we to substitute some sort of straw, we should only increase the mis- chief, since it would be found we must give more straw in proportion than hay, the former containing less nutri- ment in the ratio of three to one. Whatever manner food is given it is to be either damped or contain a por- tion pf bran mash, and it ought to be of the most nutri- tious description, at the same time readily digestible in kind and form, in order to keep the dung in a softened state. A manger food, such as the following, seems very applicable :—One part ground maize, and two parts ,ground oats, with the addition of sliced carrots, when they can be readily procured, as they seem to act bene- ficially in preventing the collection of flatus, which is so distressing to the animal. The quantity of foods, and the proportions, mainly depend on the size of the horse and the work he is to perform. if carrots are used in any quantity, a proportion of hay may be dispensed with, accordant with the relative nutritious value. The horse ought to be fed at least four times a day, but nothing for two hours before work. The broken-winded horse, like the roarer, is always eager for water; but give it sparingly, very often, and only a little at a time, the greatest quantity in the evening, and debar him from it for some time before his ;work. If fed on car- rots or any succulent food, he will require less water. . RESULTS OF THE HARVEST. The Times publishes a lengthy and interesting article giving the results of the harvest. The general average yield of wheat has been about 30 bushels per acre or slightly above a standard normal produce, the standard average yield being 29i bushels per acre. The acreage under wheat in the present year has been 2,751,000, and the wheat available for consumption, after deducting seed, has been 9,504,000 Imperial quarters. The average acres under wheat for the nine years ending 1883 was • 3,14060, and the produce 9,182,000 Imperial quarters, or 25* bushels per acre. It appears that the wheat area has fallen from nearly four million acres in 1869 to 2/ millions in 1884. The Average for the past 19 years is 3,434,000 acres. With a total home production of 9,504,000 quarters for the past harvest available for con- sumption, after deducting seed, we require an importa- tion of 16i million quarters of wheat and flour during the current harvest year ending August 31, 1885. Last year the imports required were put at 16! million quar- ters, the quantities actually received from September, 1883, to August; 1884, being—wheat 11,803,220 quar- ters, and flour 4,289,162 quarters, total '16,092,382 quarters. The exports to be deducted were 276,515 quarters. In stating the ensuing year's total re- quirements at 26,000,000 quarters, when the total available for consumption has averaged 24,795,000 quar- ters during the nine years ending 1883-4, and the average for the last sit years has been 25,723,000 quarters, The Times takes into consideration not only the increase of population and the encouragement to extra consump- tion furnished in the excessively low price of bread and flour, but also the fact that a larger proportion than usual of the home produce of wheat will be withheld from market and aaropriated as food for animals. The average of 18 years, 1866 to 1883, shows 10/ million quarters annual production of wheat, and 12fr million quarters imported; amounting to a total of 23,311,000 quarters per annum available for consumption. For the first nine years of that period the home growth was 12,278,000 quarters, and the importation 9,548,000 quar- ters per year. For the last nine years ending 18834, the home crop gave only 9,182,000 quarters, while the imports swelled to 15,613,000 quarters per year. Barley, in spite of its fine promise in some parts of the kingdom, turns out 33 bushels per acre, thus being below a stan- dard average of 35 bushels per acre. The production has been extremely variable. The area is short this year baying shrunk from 2,663,000 acres in 1881 to ,336,000 acres in 1884. On this, deducting three bushels per acre for seed, there have been grown 8,760,000 4uar- ters. If the total requirements for maltsters, brewers, distillers, and feeders of animals be 14,900,000 quarters, there will be required 5,240,000 of imported barley, which is 1* million quarters more than was received from abroad last year. Oats, peas, and beans have yielded short crops. Failing or moderate crop of roots, relieved only by fine yields of potatoes, nearly free from disease, form a sad compensation for a vast loss in the produce of hay and a poor summer grazing of pasture. From all parts of the coun- try there have come lamentations to The Times. The burden of these is the preposterous price to which corn has descended, with little prospect, indeed of recovery to a reasonable level; the fact that corn still remains a pro- duct of husbandry which cannot, at present, be dis• plaeed, while the alternative of more live stock produc- tion is met also by a fall in the price—store beasts being worth 30s. to 495. per head less than at this time last year, and sheep at the great fairs making Bs. to 12s. per head less value. The report from the district nearest Lancashire is from a well-known agriculturist in the North Riding of Yorkshire, Who says that the prophecy a those who declared that one fine weather seapn would retrieve the position of farmers has been quite falsified. The pototo crop varies, but, as a rule, there are plenty of tubers, though on Fniis where rain fell upon hot ground the disease is pressalent. Prices are very low, £2 per ton be- ing as much as they are worth in the market. ' Store beasts are worth no more than at last spring, and are worth £3 per chead less than they were a year ago. Many farmers have summered them for nothing. Sheep have done very badly, and landlords have reduced their rents in many instances with serious effects upon themselves. All the farmers agree in de-

SCIENTIFIO NOTES.
Acting under the orders of his medical advisers, Prof. Huxley has left England for some months of absolute rest. He has proceeded in the first instance to Venice. . . . .

An interesting discussion on the alleged shifting of the earth's axis of rotation is being carried on in Nature. Professor Piazzi Smyth writes this week in support of the opinion that a slow change is going on. Many years ago Mr. T. P. Bunting began a memoir of his father, the Rev. Dr. Bunting, the noted Wesleyan minister. One volume was published more than twenty years ago. Mr. Bunting is now finishing the work, and will publish it in a complete form..

Great is the task, writes the Athentmenz, before those zealous for popular enlightenment! Last week one of the librarians of the British Museum, passing through the King's Library, was stopped by a well-dressed man, who had been examining the cases in which manuscripts and other documents relating to Wickliffe are exhibited, and was asked by the visitor, "Pray, sir, can you tell me who the Mr. Wickliffe was who formed this col- lection 2"

The Rev. John'. S. Moffat, who returned from South Africa mainly for the purpose is now engaged in writ- ing a memoir of his father, Dr. Moffat, the well-known missionary, and father-in-law of Dr. Livingstone. Mr. Moffat has lately brought to light several letters written by both his father and his mother at the period of the first arrival of the Boers in the country now known as the South African Republic. These letters are said to be almost prophetic in their tone as to the relations of the Boers with the natives, especially with the Bechuana tribes. The work will not be published before the spring. —Athenauns.

A letter /purporting to give a descriptian by an eye- witness ,of the execution of Queen Mary will be pub- lished at the end of the present year. It has been ' found in a manuscript book among the papers of Lord Eliock, the Judge, who died in 1793. The book is all written in one hand, apparently in the first half- of the eighteenth century, and the account of the execution is ' a copy of a letter sent by special desire. Lord Eliock's father managed the affairs of the Duke of Perth and of ' other families devoted to the Stuart cause, and it is con- jectured that the document now discovered is a copy of a letter written by a member of one of these. ' At a recent meeting of the Paris Academy of:Sciences, M. Tresca• read a communication on experiments re- cently made at Turin and Lanzo to distribute the electric light to' great distances. These experiments, carried out by Messrs. Gaulard and Gibbs in connection with the International Electrical Exhibition at Turin, are stated to have been attended by a large degree of suc- cess. A Siemens' dynamo-electric machine of 30 horse- power generated an alternate current, which was simul- taneously utilised by the Swan, Siemens, and Bernstein systems distributed over a circuit of 24 miles between the Exhibition, Lanzo, and intermediate stations. A Nrw NoSE.—Fancy making a man a new nose out of the middle finger of his left hand and by borrowing a bit of flesh from his cheeks. This is what Dr. Sabine has just accomplished in the Bellevue Hospital, New York, in the case of aman who had lost his nose through hepuline cancer. To make a new nose of flesh alone would not do, as it sinks into the face, anci does not stand prominently forth as a nose should. Conseouently Dr. Sabineborrowed the little bones of the fingel to make a bridge and septum and then covering these with a strip cut from tho cheek, manufactured an artificial but living nose! The man is said "to be much improved in appearance," and to be very proud of his second nasal organ. PREADAMIC REPruEs.—Professor Marsh, the distin- guished American palceontologist, continues to enlighten the world concerning the strange preadamic reptiles which the geological sucvey of his country are unearth- ing in the Far West. He has just published a memoir on the Thereopa a, an order of extinct carnivorous reptiles which existed during the oolitic period. An almost per- fect skeleton has been named by the professor Cerato- saurus. It must have been a strange beast, 17ft. long, with a large horn on its skull. It had what is to natura- lists anew, strange, and unexpected type of vertebra, a pelvis, in which all the bones were ossified together, as they now are in birds, and a set of bony dermal plates which extended from the base of the skull along the neck over the vertebne.

- ME OLDEST CHI:TECH IN AMERICA.—IL is alleged that the oldest church in America is situated in the village of Tudousac, where the Canadian river Saguenay flows into the St. Lawrence. The church was built by the French discoverer, Jacques Cartier, for the French colony he had founded. It is only a small building, be- ing only about twenty feet square, with a very low ceil- ing, and was erected in 1517, twenty-five years after the discovery of the Continent. It contains a very remark- able picture of the Virgin Mary, painted more than 300 years ago by one of the Jesuit fathers at the mission. The objects of interest in the church—for, besides this picture, there are some ancient vestments and a very curiously embroidered altar-cloth—are freely exhibited to strangers. , ME CHOLERA BAcurus.—The Bombay papers, in ex- plaining the failure of the local medical men to identify Dr. Koch's " Comma " bacillus in Bombay, until shown the actual microbe by Dr. Klein and his colleagues, point

out that the organism only slightly resembles the Eng- lish cobima, either as written or printed, the corres- ponding German punctatory sign having been drawn upon by Koch for purposes of description. It is added that the cholera microbes resemble small caraway seeds rather than the English comma. The Bombay Gazette recommends the practice of a series of inoculations oia men lying under sentence of death, the criminals being allowed the option of running the risk of cholera in re- turn for a commutation of their sentences. It is obvioul that negative results from one experiment merely would not settle the question as to the relation between Keelea cholera bacillus and the disease. • IRON ORE IN LlBERlA.—According to a report by Mr* J. H. Smith, the American Consul-General at Monrovia, extensive deposits of iron ore exist in Liberia, Wee° Coast of Africa. Mr. Smith states that he has found, without any difficulty or careful search, very fine speci- mens of iron ore on the surface of Cape Mount, on the seaboard, and at Carysburg, about forty miles by water- zjai and land from Monrovia, and about twenty-fivP es from Grand Hasse. The specimens were esti- mated to contain at least 50 per cent, of pure iron. TbsY were shipped to the Whitney Arms Company, at New Haven, Connecticut, United States. Mr. Smith also states that there are deposits of almost pure iron near the banks of the river St. Paul, above the rapids, twenty miles east of Monrovia. These deposits continue to be found all the way to Musardu, the extent of the furthest exploration, a distance of two hundred miles from the coast. A Liberian explorer, Mr. Anderson, in an account of a journey to Musardu, says that in one district which he visited the road led through a country :which 41' peared to be a solid mass of out-cropping iron ore, a short reddish grass struggling for existence on an ex" tensive plain of metal. The iron is reported to be so 1311„..ra that the road leading through it was a polished -mew pathway, smoothed over by the constant treading of tbe travellers. It is said to be hardly treadable in the drY season, because it becomes so thoroughly heated. ktrs time occupied by the traveller in passing over the to and plains of metal was thrpe hours and a half.----rre74,,, TELEPHONIC COMMITNICIiTION BETWEEN VESSELS "- MonoN.—At the recent meeting of the American ciation for the Advancement of Science Professor A-- Graham Bell, the inventor of the telephone, read a Paper giving a possible method of communication betweet; ships at sea. The experiment that illustrates the methou -which he proposed is, according to Science, as follows ; Take a basin of water, introduce into it, at two witleir separated points, the two terminals of a battert circuit which contains an interruptor, making se° breaking the circuit very rapidly. Now at two etbe.rt points touch the water with the terminals of a drew containing a telephone. A sound will be heard,,excep, when the two telephone terminals touch the water at points where the potential is the same. In this way the equipotential lines can easily be picked out. Now, t° apply this to the case of a ship at sea: Suppose one ship to be previded,with a dyname machine generating a powerful current, and let one terminal enter the water at the prow of the ship, and the other be carefullY insulated, except at its end, and be trailed behind the ship, making connection with the sea at a considerable distance from the vessel"; and suppose the current be rapidly made and broken by an interruptor ; then, ,the observer on a second vessel provided with similar ternn-._ nal conductors to the first, but having a telephone stead of a dynamo, will be able to detect the presence oi the other vessel even at a considerable distance; and bi suitable modifications the direction of the other vesse may be found. This conception Prof. Bell has actuallY., tried on the Potomac River with two small boats, an" found that at a mile and a quarter, the farthest we' tance experimented upon the sound due to the seti°° of the interruptor in one boat was distinctly audible in the other. The experiment did not succeed quite 9°` well in salt water.

COTTAGE GARDENING. Our remarks on fruit trees which we concluded lest week for the present would be imperfect if we omitteo to give a list of the most suitable varieties for the die' trict and the north generally. There are, no doubt, many worthless varieties in cultivation compared with those enumerated below, which have been raised free' seeds.*'• This is because persons overlook the fact that pips of an apple or pear do not produce their like, and a score of pips may be sown and not one produce a gel variety, and many will be as worthless as crabs. sm` inferior sorts are capable of being renovated by cutting them down at the right time and raising their roots aS directed in previous papers, and then graft on them anY of the following :—Kitchen or cooking apples: Carlisle Codlin, Keswick Codlin Hawthornden, Manks French Crab, Livsey's or Tower of Glammis Golder' Spire, Wellington, Scotch Bridgets, and Grenadier. Dessert:: King Pippin, Stunner Pippin, Goldin Pippin, Court of wia, Cox 's Orange Pippin, Blenheim Orange, Greenup Pippin, and Margil. Pears: Marie Louise, wil" ham Bon Chretien, Beurre d' Amanlis, Benne Box, Louise Botua,3 of Jersey, Eyewood, Hessle, and Suffolk Thorn. , Pas,—Prince of Wales, Early Rivers, Victoria, seu the Damson. CHERRIES are not satisfactory unless they are placed against a wall. We, at the same time, would like the Morello:to have a trial, as it succeeds almost anywhere. GENERAL WORK IN THE VEGETABLE GARDEN Will COTP. SiSt of clearing away exhausted crops as well as those destroyed by the frost, of which the dvvarf French Beans and Scarlet Runner look very conspicuous, as there is not a vestige of green in them. Of the first the Pe° haulm and the potato tops may still be seen in sane gardens. A writer of note recently remarked that if we wished to see the 'potato murrain for the first time in anY season, we must keep our eye on small, dirty, and ev'T- shadowed gardens and more especially where all potatO tops were allowed to remain on the surface till far on in the following season. Such gardens he declared to be the very hotbed of the disease, and all the conditiOnft were present to propagate it freely. We have contended in this column for the immediate removal of the toPt "Hogged" potatoes should be examined, as we Openea some of the second Earlies the other day, and found them decaying rapidly consequent upon some that had a touch of the disease being enclosed with them. If it its intended that they should be replaced, a dry day timul_i be selected for opening them, and if the whole are sprew out and examined, they will dry in a few hours, and the clump can be made up again, where the potatoes are likely to keep for some time better than in rooms in or under the dwelling. FRONT GARDEN.—This department of the garden • seems to have suffered worse a few miles round Prestos than elsewhere. Even so near as Lytham the Dahlias, which are as tender as anything, are uninjured; but further away from the coast, front gardens wear a dif-' ferent" aspect. Geraniums are not so Much damaged but what they will be fit to preserve through thewinters and we advise that every effort be made to save theta, as old plantellower mbre freely than the young_ onet All the leaves should be moved except a few small em" on the point:of each shoot. It is not a safe practice to shorten any shoot, and should the plant have too much of a spread, we would remove a few shoots and 0e,.1f them close to tip old wood, as in that case there is 13.31' so mitch danger of gangrene setting in. But the lesg cutting of geraniums at this time the better. They 1n21,4 be placed close together in boxes in dry, light soil, an exposed to currents of air, but not rain. When we sal dry soil,-we,do not mean dust dry, but so dry that n° moisture can be squeezed out, or if it is pressed in tt° hand the paqicles will not adhere; that is what gar.; deners generally understand by dry soil. In such a son they will exist without 'water for weeks; and when it it absolutely necessary to supply them with moisture, we would prefer to immerse the pot or box containing them half its depth in water, and hold it so for a feV7 minutes. The soil being in a partially dry state, would take a large quantity before it reached the roots whet' applied in the ordinary way; and as several applicationg would be required, the soil on the surface would be con- stantly wet, and that in the immediate vicinity of the roots dry. THE Wiwnow.—Last week we gave preparatory in" structions respecting Hyacinth potting. This plant is annually increasing in popularity, and when we consider the beauty and fragrance of the various sorts, as well at the ease with which they are cultivated, we are not so much surprised. Seedsmen devote special catalogues W them and other bulbs,.and their travellers make special pilgrimages up and down the country seeking orders, and in London two auctioneers, at least, conduct three sales each weekly during the season, and now and then one is held in the large provincial towns to dispose of these Dutch bulbs. Porzixo.—All cultivators agree that the bulb should not be buried in the soil, but they differ slightly as to how much should be exposed above it. Some maintain one-half, others a third, and some a fourth. We usually allow one-third, and when the bulbs are covered with; ashes orjsand after being potted they are as much buriel as if overhead in the soil. Even if a small pot is place° over each bulb, which is advisable (where only a few are grown, as it protects them from mice), if the whole is covered with about 81n. of either of the substance°, named, their condition will not be materially chan,,aeol But when the bulbs are taken out and become expose' to the sun in February and March, it is a question if the practice of allowing too much of itto be exposed is no„s a pernicious one. We append a list of good sorts whie° we have noted in winninc. collections at different showS. We select those that are cheapest ;—Single Blue—charlee Dickens, Decandotte, Sir C. Napier, and King of the BlueS. Single Red—Norma, Sultan's Favourite, Lord Wellington, and Gertrude. Single White—Snowball, Voltaire, All Superbissima, Queen Victoria, Mont 'Blanc, and Graria Vamqueur. Double red and shades of the same are the following :—Grootroost, Bouquet Tendre, Lord Welling' ton, Waterloo. Double White—Anna Maria, Florenee Nightingale, La Tour d'Auvergne, and Prince of Water: be. Double Blue—Grand Lilas, Laurens Koster, Lora Wellington, and Garrick.

In each case the pawnbroker b found the metal to stand the test, and had lent more tban one hundred times the actual value.

_ -- HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. The Speaker took the chair shortly before four o'clock. A new writ was ordered for South Warwickshire, for a Member in the place of the late Mr. Gilbert Leigh. THE M7RDER OF MR. BETHELL.-1D reply to questions from Sir F. Miler, Mr. Dawnav, and others, Mr. ASHLEY announced that a telegram had -been sent to Sir H. Robin- son directing him to take all possib'e means to bring to justice the murderers of Mr. Bethell, whose names were knewn. Asked when the despatch had been sent, he Said "To-day," at which there was some ironical cheering. Mr. ASHLEY said that the first official despatch giving the particulars was only received three days aeo, and Mr. Camara pointed out that the murder took place three months ago. SCHOOL BOARDS AND NONCONFORMISTS.—Mr. ILLING- WORTH called the attention of the Vice President of the Council to an advertisement in the School Board Chronicle from the North Mundharn, Hunstan, and Merston U.D. School Hoard, for "an assistant mistress. Churchwoman.— Mr: MUNDELLA found that a similar advertisement appeared in 1876, and then counsel advised that the Act of 1870 gave the Department no power to interfere. The present adver- tisement savoured of intolerance, and was entirely contrary to the spirit of the Act. It was the only case of the sort which had been brought to his notice daring the last four years, and he hoped it would not be repeated. THE SHIPBUILDING TRADE.—Mr. GLADSTONE was ques- tioned by Mr. Gourley as to the willingness of the Govern- ment to relieve the distress in the northern shipbuilding districts by means of orders for naval shipbuilding or by a vote of money as in the case of the Irish and Indian famines. The right hon. gentleman pointed out the irregularity of asking the Treasury to interfere with the arrangements of the Admiralty,and expressed his regret that any hon. gentle- man should suggest an Imperial grant in aid, there being no analogy between the circumstances of the existing distress and those of the calamities referred to. THE ASTON RIOTS—ATTACK ON MR. CHAMBERLAIN A motion by Mr. GLADSTONE to give precedence to the Ad- dress on Monday and Tuesday gave rise to an animated conversation in reference to the Aston riots.—Mr. CHAM- BERLAIN. asked by Lord G. Hamilton when he meant to ex- plain his share in them, said he had been expecting that Lord R. Churchill would have had the courage to repeat in the House the charges whieh he had made out of it. He had not thought it necessary to reply to charges made by persons who were not present, but if Lord R. Churchill had any charge to make against him he was ready to meet it.—Sir H. WOLFF remarked that the right hon. member had spoken with his "usual insolence," but on a reproof from the Speaker he withdrew the expression.—Lord R. CHURCHILL said the President of the Board of Trade had charged him with want of courage in having stated outside the House what he had not repeated inside. He said that the right hon, gentleman was the author of these outrages. No denial having been made to that charge, he thought Mr. Chamberlain accepted the responsibility. If he was afraid of giving a reply, he would take the earliest opportunity of seeing what be could do to "draw the badger." (Loud laughter.)—Mr. CHAMBERLAIN: The noble lord has just brought a very strong charge against me as a minister of the Crown. I shall be prepared to meet that charge on the oc- casion to which the noble lord referred, and for the present I shall content myself with absolutely denying that charge. —Mr. GLADSTONE said it was not intended to interfere with the progress of the debate on the Address, even if it were not finished by Thursday. THE ADDRESS.—THE MA AMTRASNA CASE. The adjourned debate on Mr. Harrington's amendment to Athe address was resumed by Mr. PARNELL, who maintained that the pledge of Lord Hartington that there should be an inquiry had not been honourably fulfilled, and, examining the main features of the case, contended that the trial RAS a farce and. that the conviction was obtained by perjury. Sir War. HARCOURT said that at the reqaest of Lord Spencer who was anxious that the case should be dealt with exactly on the same principles as if it had been an English case, he had carefully considered all the circum- stances before the letter was written to the Archbishop of Tuarn, and had come to the conclusion that there was no grotand for interfering with the course of the law. Mr. E. CLARKE while recognizing the anxious care of the Home Secretary in the administration of justice, ridi- culed the idea that the Lord Lieutenant of Ireland could have been concerned in such a conspiracy as that which was charged against him. Mr LABOUCHERE. speaking in 'favour of the amendment, contended that the dying declarations of the two boys had been improperly withheld from the jury, and he did not doubt that if similar circumstances had occurred in Eng- land an inquiry would have been held. He suggested that the amendment should be amended by leaving out the words of general condemnation of the administration of the law, and confining the amendment to the special case under dis- casein]. The amendment having been accepted by Mr. Harrington, Mi. Gregory spoke against it, and was followed by Mr. W 6 Redmond, who declaimed against the action of the Government in refusing a further inquiry. Mr. Mellor continued the discussion in opposition to the amendment, and Mr. C. Lewis, speaking on the same side, considered it highly improper for the House to countenance an attack upon the Government when they appeared to be doing all In their power to support the due administration of jus- tice. Mr. MITCHELL HENRY supported the amendment, but refused to join in any charge against the bona fides of the Lord-Lieutenant or the Home Secretary. Mr. MACFARLANE supported the amendment, while Mr. C. S. ROIINDELL censured in strong language the wicked recklessness ef the charges which had been made against the Irish Government. Mr. Guasos, in reviewing the facte, reminded the House 'that nine out of the ten men accused had in one form or another acknowledged their guilt. and that the evidence of the three principal witnesses, given at once, had never been impugned. Mr. O'BRIEN supported the amendment, and waned the House that the refusal of the inquiry would be regarded as an intimation that it was determinad to shut its eyes to what was passing in Ireland under the guise of law.-- Mr. O'DONNELL, speaking in support of the amendment, ex- pressed the determination of the Irish party to continually harass the Government and its successors until the subject had been properly and fairly inquired into.--After some remarks by Mr. Deasy, the debate was adjourned, on the motion of Mr. M'CARTRY.
„..-- The Heuse adjourned at 12.30. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at 4.0. In answer to Mr. F. H. Fowler and Mr. Corbutt, Mr. J. K. CROSS said not a single rail had been furnished from abroad for the indian railways during the last 10 years.— In reply to Sir H. D. Wolff, Sir THOMAS BRASSEY said that a scheme for the reorganisation of the constructive depart- ment of the navy had been under consideration. No other alterations were contemplated. FRENCH SHIPBUILDING.—RepIying to Mr. Maclver, Mr. CHAMBERLAIN said he had heard that some few operatives inthe shipbuilding interest from the East Coast, where the depression of trade was severely felt, had found employment in France, chiefly in the repairing of vessels, but no consider- able number of men had taken part in the movement. THE IRISH CHIEF SECRETARYSHIP.—Mr. FIRTH gave

- notice to ask the Prime Minister, in filling up the vacancy of Chief Secretary, that the Lord Lieutenant's consideration would be given to the propriety of appointing an Irish mem- ber of Parliament familiar with the requirements of the country, and able to inspire Irish confidence: ("Oh, ob.") LORD R. CRIMCBILL AND MR. CHAMBERLAIN.—Lord R. Cituacntm., in view of what fell from the Prime Minister on the first day of the session with respect to violence and outrage, and in order to enable the House to come to a decision on the matter at issue and in justice to the Presi- dent of the Board of Trade, gave notice of the following amendment to the Address Humbly to assure her Majesty that we regret to find in recent opeeches and actions . of one of Her Ministers, holding the high office of President of the Board of Trade incitement to interference with the freedom of political discussion and justification of riot and diserder." (Hear, hear, sad "Oh. oh.") Kriairroum.—Mr. R. FOWLER asked had the Government

any information in reference to the rumoured fall of lihar- toum.—Lord HARTINGTON said no such information had been received at. the War Office or Foreign Office.—Mr. MARRIOTT gave notice that he would call attention to Rorpt, Khartoum, and the Soudan, and move a resolution. (Hear, hear.) MILITARY EXPEDITION TO SOUTH AFRICA.—In reply to Mr. S. Leighton, Mr. ASHLEY said that the War Office were in close communication with Sir Charles Warren and the officers in South Africa as to the nature and scale of the military forces by which it was desirable that Sir Charles Warren shall be supported its Bechuanaland. The nnmber of the eight forces in South Africa was now about 8,000. Sir Charles Warren would be under the orders of Sir Her- cules Robinson, as High Commissioner. He was not pre- pared to give a detailed statement of the expedition that would be sent.—Mr. FORSTER : May we consider it settled that Sir Charles Warren is going out ?—Mr. ASHLEY: Yes air.

DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS.—THE trAitatTuASNA CASE. The adjourned debate on the amendment to the Addre2e in reply to the Queen's Speech was resumed by Mr. JUSTIN MCCARTHY, who regretted that so far members of the Lions° were unacquainted either with the locality or the people of that part of Ireland in which the Maamtrasna murders took place. Mr. GLADSTONE said the great importance of the question raited by the amendment was not orly as touching the con- duct of judicial persons, but in regard to the proposed re- opening of a • grave and serious case. Of Lord Spencer personally he could say that no man throughout the king- dom enjoyed in a larger degree the esteem, the confidence, the veneration, load the respect of the people generally. (Cries of "No" from the Irish benches.) The right hon. gentleman also bestowed ahigh enlogium on the character of the Lord Chancellor of Irelind, and remarked that the hon, members spoke in what was to that House a foreign language when they preferred the charges that had been made against two such individuals. (Loud cheers from the Irish members, and a voice "Foreigners we are.") Reviewing all the circumstances of the case, the right hon. gentleman remarked that the appeal which might have been made to the clemency of the Crown had in this instance been shut out by the mode of procedure which had been re- sorted te, and, as to the demand for inquiry, he pointed out the difficulties in the way of inquiry by means of a Select Committee of that House, and in reply to the suggestion that some impartial judicial person should be employed for the purpose, he asked whether that individual was to examine the boy who was held to be unfit for examination at the

trial, whether the convicts who bad pleaded guilty were also te be questioned, and in what mode the examination was to be taken? If it was desired that the examiner should not have power to administer an oath, was it on such a basis that they should establish a machinery, the effect of which would be to upset the verdict solemnly arrived at by a pro- perly-constituted judicial tribunal. (Hear, hear, and a voice : "‘ About Kilmartin's case." Kilmartin's case, which was distinct from the present, in which the House was asked to adopt a method totally unknown to the Constitu- tion, and create what would amount to a Court of Criminal Appeal totally insufficient for the purposes involved and altogether inferior to that which it was intended to supplant. (Cheers.) Mr. T. P. O'CoNrroa expressed disappointment at the Speech of the Prime Minister, and, disputing the eulogium be had bestowed on Earl Spencer, unhesitatingly de- clared that there was not a man in Ireland who was more despised by the Irish people. (Cheers from the Irish benches). Mr. HOPWOOD, in opposing the amendment, pointed out that at the time when the Liberal party supported the estab- lishment of a Court of Appeal the strongest opponents of that proposal wero found among the members of the Irish party.--Sir JOSEPH McKEpare was of opinion that the inquiry asked for ought to be granted in this case. He ad- vised the Government therefore to "Be just and fear not." --Mr. C. THOMPSON supported the amendment.—Sir EARDLY WILMOT had come to the conclusion that a great wrong had been done. In his opinion the Lord-Lieutenant had made a mistake. He argued for a Court of Criminal Appeal. The ATTORNEY-GENERAL severely condemaed the Irish clergymen who had advised the men who protested their in- nocence to plead guilty. The o.Gortmarr MAHON supported the amendment, Mr. CALLAN, who rose amid loud cries of 'Divide," sup- ported the motion. The House then divided— For the amendment 4B Against

Majority against On the motion of Sir H. HOLLAND, the debate was ad- journed. The House adjourned at 20 minutes to 1 o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at twenty-five minutes pet twelve. THE TRANSVAAL: The House, which was vero thinly attended, was occupied throughout with discus- sion of affairs in the Transvaal. The subject was cursorily introduced, without tabling an amendment, by Sir Henry Holland in further debate on the Address Sir Henry did not undervalue the difficulties of the Government in South Africa, but contended that they had been increased by a policy of drift and concession. Mr. Wodehouse expressed his misgivings at the establishment of a partnership with tbe Cape Colony, contending that in dealing with turbulent and barbarone communities affairs could not be conducted with credit and success by by a rigid adherence to the limi- ted liability principle. Sir Frederick Milner drew attention to the circumstances connect- d with the murder of Mr. Bethell. Mr. Cropper, the Lord Mayor, Sir Donald Currie, Mr. Dawnay. and Mr. Evelyn Ashley continued the debate. Sir M. Hicks-Beach, whilst in favour of leaving the colonists to settle the difficulties among themselves, thought the pre- sent was a case in which her Majesty's Government were bound by definite obligations and engagements, and matters could be left to be settled by the Government of the Cape Colony only if they were prepared to fulfil the engagements this country had entered upon. Mr. Forster unfavourably reviewed the action of the Government in relatton to the Transvaal. The right hon. gentleman extended his speech till only seven minutes were left to Mr. Chamberlain, the Minister in charge of the debate. Mr. Chamberlain man- aged to compress what he had to say into this limited space, pointing out that four-fifths of the colony were Dutch ; that action of the kind hinted at by some of the speakers would have brought about a revelution, and that it was only by the patience—the long-suffering, if they would—of the Go- vernment that a crisis bad been avoided. The Government were now in a position amicably to settle matters to their own satisfaction.—Mr. Redmond and Lord R. Churchill struggled for precedence to move the adjournment of the debate, it not being clear which had succeeded. The House adjourned at a few minutes to six. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Tetunsnev. The Speaker took the chair a few minutes before four o'clock. QuEsTiorrs.—Lord R. GROSVENOR was questioned by Mr. Raikes respecting the omission of the Morning Post from the list of newspapers receiving Government commu- niques. His lordship said he saw no reason for departing from the principle hitherto acted upon. He further stated that the redistribution scheme which appeared in the Standard was not furnished to that journal by any member of the Government.—The HOME SECRETARY informed Mr. Macfarlane that the local authorities in the Highlands and the islands of Scotland would in the agitation now going on have the support of the Executive in upholding the law. The question of legislation was receiving the anxious atten- tion of the Government.—Replying to Mr. Bartlett, the PREMIER said preparations were being actively made to en- able an advance of the Gordon relief expedition to take place. LORD R. CHURCHILL'S ATTACK UPON MR. CHAMBER- Lem—The debate on the Address was resumed by Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL, who moved as an amendment the addgion of the following words :—" And we humbly assure your Majesty that we regret to find in recent speeches and actions of one of Her Majesty's Ministers bolding the high office of President to the Board of Trade, an incitement to interference with the freedom of political discussion and a justification of riot and disorder." His lordship, remarking at the outset that he hoped to prove a deliberate and syste- matic attempt on the part of Mr. Chamberlain to incite the people of this country to riot and disorder, and also that be was morally and directly responsible for the breaches of order which had taken place, quoted from a speech which the right hon. gentleman delivered at Birmingham in Aug. last, and then went into a narrative of what bad occurred on the occasion of the visit of himself and Sir Stafford I Northcote to Birmingham. The noble lord claimed to have shown the direct complicity of the Bir- mitigham Liberal Association in the Aston riot, and said the Birmingham Liberal Association was the President of the Board of Trade. They were "one and in- divieible."—Mr. CHAMBERLAIN said the charge made against him at Birmingham was that he had direct personal complicity in the Aston riot, but in the amendment before the House the ground was shifted. The fact was that the noble Lord did not believe in these charges himself. If the proceedings at Birmingham were disgraceful why did his Lordship at a meeting which immediately followed suggest retaliation in the same way? The right hon. gentleman I proceeded to deny in detail several of the statements of the noble Lord. On becoming a Minister of the Crown he (Mr. Chamberlain resigned all his municipal offices in Birming- ham, and be had DO part whatever in the Liberal Association except that he was a subscriber to it. He had never in his life hired a rough; he had never contributed directly or in- directly to hiring roughs, or connived at hiring them; and he did not believe any of his constituents hired roughs. He did not believe that a single ticket for the Tory meeting was forged, and if there was be had nothing whatever to do with it. He was authorised by the leaders of the Liberal party to contradict the charge of forgery. There was no need to forge tickets which were available without forging. As to the allegation that he should have prevented the counter demonstration, he replied that he could not have stopped it if he would, and he would not have stopped it if he eould. —ln the de:ate which ensued Sir Stafford Northcote and the Premier took part.—After further discussion the House divided—For the amendment, 178; against, 214; majority for the Government, 36. The announcement of the result was received with loud cheers by the Conserva'ives. On the motion of Mr. Maclver the debate was adjourned, and the House rose at a quarts-past one.

At the Stratford Petty Sessions on Wednesday, six bakers were each fined .E 5 and costs for not carrying weights and scales when selling bread. The full penalty for this offence is .£lO. Considerable damage to rolling stock was caused by a goods engine running off the Midland Railway line near Luton early on Thursday morning. A number of waggons were smashed, and traffic was delayed. MURDER NEAR Cons.—An inquiry was held on Thursday into the murder of Corporal Ashworth, of the Lancashire Fusiliers, at Ringabella, near Cork. Ainsworth and a comrade were attacked by a number of labourers, who fractured the skull of the former by kicks, and threw his body into the seat Two men, named Murphy and Casey, were committed for trial on the capital charge. THE Borfrox MIIRDER.—During the week Kay Howarth, charged with the murder of R. L. Dugdale, a commercial traveller, at Bolton, has had a short interview with the young woman to whom he was about to be married and his uncle. Howarth again asserted his innocence of the crime imputed to him. He is somewhat reserved in manner, and spoke but little. Professional assistance has been en- gaged on bee behalf, a Bolton solicitor haying undertaken his defence.

AN EXTRAORDINARY MURDER TRIA.L.—A very remark- able trial for murder at the Maidstone Assizes was concluded on Thursday. The victim was a gunner named Hunter, and he was shot by a comrade in mistake for a non•com- missioned officer named Bradford, who was sitting with him at the time. Bradford had caused the prisoner to be court- martialed for misconduct, and the crime *as clearly pre- meditated. The defence set up was that the prisoner was insane at the time he committed the murder, and the jury found him not guilty on that ground, although the evi- dence of sanity and premeditation was remarkably strong. He will, of course, be detained for life in the asylum for insane convicts. _ . . .

Ax Ex-M.P. IMPRISONED.—At the Central Criminal Court, London, on Saturday, Mr. George Hampden Whalley, ex-M.P., for Peterborough, and son of the former represen- tative of that constituency, was charged along with a young man named Thomas Herbert, with having stolen articles valued at £2OO, the property of Mary Gamble. Mr. Whalley took a furnished house in South Kensington, and in it his landlady, Mrs. Gamble, left certain valuables of her own , under lock and seal. These things Mr. Whalley appropriated to his own use, and absconded to Boulogne, where he was arrested. The prisoner Herbert admitted pawning some of the articles and of participating in the profits in cense- ' quence of his living with Mr. Whalley. Another person, who was a man of education, and had been brought up as a gentleman, whose name was Fraser, but was not in custody, had also pawned several of the things. Mr. Whalley was sentenced to nine and Herbert to three months' imprison- ment, with hard labour.
