div.head: FOREIGN NEWS.
div.p: FOREIGN NEWS.

EGYPT AND THE SOUDA.N. GENERAL WOLSELE ADVANCE.—THE FATE OF COLONEL STEWART. CAIRO, SATURDAY.—A circular issued by Nubar Pasha to the Powers announces the resumption of the regular pay- ments to the Treasury of the Public Debt, as provided by the Law of Liquidation. The amount realised by the Egyp- tian Government during the period that these payments were suspended, is about £4OOOOO. CAIRO, SUNDAY.—An official telegram from Wady Haifa states that the two messengers sent to inquire into the wreck of Colonel Stewart's steamer, near the Fourth Catar- act, have returned, and state that a vessel was towing two boats, which, being overtaken by the enemy, they cast adrift, Nahoum and his relatives, who were on board the boats, and were taken prisoners. The steamer continued on its way, but struck on a rock near the Fourth Cataract. The 45 persons on board, including four women, Col. Stewart, two Consuls, one named Nicola, weie all killed with the ex- ception of two natives. The messenger-saw one of the !liar- vivant, who furnished the above information. WADy HALFA, SATURDAY.—Lord Wolseley and Lieut. Colonel'Swaine will start up the Nile on Tuesday. Gen. Sir Redvers Buller and Gen. Earle will remain here for the present. One hundred men of the Mounted Infantry, under the command of Major Barrow, will leave here for Dongola on Saturday. The remaining portions of the Yarrow stea- mer have arrived here. WADy HALFA, MONDAY.— Lord Wolseley to-day visited the Canadian boatmen at their camp, five miles above this place. The canoe which his lordship used on the Red River has arrived here. SARRAS, MONDAY.—Yesterday I passed the wrecked stea- mer Gileh. The crew had a narrow escape. The natives who were hauling her let go the hawser. and the vessel at once struck on a rock. The water poured into her engine room and quenched the fires, and the stream carried her down at a terrific rate. Fortunately she sank close to the shore. Although half out of the water, she is a hope. I less wreck. The officers and crew, who have lost all their private effects, are now encamped upon the bank awaiting orders from Dongola.—Standard. • WADY HALFA, TuEsDAy.—Lord Wolsaley and Colonel Swaine, with their aideetle-camp, left here by train at 6-15 this morning, stopped for a few moments at Genial, where all the whalers will receive their gear, and arrived at Sarras at nine o'clock Assonew, TUESDAY.—CoIoneI Clarke has arrived here with the heavy division of the Mounted Infantry. WADY HALFA, WEDNEsDAy.—Forty more of the whale boats arrived hereto-day. The Canadians have passed 120 boat:, over the Second Cataract. A company of the Stafford- shire Regiment left this morning for Sarras by route marches as an experiment. Lord Wolseley has reached Ambikol. RUMOURED FALL OF KHARTOUM. CAIRO. TUESDAY.—Persietent rumours are circulating this ' morning alleging that Khartoum has fallen. Nothing is known officially. THE NILE EXPEDITION. DONGOLA, TIauRSDAY.—The steamer Nasslf Kheir, on her return voyage from liannek yesterday, discovered the body of a white woman, who is supposed to have been one of the victims on board the steamer that was wrecked at Wady Gana. The body, which had apparently been about three weeks in the water, bore nn trace of violence. Lord Wolseley and staff are expected here on Monday next. FUNERAL OF THE DUKE OF BRUNSWICK.—THE SUCCESSION QUESTION. BRUNSWICK, Seatranay.—The funeral of the Duke of Brunswick took place to-day in the cathedral. The streets of the town were thronged. Dr. Liebe, representative of Brunswick in the Federal Council, has presented to the Diet a communication from the the German Emperor, in which his Majesty rejects the Duke of Cumberland's claim to the succession, and approves the measures taken by the Council of Regency against the Pretender. BERLIN, MONDAY.--The Federal Council to-day adopted the proposal made by Prince Bismarck on the 23rd inst., that the delegates to be deputed by the Brunswick Regency Council as representatives in the Federal Council should be recognised by the latter body. BRUNSWICK, MONDAY.—In to-day's sitting of the Diet Herr Von Veltheim read a letter from Prince Bismarck to Count Goertz Wrisberg, Minister of State, in which the Im- perial Chancellor says that he has communicated to the lEmperor the letter of the 18th inst. from the Regency ' Council. His Majesty has declined to receive either Com- missioner Grote, the Duke of Cumberland's delegate, or the Duke's letter. The Emperor is anxious to solve, in a cen- stitutional manner, the questions affecting the Imperial con- stitution which have arisen out of the present state of affairs, at the same time legally securing the rights and in- terests of the Duchy and its people. The Diet was subse- quently prorogued by the Council of Regency. FRANCE AND CHINA. PARIS, MONDAY.—The French reinforcements to be sent to Tonquin in the middle of next month mill number 7,000. Intelligence received here from Tangier states that the news of an attempt upon the life of the French Con- staler agent at Fez is officially confirmed, and that the matter has been diplomatically represented to the Sultan of Morocco. TIENTsiN, SATURDAY.—Imperial audiences will be held at Pekin on the sth and 7th proximo. All the Princes of the Empire have been specially summoned to attend. THE PRUSSIAN COUNCIL OF STATE. BERLIN. SATURDAY.—The Prussian Council of State, after being in abeyance 300 years, was opened at two o'clock this afternourPin the Elizabeth Hall of the Royal Castle by the Crown Prince, in the presence of the Princes of the Royal House' Prince Bismarck, Count von Moltke, all the Ministers of State and about 100 members of the Council of State. The drown Prince read a speech speci- fying the objects of the re-establishment of the Council. BELGIUM. BRUSSELS, SUNDAY.—The following Ministerial list was I approved by the King at five o'clock this afternoon i—M. I Bernaert, President of Council and Minister of Finance ; M. de Voider, Minister of Justice; M. Thonesson, Minister of Interior and of Instruction; General Ponies, Minister of War; M. Van den Peerenboom' Minister of Railways; M. Caraman Chimay, Minister for Foreign affairs; M. de Moreau, Minister of Agriculture. RUSSIAN NIHILISM. BERLIN, MONDAY.— Intelligence from St. Petersburg states that a printed sheet has been issued in the Russian capital, announcing fresh revolutionary designs. It also ex- plains the murder of Colonel Sudeikin, and the measures ' adopted by the revolutionary party to rid themselves from the traitors to whom they ascribed their failures. Intel- ligence from St. Petersburg states that the news published by a London paper of the discovery of the mine in the Kronoverski prospect in that city is wholly unfounded BERLIN, THURSDAY.—lntelligence from St. Petersburg states that the condemned Nihilists Lieutenant Rogatcheff and Naval Lieutenant Stromberg, whose execution has been already announced, were hanged in the Schluesselburg prison, where al executions are to take place in future. LORD NORTHBROOK. MALTA, TUESDAY.—Lord Northbrook has arrived here in the Iris from Alexandria. He continues his journey to Marseilles to-day TERRIBLE COLLIERY EXPLOSION. NEwl:Yonx, Trasnev.—An explosion of fire damp has occurred in the coal mines of the Yougstown Coke Co., in Pennsylvania. The bodies of two miners who were killed and several others who received fatal injuries have been recovered. There are, however, still more than 20 men buried in the mine and believed to be dead. THE NEW BRITISH AMBASSADOR. BERLIN, TUESDAI .—The National Zeitung, commenting on Sir Edward Malet's appointment, declares that he has al- ready everywhere created a favourable impression. Prince Bismarck, adds the journal, shows he is anxione to maintain with him the same good relations which existed with the late Lord Ampthill. 'THE ELECTIONS IN GERMANY. BERLIN, WEDNEsDAY, 3-10 F.M.—The definite results of seventy-four elections are now known. They include twenty- nine second ballots, in which thirteen Socialists will contest seats with candidates of other parties. AUSTRIA. ATTACK ON A MAIL CART. VIENNA, WEDNESDAY.—The mail cart was attacked and plundered last night at Gyarmarth, a village in Central Hungary. The driver and horses are missing, but the cart was found overturned by the road side, with its con- tents gone.

IHE MEXICAN DEBT. NE-W Yon, WEDNESlDAY.—ktellignee from Mexico announces that the Senate has ratified the agreement be- tween England and Mexico for the conversion of the Mexi- can debt. THE POPE AND IRELAND. ROME, THURSDAY.—An authoritative denial is given at the Vatican to the statement made in a New York telegram recently published here representing the Pope to have ex- pressed to the Bishop of Trenton (New Jersey) a hope for the speedy liberation of Ireland from English rule.

One of the Liverpool magistrates on Monday pointedly informed the lessee of a theatre that the posting of offensive placards might lead to the refusal of his license. SHOCKING RAILWAY FATALITY AT ST. HELENS.— A sad discovery was made on a branch line of rails near the premises of Messrs. Kurtz and Co., chemical manufac- turers, about eleven o'clock on Saturday night, when the remains of George Carruthers, 46 years of age, and residing ,in Higher Parr-street, were found in a mangled condition. It seems the deceased was employed as a labourer by Messrs. Kurtz, and was working until a late hour on Saturday night. On 'finishing his work he proceeded to the Stanley Inn, Peasley Cross, where he had some drink. On his way home he went along the railway, and nothing further was seen of him until his dead body was found as stated. At that time shunting operations were being carried on, and it is supposed that the deceased was knocked down and run over. Both his head and right arm were nearly severed from the body. The occurrence created a sad impression in the neighbour- hood of the deceased's residence, as a widow and six chil- dren were left to mourn his loss. At an inquest on the body of the deceased on Tuesday, it was stated that the deceased had three glasses of whisky at the Stanley Inn, and that he was trespassing when returning along the railway. The deputy coroner remarked that he considered no one was to blame but the deceased himself. He was afraid the whisky had got into the deceased's head, and confused the deceased when the accident occurred. The jury returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased was accidentally killed when trespassing.

1 FE FX A MINFR. SATURDAY. NOVEMBER 1, 184 WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. A meeting of this Council was held in the Town Hall, on Tuesday evening, for the purpose of winding up the busi- ness of the municipal year. There were present the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) ; Aldermen Burgess, Holmes, Kean, and Davies; Councillors Crosfield, Barker, Brown, Platt, Broadbent, Ashton, Marsh, Burgess, Francomb, John Pier. point, Wm. Pierpoint, Sutton, Taylor, Wright, Whittle, Litton, Hutchinson, Milner Tinsley; Brook (town clerk) and Whittle (dtputy town clerk.) THE comstirrEns. The minutes of the Watch, Finance, Street Improve- ment and Lighting, Paving and Sewerage, School Attend- ance, Museum., Library and Arts, Cemetery, Sanitary, Gas, and General Purposes Committees' were confirmed without discussion, and contained nothing of public impor- tance.

_ THE BATIIS.—MKSIC IN THE PARK, In the minutes of the Town Hell, Park and Baths Com- mittee, it was stated that the Bathkeeper had reported that the income from the beths for the pest four weeks was .610 161 101, and for the corresponding period of last year £8 123 61. It had been resolved by the committee that the sum of £5 be voted to the 9th L.R. Volunteer and the Legh- street bands for playing in the park during the summer months, the amount to be equitably divided, viz., £3 10a to the volunteer band and .£1 103 to the Legh-street band.

The minutes were centirmed. STAMPING WEIGHTS AND MEASURES. The Markets Committee recommended that the Town Clerk be instructed to apply to the Board of Trade to increase the scale of fees for stamping and adjusting weights and measures._ .

Councillor TAYLOR moved, and Councillor ASHTON se- conded, the confirrnation Of these minutes. Councillor BoiroN said he Wished to knew why the com- mittee desired to increase the fees for stamping weights and measures. Councillor JOHN PIERPOINT said that from a calculation made the committee found that the expense of stamping the number of glasses they had to stamp would more than swal- low up the amount of fee already fixed upon, and the com- mittee considered they had no right to run into the rate- 'payers' pockets to find the sums to execute this stamping. (Hear, bear.) Conucillor Swami: I ana rather sorry that question is not quite satisfactory. (Several voices " Ile has already spoken.") I asked a question. Alderman BURGESS objected to Mr. Bolton speaking again. The MAYOR said he was, of course, in the hands of the Council. but he really thought the simple asking of a question could not be deemed making a speech. Councillor BOLTON: Mr. Alderman Burgess is in the habit of speaking three or four times. Alderman BURGESS: I beg to tell you, Mr. Mayor, I am not in the habit of doing anything of the kind. Councillor PLATT : I move that the standing orders be suspended until Mr. Bolton asks his question. ("Oh, oh," and laughter.) Councillor JOHN PIERPOINT said he might save the trouble by explaining that in other towns the charge was Id per glass; unfortunately in Warrington it was fixed at d. Councillor BOLTON said this Markets Committee seemed to be against all the shopkeepers and traders in Warrington; to those who came into the town and paid no rates they were more lenient. Ile could not see why they could not stretch a point, as the ratepayers would receive all the benefits. He would move that the minutes be passed, with the excep- tion of the resolution t 4 apply to the Board of Trade to in- crease the scale of fees. There being no seconder to this amendment, the minutes were passed.

NIGHTSOIL REMOVAL. Councillor BURGESS moved "That the Conacil is of opinion that the nightsoil pails should be collected during the night, and recommends the Sanitary Committee to make arrangements accordingly." This resolution, he said, was exactly the same in words as the one which he moved a month ago. He felt it necersary to bring it forward again on account of the manner its which it was met on that occa- sion. Before ha said anything more about it he should like to make the remark that as long as he was a member of that Council he should not submit to be told by any committee that not being a member of that committee he ought not to criticise its work. He was not gaing to say that the work of the Sanitary Committee was not carried on as satisfac- torily as the work of any other of the committees, but if in any particular part of its work it seemed to him that any alteration should be made, and if the committee could not be induced to make the alteration unless the matter was brought before the Council, he should not hesitate to call attention to the point on which he thought the committee was not acting fer the public benefit, As he had said he brought that matter forward that night because of the way in which it was treated on the last occasion it was before the Coun- cil. He did not object to people differing from him; he was perfectly willing that they should vote against him. More than that, if the majority of the Council was against him he was perfectly willing to give way; but when he thought a matter was of sufficient importance to bring before that Council he was not going to be satisfied withoet the deci- sion of the Council being given. That was not the first occasion on which a motion vihich he had brought for- ward had been treated in that Way. Almost at secei as he became a member of that Council he thought it his duty to call attention to another matter connected with the sanitary work, and on that occasion, as on this, the Council was counted out. He delayed for several months to bring forward the matter again, but an outcry arose in the town and he brought for- ward the resolution again, and it Was carried with a large majority. At the end of the last debate on his present re- solution he had no opportunity, on account of its protracted nature, of saying why, in spite of all that was said by those taking the opposite view to the one he took, the opinion which he originally entertained was entirely unaltered. The question of expense was dealt with and he stated what he thought would be the expense, and although some state- ments were made to the contrary he still entertained the same opinion that he held then. But the objections that were made to his resolution practically narrowed them- selves down to this : that tbe alteration was impracticable and that the difficulties in the way ot putting them into practice were simply insuperable. He then explained that on the previous occasion his resolution was debated he men- tioned that Wigan was one of the towns where there was a removal of night-soil by night. He bad informaticn to that effect, but the information was incorrect. He had, however, made very careful inquiry with regard to Birming- ham and other towns, and what he had said on the last oc- casion with respect to Birmingham was undoubtedly cor- rect, and he at any rate would not follow the example of Lord Randolph Churchill and decry the corporation of Bir- mingham. (Laughter.) He had inquired about other towns and found that in Blackburn the collection was made In the night. In Glasgow it was made in the night almost entirely, the exceptions being with regard to a few works where there were no night watchmen kept. In all other cases the collection was made by night, and a member of the sanitary department of Glasgow said that they had ex- perienced no difficulty whatever in collecting the night-soil at night. He thought these facts showed that there were ' no insuperable difficulties in the way of what he proposed. The objections to his proposals had mien, he thought, sta- ted most fairly by Mr. Francombe. He did not display what was displayed in other quarters, perhaps for the admi- ration of the Council, a quantity of rhetorical gymnastics— (laughter)—and he (Mr. Burgess) could only suppose that performances of that description were intended perhaps.to amuse and possibly to distract the attention of the Council from the question that was before it. Mr. Francomb told them that in all probability, at some time or another, they. would be able to remove these pails in the night. That was a distinct admission. But Mr. Francomb pleaded for delay, because, he said, and it was after 15 years of these delays, in Warrington they had not arrived at such a state of perfection as to admit of its being done at present. This was a rather startling confession from a member of the in- fallible Sanitary Committee—(laughter)—and he might say that it hardly seemed to coincide with the very glowing des- cription of the absolute perfection of all sanitary matters in Warrington. (Laughter.) Mr. Francomb said they had not got to that perfection yet, and after admitting this, and saying that some time or another they should be able to re- move pails at night' he enumerated some reasons why the removal could now be made. If he were to describe those arguments he should describe them as the front and bock door arguments. (Laughter.) The trent door argument was this, that there were in Warrington certain houses where these pails could only be reached through the house, and, therefore it wouldbe impossible to remove the pails by night. All this he had heard before, but he hardly believed it was possible with such a perfect Sanitary Committee, and he did netlike to mention it. Now, however, he was in- clined to think it very likely to be true in the case of some of the workingmen's houses in Warrington. He had heard of a family living in one of these houses who, while getting their dinner in the middle of the day, were disturbed by the servants of the Corporation going through the house to bring out these "honey tubs," and the family had to go out owing to the stench. He did not think the front door argu- ment was a very good one, he thought the best argument would be to alter these houses to which the argument applied. (Hear, hear.) He would have as much consideration for the property-owners as his friend Councillor Wright ; but the Corporation had put property- owners to a great deal of expense with regard to these Nat, and whilst making those alterations they might have got them to make such alterations as would have knocked this front door argument out of the field. With regard to the back door argument, the Town Clerk gave a very guarded opinion. His reply to the question put to him by Alderman Burgess, whether the committee had power to compel people to leave open their gates and back yards, was I do not think you have the power to compel people to keep their , back yards open." The Town Clerk was not positive, but I he (the speaker) would suppose the committee had not the power to compel people to keep open their back doors. Who wanted them to do so ? He did not wish it. It was quite possible to get into the yards without the doors being kept open as Councillor Dr. Mackie stated on the last occasion of the debate. He had written to Birmingham and asged for information upon this point, and the reply was that the authorities used a key. So then what Councillor Dr. Mackie had mentioned was absolutely the fact, and being carried out in Birmingham. [Councillor Bolton : What about the bolts?] People would not require bolts and locks also. There was only one other point urged against his motion to which he wished to refer. He had been asked to postpone his motion, and he had no doubt that he was asked with the very best intentions. He was asked to postpone it until Mr. Longdin's scheme had been completed and laid before the Council. If anyone would explain to him—and he would challenge the Sanitary Committee to show this— in what way the nuisance of which he complained would be

abolished or even seriously diminished by the Borough Sur- veyor's scheme he would listen to it, and if this could be proved he would willingly withdraw his motion. (Hear, hear.) He did not see how it could possibly be so. He was not going to discuss the plan and the details, of which he knew very little. He understood the plan would be that there would be depositories in various parts of the town for the reception of the excreta. The excreta would be carried from the houses as at present, and would be taken to these depositories instead of to Longford depot. He could see that such a plan might materially diminish the existing nuisance, but he did not see what the difference in the nuisance itself would be. It would have to be removed then just as it was now, from the same houses and through the same streets. Probaby less carts would be used, but they would, in all probability, be so much the dirtier on that account, and quite as frequent. The only difference he could see that it was possible to make in 'the nuisance would be a difference in the amount of inconvenience suf- fered by those people living near the depositories to which the excreta would be removed. He considered the present system a disgusting and abominable nuisance, and the sooner an alteration was made the better it would be. With regard to the motion, it did not compel the Sanitary Com- mittee immediately to commence the alteration suggested. It asked them to take steps which would eventually, at any rate, bring about the end,intended by this motion. He did not think it an unreasonable request, but one which the people of the town would generally make if appealed to. • Councillor Jotter PIERPOINT rose to second the resolution. He thought that the matter did not call for any lengthy speeches that night, inasmuch as the resolution only recom- mended the Sanitary Committee to "make arrangements accordingly." He inferred that meant that they should consider the advisability of the proposal, and come before the Council with their decision. He should be glad when the time came that an arrangement could be made by which the nightsoil could be removed during the night instead of day, for they had many complaints of the stench in the streets, and the sooner it was done away with the better. With regard to the plan of Mr. Longdin, he thought it would prove a success and diminish the nuisance to a greater extent than Mr. Burgess had acknowledged. The long dis- tance that the vans lead to be carried created a great disad- vantage, and lithe distance were less the nuisance would be reduced. At present he thought it would be sufficient for the committee to consider the matter, and as Mr. Burgess said that he was not particularly in a hurry to know the result of their deliberations, the question was really at an end for the present. Councillor FRANCOMB said that he had asked for delay simply because they were in the midst of experiments that would wonderfully alter the state of things if they proved successful, and because the time was inopportune to inter- fere with the work of the Sanitary Committee. Mr. Bur- gess was surprised that they should ask for delay, consider- ing that they had had fifteen years, but he had only bad two or three years on the Sanitary Committee, and be had seen more hard and anxious work done on that committee than he had seen en any other committee with which be had been connected. They had met the thing manfully. It was a difficult question, and one that had bothered not only War- rington, but almost every part of the civilised world. He saw from a report that in 1873 the death rate of the town was 30 in the 1,000, and at the present time it was about 20, so that Ile believed the Sanitary Committee had good results/0 show for their work. They had got some wretched build- ings which he did not think they at present had power to pull down, and all they could do was to make the best of things as they found them. Wherever he had been—in the poorest courts of the town—he had seen the work of the Sanitary Committee, The scheme in preparation would take ten of the fifteen vans put of the streets. He believed, with Mr. Burgess, that an abominable nuisance existed, and did not think that the Sanitary Committee had gone thoroughly into the matter because their time had been spent in what seemed more important—getting rid of the raw material. lithe committee went into it thoroughly he thought that in a short time, with the five vans or per- haps a few more, they could get every van out of Warring- ton by 10 o'clock in the morning, which would be as much as they were doing at Birmingham. Councillor BROADBENT said that he saw no reasonable or possible objection that could be taken either to the manner or matter of the speeches of Mr. Burgess at the last and pre- sent meetings. He should, had the question come to a division, have supported the committee, as he thought that the answer of the Chairman was conclusive, but he con- sidered it desirable when there was a feeling in the town on any particular subject, as there was on this question, that it should come boldly and fairly before the Council. Mr. Burgess wished the matter to be removed with the least possible inconvenience and nuisance to the public, and so did the committee, and, as had been hinted, they were tak- ing measures to accomplish that end. Councillor Pram said that he sheuld support the com- mittee because he tho'ught it was to be trusted to pursue its own work to the best advantage. He knew from experience what anxious and laborious work was performed by the committee, and he thought the members were prepared to do their best for the borough, and that if they saw their way to bring the matter to a satisfactory issue, they would do it , without any pressure from outside. Alderman Warm said thit thQ ra,mbere of the Con. I mittee Were riot taklng up the time of the Courieil, because they thought that the matter was thoroughly discussed be- fore, but it must not be thought that they were not pre- pared to say a deal against the motion, and they hoped that the Council would assist them in resisting it• The MAYOR said that he should have no difficulty in supporting the motion, and should not feel that he was act- ing in antagonism to the Sanitary Committee. (" Oh !") It was a mild resolution, and simply went to the extent that the Council was of opinion that the nightsoil should be re- moved during the night, and recommended the Committee to make arrangements accordingly. It after all rested with the Committee. ("No.") The Council would simply be recommending, but not making it imperative on the Com- mittee to do it. If the Committee thought it was im- practicable they had only to say so and there was an end to the matter. He thought there would be no harm in vot- ing for the motion. Of course, he might be mistaken, but he should have no hesitation in doing so, because he knew it was a matter for the Committee.
On the motion being put to the meeting there voted for it Councillors Burgess, J. Pierpoint, Hutchinson, and the Mayor, and the remainder against. The motion was therefore lost.

div.head: THANKING THE MAYOR.
div.p: THANKING THE MAYOR.

Councillor BROADBENT moved :—" That the best thanks of this Council be presented to Joseph Harrison, Esq ,alder- man of this borough, for the able and satisfactory manner in which he has discharged the responsible duties devolving upon him as Mayor and Chief Magistrate ef this borough, and for the unvarying courtesy, kindness, and impartiality displayed by him when presiding over the deliberations of the Council, and in his intercourse with its members." He said that whatever difference of opinion there might be amongst them about the removal of the pails, and there did not appear to have been a great divergence, there would, he was sure, be none as regarded the resolution which he had the honour to place before the Council. (Applause.) They had all experienced the unvarying courtesy and kindness Of the Mayor during his year office. He didn't remember a single occasion in this Council where there had been any failing in that uniform courtesy; in fact, if one might ven- ture to make a criticism in moving that vote of thanks, perhaps he might say that the Mayor's courtesy and kind- ness had been sometimes a little in excess, and possibly sometimee a little sterner administration of the duties of the chair might have been better for some of them. But the Mayor in his good nature, when he saw a member of the Council yearning to address them, was very unwilling to check his ardour. He (Mr. Broadbent) thought they ought to recognise in the Mayor his unfailing punctuality and devotion to the duties of his office. Perhaps be might be excused for saying that, unfortunately, the Mayor was not quite so agile as some of the members of the Council, but that had in no way interfered with his constant attendance on every and all occasions when he deemed it his duty to be present. (Applause.) His duties as chief magistrate had been fulfilled with the same steady devotion and self-sacri- fice. And here again, if he might venture upon the slightest possible criticism, he might say that it was that in the -,,ndioions mixture of justice and mercy sometimes the mercy had rather the preponderating influence in his mind. (Hear; hear.) The duties of the mayoralty. which those who have occupied the office knew very well, were of no light character, including as they did attend- ance at various public meetings, where it was a pleasure to the people of Warrington to have the presence of the Mayor, and if possible to be presided over by him. And he believed the Mayor had seldom, if ever, absented himself, whenever he had been requested to take part in public or private meetings, where his presence as Mayor of the Borough had been desired. On all occasions his presence had given the greatest possible pleasure. (Applause.) In moving that vote of thanks, they wished to recognise the hospitality which not only they but the town in general had received at the hands of the Mayor; and he congratu- lated him on the kind of hospitality which had been exer- cised. It had given pleasure to the greatest possible num- ber, and had not been confined to one sex. (Applause.) He (Mr. Broadbent) did not undervalue the importance of a good dinner on the mind of an Englishman, and the turtle soup and punch and that sort of thing, which seemed to be connected in some way with aldermen and councillors— (laughter)—but he thought those entertainments where both sexes could meet perhaps, on the whole, give the greatest pleasure. (Applause.) Ile should also like to allude to the very happy manner in which the Mayor was always able to give expression to his own feelings and to the feelings of the Council on public occisions. (Hear, hear.) They all knew that the Mayor had the gift of speech; and that he had a very happy way of illustrating by apt quotations his utterances to the public, and it was at all times a pleasure to hear him. He had the greatest possible pleasure in mov- ing the resolution, and he felt proud that so excellent a Mayor had come out of Latchford. (Applanse and laughter.) Alderman Howass seconded the resolution. He frilly endorsed all that Mr. Broadbent had said, and he was sure that if Alderman Harrison didretire from the seat of Mayor he could look back upon his year of office with great plea- sure. He was sure the Mayor had had the cordial support of all the members of the Cbuncil, and he believed that the whole town had been pleased with the manner in yrhich he had fulfilled the duties of the office. Alderman DAyins supported the resolution. He.thought they had had a good example of the Mayor that night. It was an example of what he would call the good feature of the failing side. What he meant was that he had always observed that when the Mayor had been giving a decision he had had a, great fear of doing wrong to anybody. He thought Alderman Harrison had made a very good Mayor (Hear, hear.)

Councillor CROSFIELD said he should like to add his testi- mooy to the valuable services of the Mayor during his year of office. He thought Alderman Harrison bad exerted him- self as much as any Mayor in his (Mr. Crosfield's) remem- brance, and that he had fulfilled the duties to the satisfac- tion of the town generally. (Hear, hear.) The resolution was passed with enthusiasm. The MAYOR, in reply, said that if he had reason to be proud on the ninth of November last, when they wcre pleased to confer upon him the honour of the mayoralty, be felt that he had now reason to feel both proud and thankkt —thankful that he had been spared with good health and strength fairly well to go through what he might call the physical duties of the office, and proud indeed he was, in a proper sense, he hoped, that his conduct in every respect had met with their approval. (Hear, hear.) He had en- deavoured to do what he could to be useful, and had not, he hoped, in the least degree done anything to com- promise the honour and respect due to the office with which they had entrusted him. (Hear, hear.) Of course his reign, to use a grand word, had not been charac- terised either by the mapificence of Alderman Pickmere's, or by the munificence of Councillor Croafield's, but in other respects he had endeavoured to emulate their goodqualities, and to profit by their example. The office of Mayor opened a wide vista for personal observation, particularly when he happened to be sympathetic aud a good listener, and h 3 did profess to be a good listener. Of many a painful domes- tic incident had he been made the custodian during the past twelve months, and in different walks of life too, which had deeply impressed him that life was not altogether a placid lake upon which they were all pleasure sailing with full baskets and plenty of champagne, but that it was a storm ridden sea, full of hidden rocks and wily and eccenti ic cur- rents, and it behoved them to be constantly on the watch to avoid coming into contact with them. It was said that the little things of life were harder to bear than great' ones, and he was much inclined to believe that it was so, and that appeared to him to be caofirmed by ex- ' perience ; his experience during the past year had amply confirmed it. It was the little things of life particularly that c, ossed the path of a man holding a public pnition, and that contrilinted most largely either to his fret and worry, or on the other hand to his peace and gladness. He should re- gard the year of his mayoralty, through the kind- ness that had been shown him as a bright green I spot in his memory which would remain with him to the end of his life. He concluded by thanking the members for the cordial manner in which they had passed the vote .of thanks, and the tewn clerk and his deputy for the courtesy they had rendered and which bad conduced so much to make his year of office a pleasant one. (Loud applause). The Council then rose.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

RENCORN RECREATION V. HALEBANK.—PIayed On the I ground of the former, and after an interesting game ended in a win for the hones teacn. Score :—Recreation, two goals, four trier, and three minor points ; Halebank, one I try and one minor point. All the Runcorn men p'ayed a good combined game throughout. RUNCORN BRIGHT STAR V. PARISH CHURCH JUNIORS. —This match was played on the ground of the former, and ended in a victory for the same by two goals and one touchdown to one goal and one disputed try. A goal was dropped by Brimelow for the Star, and shortly after a try was gained by Harvey, from which Royle kicked a neat goal. The tries for the Juniors were gained by Whitfield, who played a good game throughout. Sr. NICHOLAS, BLUNDELLSANDS, V. WIDNES WASPS.— The above clubs played their first match on the ground of the former, at Blundellsands, in the presence of a goodly number of spectators. A remarkably good game was placed, and St. Nicholas, the first time for 4 yeare,were able to bold their own against the splendid dribbling play of the Weeps. The contest throughout was very even, and great interest was shown by the spectators, as both sides were often on the verge of scoring. The game ended in a draw, as neither side scored a major point. After the match the visitors sat down to a substantial tea, which is always provided by St. Nicholas for visitors to Widnes. WALTON V. WIDNES —The above teams met at Walt( n on Saturday, and a thoroughly well-contested game ended in favour of Walton by one goal, two tries, and one touchdown to one touchdown and a dead ball for Widnes. Teams : Walton : T. Rutherford, back; J. Faircloogh, Parry, and W. Legge, three-quarter backs; J. Butcher and J. Alsopp, half-backs • J. Brodie (captain), H. Barker, E. Brown, J. Rancor, H. Smethurst, F. Fowler, J. Owen, F. Tattersall, and W. Charnley, forwards. Widnes :S. Bingham, back; Monis, Parkinson, and Harding, three-quarter backs; Far- rell and Mason, half-backs; Kendrick (captain), Brown, Meagher, Ridyard, Corns, Smith, Golding, A. Bingham, and Longton, forwards. RUNCORN WANDERERS V. RUNCORN RANGERS.—These clubs met on Saturday on the ground of the latter, and. throughout, the game was of the roughest possible char- acter. With the wind in their favour, the Wanderers during the first half had slightly the best of the play, the home team after scoring a disputed try being driven book, and a try registered to the visitors. This, however, was disputed, and a good attempt at goal failed. The Rangers were several time* forced to save tees) half time was called. In the seCond half the game get very noisy, and the Wanderers were pressed hard, though at times they made a combined rush and brought the ball back into the home quarters. No major points were scored by either side, and though the home team tried hard to cross the line, their opponents defied all their efforts. After time WAS called, and the Wanderers were leaving the field, the Rangers being determined to score something of importance, and having no one to stop them, got a try, from which they placed a goal, amid their own shouts of triumph and the laughter of theon-lcokers• The game ended in e draw. WARRINGTON ASSOCIATION V. EARLESTOWN WAN. nannns.—The first teams of these clubs met each other on

the Warrington ground, Knutatord-road, on Saturday after- noon last, with the result that Earlestown came off victors by seven goals to none. The ball was set agoing shortly after three o'clock, and up to half-time the game was pretty evenly contested, and though the Earlestown scored goals they bad not unfrequently to make very vigorous defences of their own posts to keep the Warrington players from scoring. The Earlestown team had the advantage, how- ever, of a very efficient goal keeper, while the Warrington team was rather weak in this respect. After ends had been changed the home team seemed to become somewnat de- moralised, for though the game was at times pretty evenly contested, the visitors scored twice or thrice very easily. For the Warrington team the backs played exceedingly well. The following were the teams :—Warrington Goal, Yonge ; backs, Davies, W. Dillon: half-backs, Walton, Royston, Parker; forwards: right wing, Pearson, Siddall ; centre, Matthews; left wing, Warren, Dillon. Earlestown: Goal, T. Champion; half-backs, R. Johnston, T. Phillips; backs, H. Selby, W. Lord; forwards: right wing, J. Shaw, W. ; centre, W. Dale, J. Lowe; right wing, J. Mather, F. Knowles. HAYDOCK TEMPERANCE V. BIRKENHEAD (IST TEAMS).— These teams met tor the first time OR Saturday at Birken- head. The Temperance team was not up to its full strength, while their opponents had the best men that they were able to procure. It was 20 minutes to four o'clock before a start could be made in consequence of the Birkenhead men not making their appearance. For about 20 minutes play was chiefly confined to the centre of the field, when a succession of rushes was made by each team alternately, in which Birkenhead scored the first point. On play being again ' resumed the Temperance men began to exhibit a good pass- ing game, but their shots were rather wide, till Birkenhead succeeded in getting a good run down the field, and again they succeeded in planting the ball through the uprights, but as the man who scored this point was rdf•side it was disallowed by the Temperance captain. At the change, of ends the visitors again exhibited some good passing, which completely eluded the Birkenhead backs, and the leather was put through for Haydock by Wedgwood. Again the ball was set in motion, and after an interval of 15 minutes Birkenhead succeeded in scoring their second goal. Owing to the darkness which was fast creeping on, and at the call of "time up," the game stood Birkenhead two goals to Haydock Temperance one goal.—The second teams of the above clubs met at Haydock for the first time, but owing to Birkenhead arriving late the fall time could not be played. The Temperance bad some new men on the field, who dis- played very good play, and eventually won by two goals to one.—lhe Ilaydock Temperance (Boys) third team also played a game with the first team of the Earlestown Victories en the second field of the former clnb, and they succeeded in defeating the Eariestothans by six goals to one.

--- EARLESTOWN V. Wrrrow (Blackburn), LANCASHIRE Cur Ti.—The Earlestown first team journeyed to Black- burn on Saturday to play off their tie with the. Witton F.C. in the second round of the competition for the Lancashire Football Association Challenge Cup. The Earlestonians were accompanied by goodly number of their supporters, and there was a large attendance of interested spectators. The toss was won by the Earlestown captain, who chose to i play with a slight breeze in his favour. The Wittonians I kicked off, but the visitors forwards secured the leather and I made an attack on the Witton goal. The goal keeper twice • fisted the ball back, but the ball was again centered by Simm, and after a short scrimmage, Earlestown secured 1 their first goal amid applause—enly four minutes having • elapsed. For the next ten minutes the play was even and I was very fast, and Witton then equalised the score by a good ' shot. The Eariestown team afterwards had wry hard lines in several capital attempts to Increase their score, bat the home &Sal keeper played magnificently, and repelled the Wanks made upon his charge. At half-time the score was three goals to one in favour of Witton—the two additional goals for Witton havinz been scored off Earlestown players. After half-time the Wittonians displayed superior tactics, and for some time they severelrpressed their opponents, rapidly running up their score to sic goals. Towards the close the visitors several times endangered the Witton up- rights, but they were unable to secure any additional points' and thus, after a good game, Earlestown were defeated by six goals to one. The Earlestown team was as follows James Appleton, goal; E. Green and J. Green backs ; J. Duxbury, J. Whalley, and R. Bowk.,r, halt-backs; W. Rich and J. Ellison, right wing t A. W. Dasmall centre; J. Simms and J. Ogden, left wins. Tha referee was Mr. Booth (of Withnell). WJARRINGTON V. ST. HELENS (IST TEAMS) --In Cold and gloomy weather, on Saturday, the return fixture between these clubs was played on the Warrington ground, at Wil- derspool, resulting in a victory for the visitors by one goal and. one minor point to Warrington two tries and ten minor points. The visitors have this Hawn scored six victories in succession, and have not vet been nlaced at a disadvan- tage, but on Saturday, although they did win, they by no Means had thine their own way, as the score ladle ttes.

and

. . as both teams were full strength and in good form some ex- citing play was seen. St. Helens kicked off, the return was made by Massey. ands scrimmage ensued at centre. From the :oose forwards play was very fast, and was carried near the visitors' line. Here the game waged for a long Hine, drops-at-goal by Barnes and Speakman taking no effect. A splendid and even game continued up to half-time. Resum- ing, Turner put the leather in motion, when Tickle punted to Barnes, who returned into touch. The visitors by bteady play gained on their oppopents' territory, and by means of a pass from Borthwick to Finney, who parted to Heseldea and took a drop-at-goal, were successful. Re-starting from the centre, the borne team pressed the visitors in their 25, when Gregson failed to return, and Gil- bert secured a try. The place was an easy one, but failed. Shortly afterwards Barnes passed to Massey, who rounded the opposing backs, and planted the leather under the posts. The place by Turner struck the goal post, ard rebounded into play. The home team from this point had the best of the play until call of time. Warrington team :—T. Walsh, back; J. T. Massey, T. Barnes and S. Bough, threequarter backs ; W. Speakman and E. Gilbert, half-backs; H. Ashtoe (captain), J. R. Calvert, J. Robinson, F. Turner, S. Hum- phries, T. Davies, W:Hayes, J. Jolley, and W. Povey, for- wards.

RUNCORN v. BALM—Played at Brooklands on Saturday, a fast and interesting game, and ended most decisively in favour of Runcorn by two goals, two tiles, and four minor points, to Sale one try. Cookson, having won the toss, Wright gave motion to the ball, when Warburton effected a quick return, which was closely followed by a clever run on the part of Baeshaw. The Runcorn quarter being entered from here, Broady emerged, and had gained the home 25 are Murray checked him. From this point the visitors still, by a storing forward effort, placed the Sale line in danger, and as the result ef a smart dribble Dean grounded the ball. Its value was not, however, increased. W. Hughes made a splendid reply to the drop out, transferring the play inside the Sale quarter flag, and after a couple of exchanges the home line became the scene of action. Speakman tried very hard to score, but losing posses-ion, Johnson very smartly completed the try, no goal resulting from the place. Reply- ing again to Cookson's drop out, Hughes again cleared his lines, the play ensuing in centre, at which point Hugh Hughes made a mast brilliant dodging run, not being checked until he had planted his charge behind the posts, Dean being very successful at the place. Changing ends, Cockson restarted from centre, Speakman replying in a short run, followed by a dribble by Stubbs, and Ughtburn bringing about play on the Sale line, they being forced to save. From this point the play became very fast Lings, I Warburton, and Murray played a hard game to avert so heavy a defeat, but the combined play of Runcorn enabled I Wright to gain a well-earned try, Andrews being also well on tne bull, Dean again being sucussi ol at goal. Starting again from centre, Cookson started the ball again, and , Lin4B securing Hughes with the ball in possession a sharp struggle followed on the Runcorn line, Bullongh getting over, Bagshaw, however, was not successful at the place, time being given directly afterwards. The splendid com- E bitted and individual play of the Runcorn team was the I means of bringing about so decisive a victory. 'Teams Sale: H. W. Smith, hack; F. Warburton, F. Bagshaw, and I J. Murray, three-quarter backs; H. Cookson and S. liar- ! greaves, lialf.backs; E. Lings, Hardy, H. Chambers, H. Marsland, E. Marsland, E. Hunt, C. Howe, Williamson, and J. Bullough, forwards. Runcorn :W. Hughes, back; W. H. Broady, H. Speakman, and T. Johnson, threequar er-backs ; H. Hughes and H. Andrews, half-becks; W. Wright, F. Joule, W. Cox, J. Gatley, J. Stubbs, J. Dean, J. Baylis, W. Dunbavand, and A. Lightburn, forwards.

NOTES BY THE WAY. The first meeting between the Manchester and Liverpool teams took place on Saturday on the Liverpool ground. A pleasant game was anticipated, but it was brought to a pain- ful close at the end of the first half by the sudden death from heart disease of one of the spectators, Mr. Rose, of Liverpool, who was well-known as a football and cricket patron. Broughton Rangers beat Broughton on tke ground of the latter, and Salford were victorious over Birch, at Birch. The ex-holders of the Yorkshire Challenge Cap, Wakefield Trinity, met Swinton after a lapse of three years, on Saturday, at Swinton, when a fine game ended in a draw, Wakefield having two touchdowns and a dead ball to Swin- ton nil. Sheffield and Birmingham had scored one goal each in their game at Sheffield when half-time was called, and no alteration took place until nearly the close of the game, when two goals were scored quickly by Birmingham, who won by three to one. - -

The following ties in the first round of the National Co competition were played on Saturday :—Blackburn Park- I road v. Low Moore: At Blackburn. In the first half Low Moor scored two goals to none, but Park-road In the second had much the best of the game, and scored three to one, an exciting game resulting in a tie—three goals each.—Chirit v. Davenham : At Chirk. Chirk non by fory goals to two. —West Bromwich Albion v. Derby Junction : At Derby. West Bromwich won easily by seven goals to none. The following ths in the sccond round of the Lancashire A,sociation Challenge Cup competitun were played on Saturday :—Blackburu Rovers v. Preston Zingari : At Pres- ton. The Rovers won by two goals to one.—Church is. Tarton :At Church. A well•contested game ended in a draw—two goals each.—Witton v. Earlestown : At Black- burn. The home team won easily by six goals to one.— ' Oswaldtwistle Rovers is. Bolton Association : At Oswald- twistle. The Rovers scored ten goals to 1301t3n one —Peel Bank Rovers is. Great Lever Rangers: On the ground of the former. The Rangers won by four goals to three. The defeat of the Queen's Park team (the present holders of the Scottish Association Challenge Cup) by Battlefield in the second round of the competition on Saturday was the sensational event of the day in Scotland. The tie was played on the Queen's Park ground, and was won by Bat- tlefield by three goals to two.—Glasgow Rangers is. 3rd Lanark: At Catbkin Park. These clubs, which played two drawn games in the first round, were both allowed to com- pete in the second round, and were again drawn together. The match on Saturday resulted in the victory of the Ran- gers by three goals to none.—Dumbarton is. l'ollockehields Athletic: The tie between these clubs was another surprise, the former losing by four goals to one.

div.head: PRESCOT-
div.p: PRESCOT-

VOLUNTEER PRIZE DISTRIBUTION.—OD 'Tuesday, the annual distribution of the money prizes, shot for by the R. Company of the 21st L.R.V., on the 20th September, took place in the Assembly Room , Prescot, under the presidency of Captain Gamble. Mrs. J. C. Gamble kindly distributed the prizes, which included a silver challenge cup, the gift of Mr. Henry Cross (this year won by Sergeant J. Jackson for the first time), and a handsome copper kettle (won bv Private A. Dennett). There was a large number of people present. Major W. W. Pilkington congratulated the men on the strength and efficiency of the corps, and suggested the formation of an Engineer Volunteer company in Prescot. BOARD OF GUARDIANS MEETING. The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guardians was neld on Thursday in the Board-room at the Whiston Workhouse. Mr. Meadows presided, and there were also present the Revs. T. Chambers, T. Finegan, and J. Barnacle; Messrs. Newsome, Fidler, Birchall, Leatherbarrow, Ashton, Mat- thews, Griffiths, Kenwright, Hulme, Jackson, Buckley. Dobell, Leigh, Lowe, Eatock, Swift, Gerrard, Tyrer, and S. Marsh.—The Late Loal Government Board Inquiry: A letter was read from the Local Government Board, dated 20th October, with reference to the late inquiry held at the Workhouse by Mr. Davy, into charges against Officers of the Prescot Union by a person signing himself " William Law." The Board had considered the report of their in- spector and the minutes of the evidence given at the in- quiry, and were of opinion that there was no foundation for the charges as affecting the Guardians, Mr. Hartley, their clerk, or Dr. Hall, medical officer. The Board added their regret that the charges should have been made, and that the Guardians and their officers should have been put to so much trouble to meet them —Mr. Dobell thought it a most unsatisfactory letter, inasmuch as there was no mention of prosecuting the man (who signed himself "William Law.") the author of the charges.—Mr. Fidler: That is jest what I was going to say.—Mr. Dobell : I should like to know whether they will take any action in the matter.—Mr. Tyrer ; I beg to move that the clerk write to the Local Government Board and ask them what further action they are going to take.—The Rev. T. Chambers: I second it. I think it is a most unsatisfactory letter, and I think the public will think so too.—The motion was carried.—The Clerk (Mr. Hartley) read a letter from the Registrar- General, relative to the appointment of a registrar of births and deaths of the St. Helens sub-district, and vac- cinnation officer of the same district: such offices being vacant by the death of Mr. Robert Kirkman. There were two applications, viz ,from Mr. James Kirkman, son of the deceased registrar, who had acted as his deputy for about six years; and Mr. Peter Ckorley, of Prescot, who has been tar 22 years connected with tile Union, 15 years of which he has acted as registrar of the Prescot sub-dis- trict. —Mr. Fidler said he had very great pleasure in pro- posing Mr. Chorley. If there were rewards for long ser- vice and for faithful servants he thought it was the duty of the Guardians to make some recognition, and he with con- fidence proposed Mr. Chorlev.—Mr. Tyrer seconded the nomination.—Mr. Silvester Marsh proposed, and Mr. Jack. son seconded, the appointment of Mr. Kirkman.—On a vote being taken 24 Guardians voted for Mr. Charley; Mr. Jack- son voted for Mr. Kirkman, and Mr. Marsh said be voted for" nobody."—The appointment is subject to the sanction of the Local Government Board.—Resignatioa of a Guar- dian: Another letter from the Local Government B card stated that Mr. Willoughby Gilbody, guardian for Ditton, had tendered his resignation, and the Board had accepted it- -The Rev. T. Finegan Galled attention to the Whines v) 'applications for the relief of able-bodied men at 'duns who could not obtain employment, and asked the G eardians to give their officer greater powers in administering relief:— The Rev. T. Chambers said he was under the impression that a rel ieving officer possessed power to relieve men in destitution. He had power to give temporary relief to men, • , women, or children who were destitute.—The Clerk said not able-bodied men. If able-bodied men were relieved they must be employed and perform a task of work. It was a very important matter, and might well be referred to a small committee, who should be autivirised to deal with the cases as they cropped up. He did not think the Guar- dians were prepared that day to adopt a special scale of relief; and the relieving officer must not relieve any able- bodied person without exacting a task, else he would dis- obey the orders of the Local Government Board and be liable to a surcharge.—The Guardians eventually decided to appoint a small committee, consisting of the Revs. T. Chambers and T. Finegan, Messrs. Matthews, Leatherbarrow, Birchall, Gerard, and Jackson, to deal with the question.

TUE CLAIMANT BEFORE THE Puumc.—Tbe Tichborne Claimant made his first appearance in public, since his release from prison, in the St. James's Hall, Piccadilly, London, on Wednesday evening, when be addressed a large and enthusiastic meeting of his supporters. The Claimant (who was accompanied on the platform by his eldest son) in the course of his speech, after alluding to the death of so many of his old friends, went on to complain of the tone of the press towards him, and said the public must have been convinced long ago that he could not have carried on such a gigantic trial unless he had a good cause, because he was penniless. He admitted that he was wild in his youth. He knew Arthur Orton, who was also wild, but then they were in a wild country. But now, having suffered as he had, be was resolved to lead a different life. After imprisonment for ten years and a half he Came Out of prison a better man than he entered it. Ile would not continue the struggle for himself, but for his children, with whom he intended to spend the remainder of his days. He felt bound to continue the tight to the end. THE CENTENARY OF SIR MOSES MONTrFIORE.—A special service was held at the Synagogue at Rainsgate, on Mon- day, on the occasion of the one hundredth anniversary of the birth of Sir Moses Montefiore, which by Jewish calendar occurred on that day. The building was crowded, the Rev. Samuel Myers, the regular minister, officiating, and Dr. Hermann Adler, delegate chief rabbi, attended and read a special prayer. In the afternoon Dr. Adler proceeded to East Cliff Lodge, the residence of Sir Moses, and again read prayers in the presence of :it. Moses and his family. At its conclusion the venerable baronet said, in a very strong voice :—" I cannot tell the thousandth nor the ten thousandth part of what I feel to-day, when, by the bless- ing of the Almighty, I have arrived at so fall an age. I thank Him for His merciful providence, and I thank all my friends fo- their great kindness." Addressing Dr. Adler. he said—" You have the happiness of seeing my excellent friend, your father, the Rev. Chief Rabbi, alive. Follow in his footsteps, and may God bless you all." Sir Moses, who enjoyed excellent spirits, received over 800 letters and 600 telegrams of congratulation in all languages and from many lands.

THE FAR WEST. I recently (says a correspondent) wrote for a young Scotch friend of mine to find out the truth about the great North-West. The reply I received from my Canadian friend is so full for the purpose and so fairly stated that I thought you would like to publish it for the benefit of such of your readers as may be thinking of emigrating. It is as follows :—( I aken from a letter from Mr. John Fraser, of Brandon, in Manitoba, dated Sept. sth, 1884 )—"I came to Canada North-West Territories in Feb., 1882, lrom Edinburgh, with 2,000 dollars, and took up 320 acres of black loam land, 2 feet deep, with clay bottom, from the Syndicate. This farm is now worth 4,500 dole. I have 40 aores under wheat crop. yielding 20 to 30 bushels per acre; 20 under oats, and 20 unaer barley ; all my veget- ables are doing well. I have plenty of hay, and cattle come out fat with nothing but prairie hay in spring. Horses and ' cattle do well in winter. As to climate, I would just say that I have been very comfortable ; it is very healthy; no bet- ter climate in the world ; the weather is very pleasant. Pro- visions have been very reasonable during the last year. People should come out here in the spring. I have travel- led through India and Turkey, and seen a great deal of Africa and other portions of the world, and I most say I never saw in any of my travels a country more adapted for , farming purposes to the European races than the Canadian North-West. lam perfectly contented, and have good pro- 1 spects ahead."—Scotsman.

THE Parliamentary Papers relating to Egypt which have been issued since the opening' of the present session show that the Govern- ment have not, as certain members of the Opposition are prone to assert, been idly "waiting upon Providence," but that they have been active and vigilant in their en- deavours to open up communication with GENERAL GORDON. An important Paper published on Tuesday last includes the in- structions given to Lord WOLSELEY before going out to Egypt, as well as interesting letters from GENERAL GORDON up to July 31st. The instructions will be read with. satisfaction by all who are not touohed with Jingoism, showing, as they do, that Her Majesty's Government have not deviated a- hair's breadth from their original lines of policy. They have from the first made it known that the Soudan was to be abandoned; • GENERAL GORDON was sent out on the dis- tinct understanding that he would aid in this work; and Lord WOLSELEY goes up the Nile equally on the understanding that the Soudanese must, when the present expedition is at art end, be left to themselves. His lordship is informed that "the primary object of the expedition up the valley of the Nile is to bring away GENERAL GORDON and ; COLONEL STEWART from Khartoum. When I that object has been secured no further of- fensive operations of any k:nd are to be un- dertaken.' And further—" You are aware that the policy of Her Majesty's Government is that Egyptian Government in the Soudan should cease." When GENERAL GORDON started on his mission he was under similar ' instructions, for whilst on his way he wrote— "The Soudan is a useless possession, ever , was so, and ever will be so. . • . I think Her Majesty's Government are fully justified in recommending the evacuation, in- asmuch as the sacrifices necessary towards securing a good government would be far too onerous to admit of such an attempt being made." This frank and emphatic expression of opinion seems to have been lost .sight of by those who have been clamouring for an expedition to Khartoum with the object not only of relieving GENERAL GORDON but of retaining the place as a basis of future opera- tions. Politicians of this class are not as a rule blessed with good memories, and their geographical knowledge is of the smallest kind. They usually refer to the Soudan as though it was no bigger than a German State, whereas it embraces a tract of terri:ory as large as the whole of Germany, France, and Spain combined. As Lord SALISBURY once said as to another matter, they should treat themselves to and study large maps; and it is due to the leader of the Tory party in the House of Lords to point out that, with all his jeering at the Government for their action, or want of action, in Egyptian affairs, he has never gone the length of urg- ing that they should endeavour to retain the Soudan: According to the instructions given to Lord WOLESLEY, the boundary line, for the future, between the Soudan and Egypt proper, is to be drawn at Wady Haifa. It • will be desirable, of course, to preserve com- munications with Khartoum, and with that object Lord WOLSELEY is instructed to make what arrangements he can with native chiefs who, if it need be, are to be subsidised by the Egyptian Government, on condition that they will preserve the peace with Egypt, encour- age ordinary trade, and discourage the slave trade. But as to managing the affairs of the country, the chiefs are to be left to them- selves; they are practically to be granted local self-government of the most extensive kind, and, as their complaint is that the Egyptian Government have in the past ruled

LACROSSE.—SEAFORTH W. WIDNES —This match was played at Crosby Cricket Ground, on Saturday. The face Was effected at half-past three o'clock. Although the Sea- forth had the best of the game, they only got the ball past the Widnes goalkeeper once, C. E. Ashworth getting the point. About half-time the contest was more evenly balanced, and Seaforth wen by one goal to nil. THE WALTON CHURCH OtsPuTE.—The dispute which has so long existed at Walton between Sir Gilbert Greened!, the patron of the living, and the incumbent, the Rev. Arthur 'Jones, will now be settled by the acceptance by Mr. Jones 'Of the living at Winlaton, Durham. The settlement of this dispute will no doubt lead to the completion and opening of the handsome church which Sir Gilbert has erected at Walton, but which has hitherto been closed to the Mourn- 'bent and his flock owing to a difference of opinion between the patron and the pastor as to the kind of exhortations which ought to be addreesed from the pulpit 'NEW BRINE AND SSALT COMPANY.—We would direct the attention of our readers to a prospectus, in another column, of the Weaver Hall Brine and Salt Corapany, Limited. It will be seen that the sew company is likely to prove attractive to investors, the advantages secured being of an exceptional character. The capital of £lOOO6O is to be raised in 20,000 shares of ES each. The land available for working is about a mile and a half in length in the Weaver Valley, and in addition to the brine it is believed that it contains extensive beds of rock salt. It will be noted that there is a solid, business-like air about the pros. pectus which, without drawing a fancy picture, makes it apparent that there is every reason to expect that a sub- stantial profit may be realised with a comparatively email outlay. The reports which accompany the prospectus are of a highly eatisfactery kind. , 1 ACCIDENT TO Mn. BRINSLEY SHERIDAN.— At the C., 080 of a successful six night-t engagement at the Theatre Royal, Accrington, on Saturday evening, Mr. Brinsley Sheridan and Miss Nellie Wright met with a serious accident. ltappears that the popular comedian was making his •final it as "Soft Tommy Shuttleworth " in the last act ef ".Grelley's Money," when he gave his bsual greeting to the audience, " Wheer are we workin' now!" A portion of the stage at the prompter's aide was taken up to allow the egress of a large portion of the audience, and Mr. Sheridan in re- tiring from the stage was kprecipitated a distance of 'l6 feet into" darkness that might be felt." Sr/nen picked up he was bleeding and insensible, but happily medical aid Was at hand, and he soon regained consciousness. Fortunately Mr. Sheridan escaped without any permanent injury. Miss Wright, who was with Mr. Sheridan at the time, was very seriously bruised. • CIIIIRCLI MISSIONARY SOCIETY AT RUNCORN.—The an- nual meeting of the Church Missionary Society was held in the Trinity Schoolroom, Runcorn, on Monday evening. There was a poor attendance,aml Mr. J. N. Lelbs oecupietl•the I'chair. The Rev. W. Preston '(hon. sec.) read the annual .report, and 4n doing so referred with regret to the abeence Of the Rev. Canon Barclay, who had been president of .the (£ociety ever eince he came to Runcorn. He regretted to I say that his constitution was not such as to enable him to take the active part in the various enterprises of the town as formerly, and they could only pray and hope that he might long be spared, if not to the town, to those who knew biat, and to those who loved him. (Applause). He and the Rev. Canon Barclay had pulled well together during the whole of the time he had been 4n Runcorn. There had been no antagonism between them. They had each had their views, and they had respected each others principles. Eaeh had gone his Own way, and they had never emus to loggerheads, but pulled together for the cause of Christ and the Church, and in various connections for the welfare, happiness and social good of Runcorn. (Applause). The hon. see, then read the following statement of receipts : c ollections : At Parish Church, after sermons by the Rev. J. Aleook, £8 13s. This was a considerable increase on last year. The Chairman and the Rev. J. div.head: EXAMINER, SA TURDXY, NOVEMBER 1, 1884:
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SA TURDXY, NOVEMBER 1, 1884:

them in order to rob them, there is some hope of their hailing the opportunity of thus becoming their own masters. It may and will be said that this is leaving the Soudan to anarchy ; but to what else has the country been subject since the attempt to govern it as an Egyptian possession ? It cannot fall back so far as government is concerned, for gov- ernment, strictly speaking, there has been none. The tribesmen may quarrel among themselves but they have always done that, and they will at least be relieved of the neces- sity of fighting the Egyptians who, it is com- puted, have lost no less than roo,ooo men in the vain attempt to subjugate the semi- savages of the Soudan. Egypt is almost bankrupt, and cannot find the means to continue to wage war with these people; and Englishmen, we are persuaded, what- ever Government is in power, will never con- sent to wasting millions of money and thousands of lives in such a " mad under- taking." Turning to the communications from General GORDON one is puzzled to know what he really means to do. Many things have happened,since he was besieged, which seem to point to the conclusion that he would not leave Khartoum if he could—that is, not until it is in the hands of someone who can hold it with a view to its being kept under Egyptian and therefore British control. He appears to have changed his mind since ex- pressing himself so strongly in favour of evacuation, for it is not to be forgotten that he has declared that it was one of his objects to " smash up the MARDI." In a letter dated July 3oth, he says :—" I shall not leave Khartoum till I can put someone in ;" and next day he adds :—" It is a sine qua non that you send me ZEBEHR, otherwise my stay here is indefinite." This is not the language of a man who is, as he has been represented, "at the last gasp." or who is praying day by day for a deliverer. We have for some time been of opinion that General Gop,DoN, great as his difficulties have been, could ere now have left Khartoum if he would and have brought away the garrison in safety. It is at any rate pretty clear that his stay at Khartoum is in- definite—that it does not depend solely on what may be called his "rescue." He has ideas of his own as to the nature of his mis- sion, and if he is to have his own way he will not be likely to stir until they are carried out. It will be a moment alike interesting and critical when Lord WOLSRLEY gets in direct communication with the "hero of Khar- toum," for there can be no doubt as to' General GORDON'S heroism, whatever doubt there may be, at times, as to his judgment. Will he allow himself to be relieved, or will Lord WOLiELEY have to "relieve" him in another sense of the word ? This is a matter of much uncertainty, but we sincerely trust that General GoaDoN will prove tractable. Once in communication with Lord WOLSE- LEY, it should be a comparatively qasy task to evacuate Khartoum, bringing away all who may be willing to leave. General GORDON has, unaided, done wonders in this direction.
In One letter' he says "We have sent down
over 600 soldiers and z,OOO people "—a brief but pregnant statement which is in itself an . .
answer to those who venture to urge that his mission has been an utter failure. It may be
that he has aimed at too high, or that he has found the difficulties of his task greater than

he expected. He has been confident for some time back that 'with a few English re- giments at his back he'could clear the country of rebels, and dictate terms at Khartoum. But this would be entering upon a war with the natives, which would ill accord with the state- _
ment that his mission was to be a mission of
peace. We are glad to know that her MAJESTY'S Government have not at any time countenanced hostilities. Lord WOLSELEY is even now instructed to limit the sphere of
his military operations as much as Possible Bring back General GORDON he must at all cost and at all hazards; but we trust he will be able to do so without entering into a pro- _ .
longed conflict with the people of- the Soudan.

The POSTMASTER-GENERAL has again been under the necessity of dealing with the cal- umny as to an "order to foreign firms" for the manufacture of post-cards which Conser- vatives have been so active in circulating. It
will be remembered that he nailed the co- un- terfeit down a few- months _ago, in reply to a

communication from Dr. GORNAL.L, Of.War- rington ; but there has since been a plenti- ful supply of bad coin from the same mint, and we regret to see that Sir RICKARD CROSS has been engaged in passing it. Speaking at Chester, he intimated that the Govern-

Meat had given an order to a foreign arm, even in the matter of post-cards, instead of employing British industry at shome. His little story was told since Mr. Fawcerr's letter of contradiction was made public, and if we were to follow the bad ex- ample of the ex-Homs SECRETARY we should designate his statement as " a wilful and de- liberate lie." But we do no such thing; we simply •say he has. shown himself grossly careless, Or grossly ignorant, or both. See- ing thatrthe repeated misstatement was doing much mischief, Mr. GEORGE SHIPION, retary of the London Trades Council, wrote the POSTMASTER-GENERA; On the subject, and has received a reply which will make Sir IttEcniim:Gnoss and. others of that ilk wince; if they are "made of penetrable stuff." Mr. Taw= 'explains. as he has done before, that the •Post Office is supplied with cards' from the Inland Revenue Department, and that thexards are obtained by that Depart- ment under contract with "an eminent firmof -private stationem in London." The bulk of the material, it has been ascertained, does come from Germany, but it iá obtained by purchase by the • contractors—a matter, over which the Government has no control, nor can they have, unless they were to go the absurd length of stipulating, as Mr. FAIN- cETT puts it, "that, where English products I are available, no portion of the material they supply should be of foreign growth or manu- facture." To mention such a thing is, as it seems to us. to rencl-N- it ridiculous. Once started on such a wild-goose chase of Protec- tion, where should we have to stop? We should have to insist, as the POSTMASTER- GENERAL points out, that "if the Govern- ment invited tenders for clothing, or biscuits for the army, no foreign wool or foreign corn should be used in making the clothes or the biscuits." Foreign countries would, as a matter of course, retaliate ; and England, the workshop of the world, would find that the game of boycott she had commenced would terminate in commercial suicide. But to the Tory slanderers the sting of Mr. FAWCETT'S letter lies in the tail, and is put forth with some effect when he states that the very firm that makes these purchases of post-card material from Germany is engaged in making foreign stamps to such an extent that "the amount which is paid away to English work- men engaged in making these stamps, and executing other orders which they receive

from foreign and Colonial Governments far exceeds the amount of their purchases from foreign countries." What, after this revela- tion? Shall we commence the process of cutting off the nose in order to spite the face? Let Sir RICHARD CROSS and Co., answer, if
they can ; and, for the future refrain from telling " the old, old, story," or it may, after all, come to be characterised as "a wilful and deliberate lie."

THE majority of our readers will hear with satisfaction of the withdrawal of the demand for a poll of the burgesses on the question of levying a rate of Twopence in the pound in aid of the promotion of the Manchester Ship Canal scheme. There could be no question in the minds of those who were present at the Town's Meeting on Thursday night week that the bulk of the ratepayers of Warrington are in favour of contributing by means of a rate. We do not say that there were no dissentients present, or that the small proportion who made them- selves conspicuous were not backed by others who did not care to hold up their hands against the motion ; but we do say that the meeting—taking it as a whole—was fairly representative of the burgesses, and that its opinion was expressed in no equivocal man- ner. Had there been reasonable ground for doubting what would be the issue of the poll, Mr. THOMAS MORRIS, who made the demand for one, would doubtless have felt justified in persevering with his opposition to the rate. As it is, having made his protest against what he regards as the imprudence of tax- ing the public for the support of what, from a commercial point of view, is a private undertakin, he, has acted wisely in giving way rather than put the town to serious expense with the view of ascertaining what, it must be admitted, was a foregone conclu- sion. But a poll was objectionable, not only on the score of the cost, but because of the bad feeling which it was likely to en- gender. Abeady there have been some hard things said, and the war of' words was ' waxing fast and furious. It will be some ! satisfaction to those who have depreca- ted the course Mr. MORRIS has pursued to' know that, if he had not taken action, the ! demand for a poll would have been made, and made too, we have reason to believe, by those who would have insisted on going forward with it. When the matter is looked at from this point of view, Mr. MORRIS may be said to have rendered a service. But we are not vet out of the wood ; it is for the Town Council now to say what shall be done as to the proposed rate. It may be that they will be confronted with the legal obstacle which previously blocked the way; or has it been removed in setting about a new scheme? The Cor- porations of Salford and of Manchester seem to have no hesitation in the matter, for they have this week met the wishes of the inhabitants of these boroughs by deciding on a levy of Twopence in the pound. It is now for the Corporation of Warrington to say what it will do.
