TRH FRODSHAM WATER SCHEME. Mr. Bancroft, the engineer for this scheme of water supply, has reported to the Frodsham Parochial Committee that on the 17th ult., the trial wells at Five Crosses yielded 18,618 gallons in 24 hours. The dry season had undoubtedly affected the quantity of underground water in the district, and they might accept this as the minimum and not the average yield of the well. He estimated the amouut of work yet to be done to complete the wells and heading, including the pipes and bricklaying of each*well, at £1,214 us 6d; this, together with the value of the work already done by Mr. Timmins, gave £1.597 19s 11 as the total cost. As the quantity of water now produced by the wells and heading indicate I that sufficient could he found on the land proposed to be pur- chased from the trustees of the late Major Hitchen, he con- sidered the work should be looked upon as permanent,and as representing tbe value of the water rights. The reparian owner claimed (exclusive of the right which three persons claimed to have water delivered to therm gratuitously iniper- petuity) £2,607 5s 6d, so that there was a considerable saving by this echeme over the others suggested. The Parochial Committee have approved and adopted Mr. Ban- croft's report, and application has been made to the Local Government Board for further powers to complete the well.

The school is a substantially built structure, two storeys in height, and is in the 18th century gothic style of architectire. div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Mr. John Ashton presided, and there wem present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner and Rev. J. Lockwood. Messrs. Highfield, Aaron, Derbyshire, Hamilton, Weir, Jackson, Campkin, Lewis, H. •Linaker (clerk), W. H. Lineker (deputy clerk), and Farrington (nuisance in- spector). THE POLLUTIoN OP OLD QUAY CANAL—The Deputy Clerk read a letter dated the 18th October from the Local tiovernm• nt Board with reference to the pollution of the Old Quay Canal, and inquiring with what object it was de- sired that the Board should cause a local inquiry to be held with regart to the alleged pollution of the stream. Therms. tion wan also asked when the Rural Sanitary Authority pro- posed to take action under the Rivers Pollution Prevention Act, 1870—The Deputy Clerk said the reason or asking for an inquiry was that the subject wan of such wide importance. It was a matter that the Authority could not Attempt to touch until there had been a proper invelligetiell by the Loci' Government Board.—Mr. Derbyshire He wrote More to ask them to take the matter into consideration.—The Deputy Clerk To assist at getting at the real facts. They don't like the responsibility.—Eventually it was decided that the clerk should reply that the subject was of such wide importance that the Authority did not feel justified in taking action until the matter bad been thoroughly investi- gated by the Board. SPECIAL EXPENSES.—An estimate of special expenses was submitted, which showed that for the township of Frodsham a call of £lOO would be required; Frodsham Lordship, £4O; and Appleton, £6O. BAD WATER AND FEVER OUTBREAKS.—The Medical Offi- cer presented a special report, which stated that an outbreak of scarlet fever had occurred at a redttage at Rock Savage Clifton. Seven children, the entire family of the occupier, had been attacked, but were now convalescent. He was of opinion that the disease had been originally contracted by infection from some inefficiently disiufected convalescent who had been attending Weston schools. At the same vil- lage a man had been attacked with tynboid fever and removed to the Workhouse Hospital. The man hate drunk of the suspected water referred to in a previous report, arid the medical officer regretted that up to the present no measures had been taken for the provision of an improved water supply, nor yet for the prevention of the fouling of the suspected water, which the inhabitants were still using. He trusted the Authority would assist him in carrying out some prompt measures for the improvement of the water supply, as he was told that water was actually being carted 'from Runcorn to Clifton. A case e.. typhoid fever had also broken out at Reek Savage Farm, and the origin of the dis- ease was very difficrett, to trace. 'The sanitary arrangement was rather defective.—lnspecter Farrington reported that he had taken a sample of the water for analysis. THE SEWERAGE t3F WESTON:IMPORTANT Ce.mat.—The Deputy-Clerk said, in company with Mr. Aaron, he had been to see the course of the sewer which drained Mr. Clarke's and other cottages at Weston Point. He ascer- tained that some three years ego the Brine Company ap- plied for the field through which the sewer Ten at WestOlti Point frem the Bridgewater Company. Mr.,Collier had ar- ranged with Mr. Farrington e'er the sewage to flow into the canal, but since the Authority had applied to the Local Government Board for a toed inquiry into the pollution of the Old Quay Canal, Mr. Collier had given the Authority notice to disconnect the sewer. He (Mr. Liaaker) was per- fectly satisfied that the sewer was vested eel under the con- trol of the Authority. It was a very important matter to the township of Weston that the tights of -sewerage should be maintained, for if they once allowed it to be taken away they would have no means of gettleg into the river„, and it would be a very expensive matter indeed to Cad a, proper oCtfall and drainage. When he -returned from his visit, he wrote the following letter to Mr. Collier:—" have been consulted by the Anthorityas to whether the sewer running-across a field at Weston Point, from certain cot-i- -tages belonging to Mr. Clarke and others to the Fellrbrook, , is vested in the Authority or not. On the facts submitted, to me, I have advised that the sewer ir question is vested, and under the control e the Authority. I understand that t' the Mersey Salt and Brine Company, Limited, have teased the fieitl in question frown your company, and contemplate beilding upon the site Of the sewer. have, therefore, on, behalf of the local Authority, to give you notice that they. object to any interference by any works that may be , injariont to such -sewer being erected or ca.ried on by any person or company. If the proposed work, Of theTrine Co. woelld,interfere with the line of sewer I would sugrest that representatives on behalf of the two compares should have-an interview with me on the reetteri",l —Mr.Collier, general manager to the Navigation Co. re- plied as follows :—" t Cave made further inquiry into, the question of the sewer at Weston Point, and cannet agree, with your clients views as to their rights of sewage across the land this compaorhas leased to the Mersey Salt and Brine Co. You will be aware that the right (if any) to pass, land or surface drainage to the Folly Brook, would net en- titlothe Authority to send house sewage-by the same course, and as the outlet of the Folly Brook is to the Weston canal, a further objection is thus raised. I think that this,yues- tion should be cleared befere we meet or discuss the leans of disposing of the Weston Point aewaee.. Perhaps there- fore, yen will inform me en what armada the claim and ob- jections you make are established. When these are with- drawn we may be in a position to deal satisfactorily with the question of both present and future requirements:"— The deputy Clerk added that the sewer acts cut by Major Orred art the time be built the cottages, and Mr. William Bankes subscribed £lO towards the cast, the sewer woe then placed under the control of the Authority and an -enor- mous fexpense would be caused to Weston,if they gave up the right to that sewer. It was only 30 garde from the oa- ten into Folly Brook to The main sewer of the Rencorn Commissioners, and an arrangement could be made with the Commissioners to turn the-sewage into their outran into the' river.e-Mr. Aaron strongly advised that the rights of the Authority should be maintains!. If they had to pat a new, sewer dewn it would cent Weston £l,OOO.—Eventually a deputation consisting of the Rev. J. Lockwocd, Mr. Aaron, and the deputy Clerk wee appointed to interview sr.: ' Collier on the matter, on the motion of MT. Aaron, ee- conded by Mr. Derbyshire. THE SKIP CANAL—The Chairman informed the Authority that a deputation had had an interview with the committee of the Manchester Ship Canal scheme, and there was no doubt they would get clauses inserted in the Bill to protect their intseaste without, the expense of opposing the Bill in rerliament.—The Deputy Clerk said the drainage of the property at Woods-row, Halton. had often been dis- tossed. If they postponed the work until the Ship Canal was made it would cost a great deal more money. He thought they might to communicate to the Ship Canal pro- moters that the Authority contemplated putting this sewer under the present canal into the Mersey. but that if they would undertake to pay the difference in cost between doing the work under the canal at its present depth and putticg it under the new canal they would try to defer the work.—The Clerk said there was no doubt that if the sewer had to be made under the Ship Canal it would cost five time as mneis as it would under present circumstences.—Coneideration of the matter was deferred.—The expenses of the deputation to Manchester (ti 18s) were ordered to be paid. A ICP,NV MEMBER.—On the motion of Mr. Ashton, seconded by Mr. Weir. Mr. Lewis was elected a member of Frodshatn Parochial Committee in place of Mr. John Chat- loner resigned. There was no other business of public interest.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON, THURSDAY.
If the debate on the Address finish to-morrow night, lea'-

log Monday free for the moving of the second reading of the Franchise Bill, the most sanguine hopes of all concerned for the progress of public business will be fulfilled. The ten days which will then have elapsed since the opening of Parliament have been worse than wasted. The House of Lords, with a rare access of common sense, adjourned the very night they met, and do not re-assemble till Monday. If , the House of Commons had taken the same course no one would be one penny the worse, whilst thereputation of the House would have been spared some heavy blows. On the part of the responsible leaders of the Opposition, there bee not been even an attempt to raise serious debate on the I Address. The two topics they are disposed to treat are Egypt and the Franchise Bill. But substquent st,,ges of the I progress of the session find full and legitimate opportunities for dealing with these matters. Everything that anyone I wants to say on the Franchise Bill can be delivered on the i second reading and at subs qaent stages, whilst Egypt can I be talked about at pleasure when the vote of credit comes on. Sir Stafford Northeote, therefore, and gentlemen on the Front Bench have stood aside waiting till the Irish members and Lord' R. Churchill have had their say. On Wednesday the question of the Transvaal was rtised. But it was an effort, scarcely disguised, on the part of half a dozen well-meaning gentlemen to deliver speeches they had prepared for a debate fixed for a Tuesday night in July, when the House was counted out. No ammdment was submitted, and the spzeches being reeled off, the subject dropped,

What has happened has been that . the Irish members have dragged the House of Commons down to the level of a squabbling vestry, and have poured oat their spite on the I heads of Earl Spencer and Mr. Trevelyan, whose crime is that they have by wise legislation and :inn administration so far undermined the influence of th 3 Land Leaguers that Ireland is at the present time more orderly than it has been for ten years. The particular ground of attack chosen was I the conviction of the Maamstraena murderers. But the Irish members evidently cared little for the murdered Joyce, whose ghost Mr. Healy said would haunt M. Trevelyaa's pillow, or for the others alleged to be unjustly incarcerated.' What they wanted was an opportunity for "going for" Earl I Spencer and Mr. Trevelyan, whose'recznt elevation and the ovation he received on Friday night in the 'House of Corn- msms, have lashed them into a condition of fury The scenes that took place and the language .n5O we written in the I Wlyspapert, and do not faini I ;:l.:ASant p.rf to dwell upon. Mr. Glettone presuming to join in the discussion which had been largely appropriated uy Irish members was treated in a manner painful to witness. He Was howled at, interrupted and jeered at by the ill-mannered crew below the gangway till the Speaker having twice int.rfered and a third warning containing promise of serious consequences ' the hubbub slightly ceased, though now and again Mr. I Biggar, when Earl Spencer's name was mentioned, was , heard calling out "He's a murderer!" When it was known Mr. Gladsone was on his feet, the Liberals crowded in anxious to hear the case as put by hirn. The Parneliites shrewdly concluded that if this clear head and persuasive tongue were permitted, undisturbed, to deal with their patched-up case, there would not be a shred of it left. Therefore they deliberately set themselves to in- terrupt him, and with any less practised speaker would have succeeded in disconcerting him, and so preventing his argument having full play. But Mr. G ladstone, though several times stopped, never lost the thread of his argument. The consequence, largely due to this speech,was that a score of Liberals who had been hesitating, honestly doubting which way their duty led them, were convinced of the true character of the Parnellite attack, and Mr. Parnell caught only five Liberals of the class of Mr. Cowen, Mr. Labon- chere, Mr. Storey, and Mr. T. C. Thompson, who are habitu- ated to distinguish themselves by voting with the Parnellites against the Government. The approaching issue of the second and third volumes of the Report of the Commission on. city guilds recalls an earlier triumph of the Standard in the direction of obtaining early copies of important documents. When the Commie- aim had finished their labours and there was, particularly in the city, intense desir to learn their recommendations, one morning the Standard came out with what purported to be, and what indeed was, &draft of the report. This gave rise te much unpleasantness on the Commission. It was evident that the document in question had either been ab- stracted from the desk of a Commissioner or had been sup- plied by him to the newspapers. The difficulty was that tbbre being no charge brought no one could meet it with a denial, thengh I believe in indirect ways, every member of the Commission found an opportunity of declaring on his honour that he knew nothing of the matter. Only recently the mystery has been unravelled. It was Mr. Vell's trapy that reached the Standard, though Mr. Pell I was innocent of the betrayal. The fact is be had thrown , into the waste paper basket at the House of Commons his copy of the draft. It appears to be the business of some astute person to edit the waste paper basket, and here this treasure was found, and was parted with for a handsome consideration to the Standard, now the favourite market for 'disposal of this kind of contraband goods. The two additional volumes of M. Froude's History of Carlyle complete the impression conveyed to the startled pi:bile mind by earlier volumes. Everybody who had learned to reverence Carlyle as the incarnation of all that was good and lofty in human nature, was shocked at the discovery that on the contrary he was, as he himself in all access of frankness puts it, a very unthankfull, ill-con- ditioned, bilious, wayward, heart-worn [and he might have added heart-wearying] son of Astern." Mr. Froude was blamed for shattering the popular idol ; but it is seen now that if a biography were to be written at all it could only be done by frankly dealing with the materials at hand. What has shacked most people is Carlyle's treatment of his wife, "The Dear Goody to whom many of his letters in the present volumes are addressed. But everyone who came in contact with the great philosopher must have had a hard time of it. One day he bought an umbrella, which the shopman promised to send home to 'him. It did not arrive, Yebereupon this calm-souled man writes—" The scoundrel umbrella vendor! Has that accursed chimera of a Cock- ney not sent the umbrella yet ? I could see him trailed thrice through the Thames for his scoundrel conduct." Another time, when ordering his tea, he told the servant she need not hurry. She thought he must be dangerously ill. "It was such an unlikely thing for the master to say," she declared to Mrs. Carlyle, "that it quite made my flesh creep." . . .

London society, more particularly the political section of it, has this week received a great shock. Here and there drawing-rooms are beginning to be opened for the autumn session. Lady Granville's was opened on the eve of the ses- sion, Lady Borthwick, one of the most ambitious and de- termined of recent leaders of fashion, has opened her famous white drawing-room, where at least one crowded and successful reception has been held. It was here that the in- cident alluded to took place. Towards eleven o'clock, when the crowd was at its fullest and the joyance at its highest, there entered the room an old gentleman with springy walk though with bowed shoulders. His hair was worn in a curl that fell over his forehead. His face was wrinkled and through an eyeglass awkwardly held between linger and thumb he curiously rgarded the crowd. He was so strikingly like Lord Beaconsfield that there flashed upon some minds the awesome thought that the late Premier, hearing of the fearful muddle Lord Salisbury is making of party prospects, had temporarily come back to see what be could do to put them straight. Butit was only Sir John McDonald, the Canadian Premier. Nature has cast him very much in tbe mould of Mr. Disraeli in his later days, and with great skill Sir John assists nature as far as a close imitation of Mr. Disraeli's dress, his manner of walking, and even his mode of speech are concerned. In other respects of a moral character (of course I mean in relation to public affairs) Sir John's enemies say that he also resembles our late Premier. But it should be said to the credit of Mr„ Disraeli that through a long life, where he had plenty of opportunities of enriching himself had he desired it, no such scandal as that of the Northern Pacific Railway is connected with his name, as it will for ever cling to that of his Canadian prototype. In some other details Sir John has come under tile censure of moralists in Canada. But be is an exceedingly able man and seems indispensible to the Dominion. Some years ago, after the Pacific scandals alluded to, he was hustled from power, and seemed to be permanently cast into obscurity. But. just as Mr. Disraeli had been in 1874, he was suddenly and unexpectedly returned to power on the crest oe a great popular wave, and has not yet suffered the relapse which in 1880 awaited Mr. Disraeli. Sir John is now, I should fancy from looking at him, about Lord Beaconsfield's age when he died, but cheerily says be is good enougli for another year or two's work. The Lyceum Theatre is now closed and the company

bard at work at rehearsals. Nobody knows very well why last week's programme has been altered. Certainly the old attrac, tions continued. The theatre was full every night—it seemed strange to abandon certain success for what might be only problematic. I believe the explanation is this, that Mary Anderson has only secured a certain term of the Lyceum, and if her Juliet is to be the great thing that it is expected' to be she may as well secure a fairly long run for it. It is of immense impottance to her that the London verdict Should be as well founded as it is favourable. The success upon which she lays most store is what may be reserved for her when she returns to New York. In the meantime, so soon as her tenure of the Lyceum ends, she will be succeeded by Modjeska., There is something very singular in the exchange. Modjeska came out here first at the Court Theatre, where she made a great hit, but a great hit on a small stage. In some pieces she succeeded, but she had her failure;, and pernaps it was unfortunate she should have pitted herself against Bernhardt, Whose strung points were exactly those in which the beautiful Pole was weakest. We were getting a little tired of Modjeska. She had been over-praised, friends and compatriots bad gushed overmuch, the reaction had set in. Then she went to the Statee, and her success was phe. nomenal. The ball rolled well at the outset, and rolled faster as it went along, and now she comes to us, or at least will do so in the spring, with a great reputation. It is ex- actly the counterpart of Mary Anderson, whose success here, though very gratifylnZ remains a puzzle to the Yankees. Another old American favourite comes to us next month. The Avenue Theatre, which has been closed for a long time, opens with a comedy by Mr. Burnand ; and Mr_ Farren, disengaged, I suppose, now for the first time for many years, is amongst the company, which also includes Mrs. Alfred Mellon (a time-honoured name), Mrs. Maddick, and Miss Sothern.
THE "STRIKE" OF THE CHOIR OF

div.head: WARRINGTON PARISH CHURCH.
div.p: WARRINGTON PARISH CHURCH.

We understind that nearly half of the old members Of the Parish Church choir, who, as repotted in previous issues, went out on "strike," resumed duty last Sunday, but the remainder adhere to the resolution by which they pledged themselves not to take their usual places in the church until the Rector had met them fairly, and an amicable arrangement could be effected. It is probable that Iwith this nucleus the Rector will be able to form a new Ichoir, hut those in a position to judge are of opinion that it will be a long time before it con be brought to such a state of efficiency as the old one. The members who have "gone in," it is said, are members of the Musical Society, and have taken such action more out of regard for the new organist than the Rector. We under- stand th3t the late organist, Mr. Rowley, who 'seat in his resignation on failing to obtain an Increased salary, contemplates communicating with the Bishop, as he thinks, morally speaking, that be was induced to take the post under misrepresentation. Mr. Rowley, when he accepted the posi- tion, was receiving a salary of £lOO, and the Rector, it is affirmed, when Mr. Rowley came to Warrington at a salary of £5O, assured him that the proper stipend would be made sip, as he would use, his influenc to promote Mr. Rowley's professional interests. Mr Rowley remained so several years, during which he had an offer of £lOO at Burnley, and at last, as the remuneration he was led to expect could not be obtained, he sent in his resignation in June last. That I resignation, he complains, was not accepted until Septem- ber, when, bad he not secured another appointment, he I be would, in a manner, have been thrown on his beam ends. The dissatisfaction seems to have affected the whole choir, who greatly esteemed the organist, and the attitude the 'Rector assumed to him and the choir has led to very un- plessant circumstances.

At Croydon, on Wednesday, a young married woman named Eleanor Liverno was committed for trial claTed with causing the death of her infant child. It is alleged that the child died from starvation. The nomination for the vacancy in the representation of the Radnor Boroughs, caused by the resignation of Mr. Evans Williams (Liberal), took place on Wednesday. Mr. Rogers (Liberal) was the only candidate, and was declared duly elected. . _

TrIE Dvstax Scarrnars.—At Dublin, on Wednesday, the trisl of Gustavus C. Cornwall, late secretary to the Post Office, and Captain Martin Orahmore Kirwan, on an indict- mont charging them with conspiracy to procure the corr. mission of certain offences, was resumed and concluded. The prisoners were acquitted, and the Judge ordered their discharge from custody.

POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.

&Tutu:wt.—Before Aldermen Burgess mid Chandley. A WANDERER FROM MANCRESTER.—Annie Leach, a good looking young woman, who said she was a fustian cutter from Manchester, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly on the previous night, and also with having broken a window in the Boar's Head Inn, Town Hill, and causing damage amounting to 255. It was stated that on the previous night the prisener bad gone to the Boar's Head and asked for some drink. The landlord, Wm. Mar- shall, refused to let her have any because she was drunk, and ultimately bad to eject her from the house. She then deliberately broke the window. She was fined ss. and costs or seven days for the drunkenness; and ordered to pay the damage or go togaol for another month. She said she only had three halfpence in her pocket and was consequently re- moved in custody. . _ .

MONDAY—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), in the chair, Aldermen Webster and Davies, Mr. John Fairclough. DECNICENNESS.—The following charges of drunkenness were dealt with :—James Farrell (21st appearance), dis- missed on promising to sign the pledge; Kate Murphy, two charges, 10s. and costs, or 14 days; Agnes Horton, fined ss. and costs, or 7 days; Winifred Noon, fined 10s. and costs, or 14 days; James Bettie?, bound over to keep the peace and pay the costs, 155.; Ann Shee, fined Sc., including costs. A WANDEREII.—Mary Smith, an elderly woman, was charged with wandering abroa 1 without visible means of subsistence, and with sleeping in a garden on Saturday night. She said that she had walked from Manchester, on the road for Liverpool, where she had relatives, and that she had only gone into the garden to rest. She belonged, she said, to the Dragoon Guards. (Laughter.) Her hus- band was one and therefore she belonged to them. She was dismissed on promising to leave the town. A HEAVY LOAD —A carter, named Samuel Platt, was fined 20s. and coats for ill-treating a horse by overloading it on the 23rd init. The total weight of the lurry dragged by the horse, and its contents, was 6 tons 4 cwt. STONE THROWING.—Thomas Oakes (12) was ordered to receive six strokes with the birch rod for throwing stones in Orford-street on the 22nd inst. BOY THIEVES.—Three boya named James Macdonald, John Ward, and Joseph Buickhard, were charged with steal- ing five pieces of timber, value 2s. 61, The property of Robert Heaton, on the nth Oct. They were each ordered to pay the costs of the case, 16s. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE —Mr. Riley, school attendance officer,prosecuted in the following cases :—Edward Harding, file cutter, Warburton-street, fined 5s ; John Robert, forge. man, Pierpoint-street, fined 5s ; Charles Higginson, labourer, Stamford-street, fined ss; James Lomax, Pinner's- brow, fined 5s ; Henry Pownall, file-cutter, Warburton- street, fined 5s ; Maria Gosling, Winwick-street, fined 5s ; Samuel Wilkinson, forgeman, Owen-street, fined 5s ; James Emson, glassmaker, Cartwright.street, fined se; Catherine Silcock, shopkeeper, Dallam-lane. In this case the Bench were satisfied that the boy was a confirmed truant, and be- yond the control of his parents, and ordered him to have six strokes with the birch-rod. TUESDAY—Before Mr. C. Broadbent.

Itobert Owen, MOM, for being drunk at the Centrsl station, on Thursday evening, was fined sa, in- cluding Costs. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. John Fairclow2h and Alderman Chandley. Darisic AND DISORDERLY.—James Vernon was fined 5s and costs for being drunk and disorderly the previous even- ing.
THtBSDAY.—There was no business.

Famay.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) in the chair, and Mr. John White. DarNx.—Alice Redfern was fined 5e including costs for being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-streot on the previous evening.--Mary Sockett, charged with being drunk and disorderly, was dismissed on promising not to offend again. CRUELTY TO ANlMALS.—Matthevo Bate was fined 5s and costs for ill-treating a horse whilst in an unfit state, and Peter Hooker, for causing it to be worked, was fined 30e and costs.--Henry Barber was charged with working a horse in an unfit state on the 13th inst. Evidence was called showing that the animal was suffering from painful warts, and that is was totally unfit to work.—Mr. Davies, for the defence, called Mr. Hopkins, F R.O S., who said that the horse was in no pain whatever, and that the appearance of the warts, which looked very painful, was den ;ptive. The horse was unsightly, but was perfectly healthy. Messrs. Ferguson and Dixon, veterinary surgeons, gave corrobora- tive evidence.—The Bench dismissed the case. Inspector Greenwell appeared for the Society. A NITISANCE.—John Hough; Widnes, was charged with allowing a nuisance to exist on premises belonging to him in New-road, Latchford.—He was fined 5s and costs, and an order was made for the abatement of the nuisance in seven days.
DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS. TrEsDAY.—Before Messrs. It. Pierpoint, W. Long, and

W. C. Jones. CARELESS DmvEns.—Themas Frank Moore was fined 59 and costs for having been drunk whilst in charge of a horse and trap on the highway at Preston Brook on the 4th October.—Peter Collins was ordered to pay 53 6d costs for having allowed a dray to travel along the roads at Moore, on the 27th August. without anyone being in charge. ADULTERATED GINGIER.—Wm. Hewitt, a shopkeeper at Stockton Heath, was charged with that on the sth Septem- ter he sold ground ginger which was adulterated with 20 per cent of farinaceous matter.—Superintendent Leah stated that he had purchased a quarter of a pound of ginger from the defendant, which he sent to be analysed, with the result that it was found to be adulterated as stated above. The defendant stated that he had sold the ginger in just the same state ache had bought it.—The Chairman said that that was the first case of the kind they had had before them, and therefore they would only order defendant to pay the costs. If anyone else came before the court on a similar charge they would in all probability be fined a con- siderable sum. THREATS. —Edward Owen, a middle-aged man, was charged that on the 3rd October he threatened to do bodily harm to Daniel Barker, and he was bound over in £5 to keep the peace for six months. ILLEGAL REMOVAL OF SHEEP.—Wm. Davidson, farmer, Acton, was charged with having moved into the county of Chester 46 sheep without having made the required de- claration. It appeared that on the 18th of October the defendant removed the sheep from Bank Quay station, and was driving them to his farm, when he was asked by a policeman for the declaration.—Defendant said the sheep had come from Dumfries, and a 3 there is no disease either at that place or in Cheshire, he did not'think he was infring- ing the law in removing them.—He was fined 5s and costs, altogether amounting to IN 6d.
WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDAY.—Bafore Mr. H. Gaskell, sen., and Mr. Fletcher. _ _

DIZZINIKEYNESS.—EIi Young, Edward Flannigan, Edward Callan, Christopher Hogan, and Patrick Brophy (19th ap- pearance) were each fined for drunkenness and disorderly conduct. WARLIKE WO3fEN.—Mary Tarply, Margaret Wall, Circe] y Riley, and Louisa McCann, married women, were convicted e fighting together in Elizabeth-street, on the 18th inst., and they were each bound over to keep the peace for three months.
RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MoNnks.—Before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. G. L. Davies.

DRUNK AND 'limits —Robert Haydock, for being drunk and disorderly at Halton on the 10th October, was fined 20i and costs, or a month.—Samuel Whitby was fined 5s and costs for having been found drunk in the Dock Hotel, Weston, on the 11th October.—Finee of I.os and costs were imposed upon Peter Orme, Thomas McDermott, and Ann Harrison for being drunk and disorderly.—For being guilty of riotous and indecent behaviour, Bridget McDonald, a bad character, was sentenced to 21 days' hard labour. BREACH OF THE MERCHANT SHIPPING ALT.—Frederick Searle was charged that on the 0111 September, at Tyne. month, County Devon, be being the captain of a British home trading ship, named the Harvestman, did unlawfully carry a seaman, William Hy. Batley, to sea without enter. ing into a formal agreemeat with him aa required by the Merchant Shipping Act, 1854.—Mr. Atkinson (of the firm of Messrs. Harris ik Co., solicitors, Liverpool,) appeared for the Board of Trade.—The defendant pleaded guilty, and he was tined 20s and costs £2 us 63.

NEWTON PETTY SESSIONS. SeTranaY.—Before Col. McCorqaodale (in the chair), and Messrs. C. Pilkington, R. Houghton, T. G. Gillespie. and I. C. McCorquodale. Dfauxxarmss.—The following cases of drunkenness were dealt with :—James Jeffries, fined ss. and costs; James ' Dowd. two charges, fined 15s. and costs; James Austin, fined ss. and costs; John Goodall, ss. and costs; Jonathan Pilling, ss. and Costs. REFUSING 10 QUlT.—Michael Costello was charged

div.p: with being drunk and disorderly on licensed premises, the Wellington Inn' with refusing to putt, and with assaulting the manager, Daniel Cullen. Defendant, who said that he had only been dancing the "highland fling," was tined 10s. and costs for the drunkenness, , and was sent to prison for a month for the assault.

BREACHES OF THE PEACE.—Henry Smith and Dominie Caffery were charged with fighting on the 17th inst. Cat- fery, who had been assaulted by Smith. was discharged, and bound over to keep the peace for six months, in his own re- cognisances of £20.--Charles Worrell was ordered to be bound over in the sum of .£2O for being disorderly and fight- ing, on the 18th inst. A CART WITHOCT A NAME.-11aM1iett Hill, for using a cart without his name painted thereon, on the highway at Newton, was fined is. and coats. OusruccrtolusTs. William Hughes, James Turton, James Edwards, and William Thompson youths, were charged with obstructing the footpath in Bridge-street, New- ton, and were ordered to pay the costs. A CARELESS BAKER.—Stephen Bethel!, baker, was fined ss. and costa for neglecting to provide a pair of scales and proper weights to his bread cart. His assistant had neglected to take the scales and weights with him. MASTER AND SERVANT.—Thomas Howard was charged with assaulting Thomas Garroty at Buttonwood on the 21st Oct. Complainant was a general labourer employed by the defendant, who admitted the assault. He was fined 101. and costs.

THREAT/MING LANGUAGE.—BeIIa Constav was charged with using threatening language to Jane Fairhurst. The case was dismissed. MaINTENANcie ORDER.--Jobn William Waterworth was ordered to pay Is. a week towards the maintenance of his mother.

ASSAULTS.—James Percival, for assaulting Mary Ann Percival at Efaydock, was bound over to keep the peace for three months, in two sureties of £lO each, or go to prison for a month in default. IGNORANCE OF TBE LAw.—Edward Everett and Robert Percy were charged with working a traction engine on the highway, after sunset on the Bth inst. They pleaded guilty but said in defence that they were delayed in Warrington through being short of water, and did not know that there was any difference between the law in Lancashire and in Cheshire, where they were allowed to travel until seven o'clock. Superintendent Jackson said that probably defen- dants were in ignorance of the existence of the bye-laws, and he did not therefore press for a penalty. The men were dismissed on payment of costs.
ST. HELENS BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
FRlDAY.—Before Dr. Gaskell and Mr. R. Pilkington.

DRUNKENNES3.—The following persons were fined for drunkenness :-ss. and costs—William Connor, Eliztbeth Savage, Parr; Edward Byrom, Sutton; Thomas McGarrity, Windle ; Ellen Martin, Eccleston. 7s di. and costs— Thomas Woods, William Johnson, Elward Ashcroft, Eliza- beth Armitage, John O'Brien, Parr ; Patrick Kelly. Sutton; Bridget McCormick, Eccleston. 10s. and cote—Patrick Griffiths, Sutton. William McCormick was fined L 1 and costs for being drunk and disorderly in Windle, on Monday night.

OBSTRUCTING THE FOOTPATH —James McNally was summoned for obstructing the footpath in Liverpool-road, on the 13:h inst. The case was odjourned in order that In- spector Whittaker might be called, and also to give defen- dant an opportunity of getting witnesses. DRUNK ON LICENSED PREMISES —Edward Dillon Was charged with being drunk on the licensed premises of John Marsh. Sefton Arms. Defendant was fined 20s. and costs. MONDAY.—Before Alderman J. Harrison and Mr. A.

DRUNKENNESS.-1 he following persons were fined the amounts stated for being drunk and disorderly :—Patrick O'Donnell, Eccleston ss. and costs; John Lee, Windle, ss. and costs; James Robinson, Windle, 53. and costs ; John Clarke, Windle, ss. and costs; John llines, Eccleston, 55. and costs; Thomas Ryan, Windle, Sc. ansi costs; William Forrest, Windle, 103. and coats; Thomas/ Tinsley, Windle, 10s. and costs; Thomas Donavan, Parr, ss. and coats; Wm. Brown, ss. and coats; Andrew Cassidy, 103. and costs; .James Carrol, ss. and costs; Bernard Cooney, ss. and costs. OBSTRUCTION OF THE FOOTPATH —Joseph Sherratt, of Eccleston, was summoned by P. C. Massey for obstructing the footpath in Waterloo-street, Windle, on the 21st inst. Tha defendant, who did' not appear, was fined 2s. ed. and costs.
CHINWEY ON Fasz.—James Rawson, of Eccleston, was summoned for having the chimney of his dwelling-house on fire on the 20th inst., and the bench imposed a file of Is. and costs.
WEDNESDAY.—Before the Mayor (Mr. H. Baxtsr), Mr. J. C. Gamble, and Dr. Gaskell.

DRUNKENNESS —John Boyle, of unsettled residence, was charged with being drunk on the previous evening, and was fined 53 and cestk—A like penalty was imposed on Martin Casey, who was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in Liverpool-road, Eccleston.

ALLEOED ASSAULT.—John Gregz, a middle-aged man, was charged under a warrant with assaulting his wife, Lucy Gregg, but as the prosecutrix failed to appear the prisoner was discharged. THIIRSDAY.—Before Alderman J. Harrison.

DRIINKENNESS.—John Reynolds, of Parr, a middle-aged man, was broaeht up for bting drunk and incapable in Boandary-road, Eccleston, on the previous night.—He was fined 5s and coats, or In default seven days' imprison- ment.

div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

fTEE RECENT FLOWER Saow.—As a result of the flower show recently held at Go[borne, there ii a balance of £lO 13s lid to be carried forward next year. The result is regarded as very satisfactory. WELSH TEA PARTY.—A tea party promoted by the Gol- borne Welsh Methodists was held on Monday evening, in the Meeting Room, Heath-street. There was a good attend- ance. An English preaching service was afterwards held in the Wesleyan Chapel, and Mr. Israel Jones, of Eariestown, preached to a large congregation. TEMPERANCE MEETING.—A largely attended temperance meeting was held in St. Thomas's School, Golborne, on Monday night, in connection with the Church of England 1 Temperance Society. The Rector's son (the Rev. J. N. Quirk, M.A., of Rotterham). was the principal speaker. The Rev. William Thorp presided, and was supported by the Rev. J. N. Quirk, and the Rev. G. F. Wills, of Wigan. SAD Acctnexr.—On Wednesday afternoon, Joseph Wood, 54, an old Golherne resident, who for the last 27 years has been employed at Messrs. Evans' Edge Green Colliery, met with a serious accident. Whilst he was engaged at work as a miner, a fall of roof occurred, and amongst the debris was a large stene which knocked the poor fellow to the ground and crushed him severely. "Ambulance men" connected with the colliery temporarily bound up his wounds, and he was conveyed on a stretcher to his lodgings in Bank-street, , Gelborne. Upon the arrival of Dr. Latham it was found that the left leg was broken and the body crushed internally and externally. _

Sr. Tnosres.'s SCHOOLS ArrNivansany.—The annual ser- vices on behalf of St. Thomas's day and Sunday schools were held last Sunday, the sacred edifice being crowded. The preachers were, moraine, Rev. J. N. Quirk, M.A., vicar of Rotherham (son of the Golborne rector) ; afternoon, Rev. Canon Fergie, 8.A., vicar of Ince ; evening, Rev. H. Siddall, of Ashton. The Rev St. Vincent Beechey, M.A., Newton Heath, was announced to preach in the evening, but sick- ness prevented his attendance. The Rev. T. C. Quirk, M A., and the Rev. W Thorp took part in the services. Mr. T. D. Grimke read the lessons afternoon and evening. The choir gave a capital selection of anthems, &c. The collections amounted to £5l 2s dd.

AN ALLEGED N lISANCE.—At Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, Mr. Johnson Walker was summoned for allowing a nuisance to exist on premises In Lord-street, off Church- street, Gollsorne.—Mr. Buckley, solicitor, prosecuted on behalf of the Leigh Rural Sanitary Authority. From his statement it appeared that the nuisance was caused by a well, and was injurious to health.—Mr. Moore. solicitor, Warrington, for the defence, said that the well was simply for the convenience of the tenants. The houses were other- wise supplied with drinking water, and the water from the well was only used for such purposes as cleansing the yards and washing. It was, he contended, the duty of the tenant, and net of the landlord, to clean out the well.—The magis- trates were satisfied that the nuisance existed, but thought that, after considering the circumstances, they had no other course but to dismiss the case. RAID ON TRADESMEN AND PUBLICANS.-0-A number of cases of interest to Golborne readers were tried at Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday.—Mary Atherton, of the Red Lion, Golborne, was charged with selling a pint of whisky not of the nature, substance, and quality demanded, on the Ist October. On that day Supt. Weir purchased the whisky at the Red Lion; on analysis, It was found to be 8 per cent. weaker than the limit allowed. A fine of 20s and costs was imposed.—James Hart, Manor Arms Hotel, Golborne, was fined 403 and costs for an offence of the same nature. The superintendent purchased from him 3i pints of rum, which were found to be adulterated 10 per cent, in excess of the limit allowed.—Samuel Barton, grocer and provision dealer, Heath-street, Golborne, was fined lOs and costs for keening a 71b. weight that was 3 drachms light; all his other weights were correct —Thomas Fairhurst, grocer and pro- vision dealer, Golborne, for having a flour scale 19 drachms out of balance against the purchaser, was fined 20s and costs.—Hobert Underwood, also a grocer, of Leigh-etreet, Golborne, was fined 5s and costs for haying a 71b. weight a quarter of an ounce light ; the defence was that the weight was not his own, but had been sent back in mistake with a number that he had lent for temporary use at same paper works —The whole of the cases were proved by Superinten- dent Weir.

ILL TREATING HORSES -A man named James Clayton was, on Saturday, fined 20s and costs, at Newton Petty Ses- sions, for ill-treating a horse at Golborue by working it in an unfit state. It was proved that the animal, which the defendant was working in a cart, was in so weak a condition as to be scarcely able to stand.—At the same court a youth named Emmanuel Pilkington was fined 103 and costs for a similar offence, also committed at Golborne.

THE Cuszon Moon RIOTS.—The trial of the eight pri- soners (three Orangemen and five Roman Catholics) char- ged with participation in the Orange riots at Cleator Moor on July 12th, was resumed at the Cumberland Assizes on Wednesday, when the case for the defence was opened. It was contended on behalf of Bawden, one of the Orange pri- soners, that in point of fact he was the victim of a savage and unprovoked attack, and that the procession in which he was takiag part was a perfectly lawful one. The Crown ultimately withdrew the prosecution against Bawden. who was acquitted. The rest of the prisoners pleaded guilty, and were ordered to enter into their own reognisances to come up for judgment when called upon.

•1114 F EXAMINER. SATURDAY, 9 NOVEMBER 1 1884. WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS, The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were present: Messrs. Cooper (in the chair), Bonnell, Kilshall, Appleton, Caldwell, Blackhurst, Greenhall, Brown, Wm. Houghton, John Houghton, Jolley, Hunt, Derbyshire, Broadbent, Owen; J. C. Sutton (clerk), and S. Sutton (deputy clerk). THE PROTECTION OF CHILDREN. A meeting of the Schools Committee was held on the 25th October, when the committee having considered the letter of Miss Gertrude Langton and that of the Rev. S. L. Wilkinson, the chaplain, apprc,ve of the purpose and request of Miss Lengton, and they instructed Mr. Mines to commu- nicate with Mr Wilkinson, and refer to the committee the question of how best to give effect to Miss Langton's pro- posals.—Mr. CALDWELL asked what Miss Langton's proposal was.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE said that the request of Miss Lang- ton, who belonged to Liverpool, was, it he understood it rightly, that an association to protect and help children, not only those which belonged to evorkhouses and reformatories, but other children of low station who had to go out to ser- vice, and to assist them in getting suitable places and to help them in any way they possibly could, should have some supervision over their children. Miss Langton mentioned Liverpool and West Derby and two or three other places that had granted her request, and she wished to have the same access to the children of that Workhouse, so that she might follow them to their situations and give them such advice and help as she possibly could in order to keep them in the proper path till they became of a suitable age.—Mr. JOLLEY said the religion of the children was not in any way affected by this supervision. It was simply a protection for young girls when they went into strange towns to situations.—Mr. CALDWELL mentioned that a resolution had been passed by the Board that no children should be allowed to go out of their own Union.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE said that resolution . would not be affected at all.—The recommendation of the committee was confirmed. THE SCHOOL CLOCK. Mr. BROADBENT slid that it would be in the recollection of those present that at the last Board meeting there was a resolution of the School Committee confirmed relative to an order for a clock being given to Mr. Alexander Blackhurst. The minutes were confirmed by the Board, but before they broke up, but after several members had left, there was a question came up, somewhat informally, as to whether the Board was in order in giving the contract to Mr. A. Black- burst. The clerk was present when the minutes were con- firmed, but he had left the room when the suheequent dis- cussion took place. He had not been at the School Com- mittee's meeting on the previous day, but he noticed that they had passed a reeolution that the order be given to Mr. A. Blackhorst. He did not know that there was any special reason to look into the matter now except this: that the feeling of the School Committee was that they could, with entire confidence, give the order for the clock to Mr. A. Blackhurst His was the lowest tender, and they had every confidence that the order given to him would be well executed. Of course the order was given on the under- standing that there was no legal or technical objection to such an order. If there was it rested with Mr. A. Blackhurst and not perhaps with their clerk, who, no doubt, would have raised a warning notice if there was anything irregular.—Mr. BLACKHURST said that at the last meeting he told the Board that he had nothing whatever to do with the contract. So far as he was concerned he was not at all interested in it, but it was to be regretted that someone, before the meeting was over, was so very busy as to carry out of that room the decision of the Board and send it down to the other competitors, and thus caused them to enter a protest before the Board had broken up. It was done in a sneaking underhand way by somebody—he could not help using strong language—and it did not reflect any credit on them to do such a thing as to carry the decision out of that room in the way they did. Mr. Blackhurst then explained that in the contract his son was alone concerned, and that no part of the work in con- uoction with the clock would be done at his premises. He also said that the Clerk, so far as his knowledge went, dis- tinctly told him that there was no legal difficulty in the way of his son teking the contract. It there had been the slightest legal difficulty in the way be would at once have advised his son to throw up the contract.—Mr. APPLETON Slid they had no right to put the Beard in a wrong position. —Mr. BIACKHURST : Nobody wishes to put the Board in a wrong position.—Mr. AneLeerme: We have no right either to subject Mr. Blackhnrst to a penaltee—Mr. DARBYSHIRE stated that the committee were advised that there had been nothing illegal done, and be considered that if there was any responsibility it rested on Mr. A. Blackhurst.—The CLERK also mentioned that the Board were in no way liable.—Mr. OWEN said he was very glad that in this in- stance the lowest tender had been accepted, for he felt very strongly on the subject of the tenders accepted at that Board of tecent date, and he Would give notice of motion that there be an alteration made in the mode of dealing with the general contracts which were sent in each six months —The CHAIRMAN thought it would be very hard if a guardian's son was debarred from tendering as well as the guardian himself.—The minutes were then confirmed. FUSTIAN CUTTERS AND THEIR APPRENTICES. On the School Fees Committee's minutes coming up for consideration, Mr. JOLLEY said the committee had had one very extraordinary case before them. A poor woman had ap- plied for school pence for her children, and as they knew the committee inquired very particularly into all the cir- cumstances of the case—as to the income and the sources whence that income was derived. The woman, when pressed, made an admission that somewhat startled the committee. She said that one of her daughters, who was /9 years of age, was a fustian cutter, and earned 5s per week. When asked the reason why a young woman Is years of. age only made 5s per week, she said it was in consequence of binding her for another year's apprenticeship) for which she got a sove- reign premium, and when pressed upon that subject she said she had done it because she wanted to keep a house over her head. The committee understood that if the daughter had not been re-bound her wages would have been something like lOs per week instead of ss. In other words, she would in four weeks repay the loan of the sovereign, and then she had to work 45 weeks to pay, as it were, in- terest. If the mother had not re-apprenticed the daughter she would not, he presumed, have had to come before them for the school fees-3cdper week. They might ask what that had got to do with the Guardians. He said that it hod to do with them. seeing that if the mother had not made such an unfair bargain the ratepayers would not have been called upon to pay the school pence. (Hear, hear.) If the committee have cases of that sort before thenn again they will refuse to give the pence, and if the children were not sent to school the parents would be summoned before the magistrates, and then the thing would be ventilated, and. he hoped, put a stop to. This, he , was informed, was not an isolated case, and he wished it to go to the public that if such bargains continued to be made they would discountenance and try and put an end to them. (Hear. hear.)—Mr. DARBYSHIRE thought a very undue advantage was being being taken of these poor people, and he hoped such cases would never occur again. —Mr. HUNT thought such bargains were an offence against the law.—Mr. JOLLEY said that the girl was a minor, and the mother could therefore bind her.—The CLERK She must be a consenting party herself.—The minutes of the committee were then passed, the remarks of Mr. Jolley seeming to meet with the general approval of the Board. • COMPLAINT. A letter was read from Mr. Caldwell, baker, Warrington, complaining that the Board had given orders to their new contractor before having completed his six months' contract, and claiming on that account £3 17s 6d as the loss of pro• fit he had sustained.—lt was, however, explained that the only order given to the new contractor was for a quantity of flour to test the quality, and that sufficient flour from Mr. Caldwell's was in store to last over the remaining period of the six months.—The CLERK was instructed to inform Mr. Caldwell to this effect.—This was the only business of public interest.
EARLESTOWN.

A fishing boat belonging to Appleeross was capsized on Thursday near Scalpa, Skye, while proceeding to lift herring nets. The crew, three in number, were drowned. One of the bodies was recovered. SHIPPING LEGISLATION.—A meeting of shipowners of the Tyne ports, held at Newcastle, on Wednesday, unanimously passed a resolution condemning the composition of the Royal Commission on Merchant Shipping, and particularly the presence of Mr. Chamberlain upon it. A letter had been received from Mr. Chamberlain, who, referring to the com- position of the Commission, stated that the object was to select fair and impartial men who should among them pos- sess an adequate knowledge on the different subjecturhich might come before them, and whose decisions should be fair to all interests and classes and advantageous to the public. EXTRAORDTNA4 ALLEGATION AGAINST A MAGISTRATE. —At Chester Assizes, on Wednesday, the trial took place of a man named William Darnton, who was indicted for sending threatening letters to Major Turner, a justice of the peace for Stockport and Derbyshire, whom the prisoner char- ged with having drowned a child of a woman be had sedu- ced, and of which he was the father. The prisoner was found guilty, and sentenced to seven years' penal servitude. After receiving sentence the prisoner again charged Major Turner with drowning the child, adding that he saw him do it. The Judge remarked that if the prisoner had made that statement before the sentence had been recorded he would have passed a heavier sentence. _

STORMS —WRECKS.—Loss OF LIFE.—At Macduff, on Tuesday, the lifeboat was capsized, but the crew were picked up. At Shields souse new houses were blown down and windows blown in. A furious gale raged over West Corn- wall on Monday night. The steamer Avebnry went ashore at Lamarna, but the crew were reported safe. A terrific westerly gale blew on Tuesday, in Dundee, and the ferry, steamers were unable to cross to Newport. Railway traffic with Arbroath was stopped by ap uprooted tree which fell I across the line, and numerous corn stacks were blown down. A heavy gale raged all Tuesday at Macduff, causing great damage to shipping. A schooner went ashore at Buckie Harbour, and was last night fast breaking up; and another schooner had foundered in Gardeustown Harbour. The steamer Greencastle had put into Macduff much damaged. , A rope works at Tarlar, near Macduff, was completely blown away. A Reuter's telegram from New York states that advices received by mail from San Francisco report the occurrence of disastrous storms on the coast of Lower Cali- fornia. The steamer Estado de Sonora, which left Mazatlan on September 29th. with 19 passengers and a crew of 38 men, was believed to have been lost with all bands. Several other small vessels with their crews were also lost. Intelli- genes was also received at Great Yarmouth, on Wednesday morning, of the loss of the fishing lugger Dispatch and her crew, numbering ten or twelve bands. It appears that she was run down by a steamboat while on the fishing grounds.

- - —• THE EARLEsrowx Foityrnam CL—The committee of the'Earlestown Football Club have protested against Harry Sharpies, one of the players for Witton in the Lancashire Cap tie between Earlestown and Witton, played at Black- burn, last Saturday. The protest is based on the assump- tion that Sharpies was not a bona fide member of the Wit- toLClub. FIRMITIVZ MICRODOT Missiowestr SocirrY.—Sen mons on behalf of this society were preached on Sunday, at Haydock, by Nil.. J. Woods; Bryn, by Mr. J. Bagnall ;. and Parr, by Rev. R. Carr (deputation). On Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday the annual meetings were held at the above places. • The report was read by the Rev. F. N. Shimmin, and addresses given by the deputation. The total raised amounted to £ll 183 4d, being £4 14s 2i-c1 in advance of last year.

THE LATE Mn. S. ARROWSMITEL—Preaching in the Primitive Methodist Chapel. Legh-street, on Sunday eveia- ing, the Rev. F. N. Shimmin (resident minister) alluded to the recent death of Mr. Samuel Arrowsmith, a prominent member and active worker both in the chapel and Sunday school. Mr. Shimmin pointed out that the late Mr. Arrow. smith had been connected with them for the last eighteen years, and he was one of the few active workers they could so ill afford to lose. STEALING Scomt3.—At Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, a middle-aged woman named Ellen Lomax- was charged, in custody, with stealing four scones, value 311, the property of the Earlestown Co-operative Society. She went into the shop of the Co-operative Societn in Earles- town, on the Friday night, and was seen to take the scones and put thorn in a bag that she carried.—Prisoner's de- fence was that she took the scones with the intention of paying for them when she paid for her groceries. She had, she said, dealt at that shop for twenty-five years, and had never touched anything before.—She was sent to prison for fourteen days. POLITICAL DISCUSSIONS AT EABLESTOWN.—The series of weekly discussions at the Earlerown Conservative Club continue to prove very interesting to the members, judging from the attendance en Wednesday evening, when the ad- journed debate on "The slackness of trade—what is the cause of it?" was resumed by Mr. William Mawdsley. The chair was occupied by Mr. Wm. Sutton, and there was a full attendance. The weekly discussion at the Earlestown and District Liberal Club, which was to have taken place on Wednesday evening was not held owing to the lecture by the Rev. J. Ferguson at the Viaduct Institute, a report ot which appears elsewhere. THE CURSE, THE CAUSE' AND THE Currx."—At a meeting of the members of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templets, held on Monday evening, Bro. G.Clarke, D.M., read an interesting essay on " The Three C's ; or the Curse, the Cause, and the Cure." The greatest curse that ever afflicted mankind was the curse of intemperance. It was the national curse of Britain, afflicting every-grade of society and every town and village in the kingdom. A great change was to be made, however, and in the country to-day there was a noble band of workers, who in the strength of their God were determined to do all they could to exterminate the curse from the land. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Bro. Clarke for his excellent paper. Two DETECTIVES OUTWITTED AT THE VirLoarr. —The details of an incident at the Vulcan, in which two detrc- lives were outwitted have recently leaked out, and have been a topic of conversation throughout that district. It seems that a workman at the Vulcan iron foundry had a wife and three children living near Crewe, and as the husband and father failed to find them the necessary support they were compelled to retire into the workboase. This was some some months ago, and the workhouse officials instituted In as to the whereabouts of the missing "head "of the house. It was ultimately ascertained that he was working and residing at the Vulcan, and a warrant was accordingly granted for his ap- prehension, and two detectives were put upon his track." A few days ago these gentlemen visited the house where the " wanted " individual was living, but he was then at the foundry. The lady of the house sent word to the foundry that two "gentlemen" had come to see her "lodger," and the detectives also visited the works. When they got there, however, the bird had flown, the hint that two visitors were in the neighbourhood evidently being not a very pleasant one. It is stated that the man actually passed his two pursuers near the foundry entrapce, but they failed to recognise him. Since then the individual, who was a prominent footballer connected with the Vulcan Club, has not been seen, and nothing is known as to his where- abouts.

SHOCKING SUDDEN DEATH AT VTILCAN. —A Case of death under circumstances of a very sudden character took ' place at the Vulcan on Tuesday afternoon. The deceased was George Simpson, 60 years of age, and a boltmaker' em- ployed at the Vulcan ironfoundry, residing at 15, Man- chester-row, Vulcan, and additional interest was attached to the sad occurrence owing to the fact that Simpson served with the army through the Crimean campaign, and boasted of having been present at the memorable charge of the Light Brigade at Balaclava. For some months past Simpson, though following his employment, had been attended by Dr. Patterson, of Earlestown, for asthma and spitting of blood, but he had not been medically treated during the last month. On Tuesday morning he went to work at six o'clockand returned home to dinner, without any complaint of being worse than usual. He again went to work in the afternoon, and at half-past five came out of the lodge gates with the rest of the men. Immediately afterwards he was seized with a fit of coughing and was seen to vomit a quantity of blood. He staggered, and a fellow-workman named Win. Travers, and another man, immediately ran to his assistance, with the view of assisting him home. , Though the house was but 130 yards from the foundry hates, the poor fellow ex- pired berore he arrived there. The sad affair cast quite a gloom over the neiahbourhood. Dr. Diggle, assistant to Dr. Watkin, attended shortly after. The man had died and be stated his opinion that :death was caused by the bursting of a blood vessel. The death was duly reported to the coroner, who, however, considered an inquest un- necessary.

LamCutts ON J. B. Get:rem—On Wednesday even- ing the Rev. J. Ferguson, of Tunstall, gave a lecture at the Viaduct Institute, Earlestown, on "Sunlight and Shadow, or the life of J. B. Gough." The Rev. W. C. Taylor pre- sided, and there was a good attendance. RI introducing Mr. Ferguson, the Chairman said that he was glad that there was going to be a course of lectures during the winter season, as those that they bad had before had been found both instructive and pleasant.—The Lecturer said that his sulaject had not been chosen because of the literary char• enter of J. 131 Gough, or of his position particularly, but because of his struggles and trials, and his chief work. A life of struggle and anceess was one of inspiration. They liked to hear of men who had struggled to gain a position, and be supposed that all men who had a position worth having had really had to struggle for it. They bad been told of late that some men got positions because they were accidentally born the sons of magnates of the empire— (laughter)—but these were exceptional cases and were outside ordinary humanity. The review of PL. Gough's life must necessarily be very brief. It was impossible to talk about all of interest that marked his life and character- ised his work. He had thought that he would devote his attention partieularly to temperance itself, but then he thought there might be some one present who took a drop for their stomachs' sake, and their oft infirmities, who ' might think he was taking advantage of his position to give a lecture against the "little habit" that was being in- dulged. But, just as much as it would be impossible to lecture on Gladstone or Disraeli, without being political, it would be impossible to speak of Gough without walking mention of temperance. The lecturer then gave an inter- esting description of the surroundings and influences:under which Mr. Gough spent his early years at Sandgate, Kent, his subsequent life in America, his conversion after giving way to habits of drunkenness to the temperance cause, and the work that he had since carried on in connection with that cause. Mr. Ferguson treated the subject in a capable manner, introducing considerable humour in various anec- dotes bearing upon the life of Gough, thus giving his audience an evening of instruction combined with pleasure.

The annual meeting of ih-e-in;rilbe-;;;F-the.-Earlestown, Widnes, Newton, Haydock, Golborne, and Ashton Building Society was held on Thursday evening, in the Infants' School-room, Market-street, Earlestown. The chair was occupied by the Rev. Canon Whitley, and the other gentle- men on the platform were Messrs. P. Chandley (sec.), R. Davies and Kirkconnel (solicitors), and Jos. Emmett. There was a large attendance of shareholders. The directors in ,submitting their 21st annual report congratulated the phareholders on the satisfactory results of the year's working. As would be seen from the statement of accounts only a comparatively small sum had been advanced on mortgage. The nett profit for the year amounted to £2,209 13s. 7 d., which with the undivided balanoe from last year of £3,426 175.2.1. made a total disposable amount of £5,636 10s. 9d., from which it was proposed to pay a dividend at the rate of 41- per cent, per annum, absorbing .132,002 19a 9d, leaving as undivided profit or reserve fund £3,633 us., which was equal to over 351 per cent. on the amount outstanding on mortgage on property in the hands of the society. The reserve fund was increased over last year by £206 L3s. 10.1. The property now in the hands of the society represents the sum of £10,159 ls 91., against £10,373 3s. last year, being a decrease of £214 Is. 3.1. During the year four members had redeemed their property, which showed a repayment of capital to the amount of £.866 Us. 5.1. The Widnes branch consisted of eight members, who were chiefly borrowers, and held 41 invested shares. In consequence of the gradual falling off in business, and the continued decrease in the number of members at Widnes, the directors have resolved to close the branch from the present time. The total number of members on the books is 526, hold- ing 4,5001 shares, being a decrease of 34. mem- bers and 3554 shares, as compared with last year. The Chairman congratulated the shareholders rnest heartily on the Society's having arrived at its majority. He was sure that on looking around them they could but congratu- late themselves on the prosperity that had attended the Society from the very beginning. He though they had every reason to be satisfied with their directors and officers. Althengla the dividend was not qnite so much as before, there were good reasons to be given why it was not. The Secretary then read the balance sheet, after which Mr. Robert Davies, in reply to a question by Mr. M. Davies, said that £214 bad been wiped off the debt on the property The Widnes property had yielded an average rent of n per cent—that was after taking the repairs out of the rent. With respect to the decrease in dividends he pointed out that the rate of interest bad declined all through the country, and was likely, if accumulation of capital went on, to decline atilt further. As to the management the directors had de.

div.head: 'ON THE ROAD."
div.p: 'ON THE ROAD."
BY AN CiLYI TRAMP,

Having frequently read accounts in the local press of prosecutions before the borough magistrates, under the Vagrancy Acts, and as Warrington is a place so much infested with beggars, it ha e occurred to me that a few remarks anent the gentlemen of the road in general—ancient and modern—might be of inter- est. Warrington householders are pretty well used to the importunities of the cadging fraternity, and by misplaced kindness do much to encourage laziness and often roguery. I should not like to assert that all tramps are rogues, but that many rogues are tramps is incontestable. Ratepayers pay taxes to assist the needy ; they pay and grumble, and straightway give aid to those who are neither needy nor deserving. One would fancy that the police court revelations of beggars' deceits would teach people sense. Appar- ently it is not so in such a degree as we might ex• pect, though, without a doubt "the profession" is by no means as lucrative as it once was. The mem- bers of it are, with a few exceptions, impostors of the worst class, though occasionally men are " jugged " for vagrancy who by the mere pressure of circum- stances are forced "on the road" in search of em- ployment. For instance, a case that recently occurred at Liverpool, where two sailors were sentenced to a term of imprisonment, who, if the reports of the case are to be relied upon, had spent two days in an hon- est endeavour to find work. Such exceptional cases excite the public sympathy, and the many impositions are forgotten in the contemplation of what appears akin to an injustice on deserving people. But as regards the " road" in general. The tramp of fifteen or twenty years agi was a very different specimen to that of the present. Then the calling was by no means a bad one. The ways adopted by these worthies to gull a confiding public were many and artful. That is not a matter for surprise, the only occasion for astonishment is that the public were so ready—and are yet so ready—to be so easily gulled. , One profitable mode was what was called in tramp vernacular, the "dry land sailor" dodge. Five or six, or perhaps eight or nine, well-fed individuals would travel together in groups or "schools," bear- ing the appearance of much to be pitied shipwrecked sailors, deserving of their country's gratitude. To use a cant phrase they" ran shallow," travelling with a scanty supply of raiment—nothing, in fact/but what wail absolutely necessary for the requirements of de- ' eency. Their usual clothing consisted of old "pants" and blue guernsey's, boots and coats, and often hats being only noticeable by their absence. These travel- lers were well acquainted with the " road " and knew almost every house the occupiers of which they could " rnsh " for a few coppers, or a good tuck out. Another stamp of mendicant journeyed under the guise of hawkers in a small way, carrying a miscellaneous stock of articles of scarcely any value, contriving to do a little honest trade and a great deal of what was not honest. They may be called the real tramps of twenty years ago, but there was still another well-known class,frequenting for the most part common lodging houses, who were, com- paratively speaking, holding a superior position. They were, in fact, the bona fide " travellers," who did not gain a living by begging, but were hawkers in a considerable way of business. Some would carry a stook worth £3O or £4O, and that in a small compass. Many had a supply of jewellery, common and other • wise, according to the needs of costomere, whilst others carried lace, some real, and a good deal imitation. The latter of course, was often passed for the former, especially if the purchaser happened to be a "fiat.' Those were the good times "on the road," but the case now is far different. It is seldom now one meets with this description of travellers carrying ware worth picking up in the street. This may be in con• sequence of the cheapening of hawkers' licenses. Formerly a license, cost £2. afterwards £l, and of recent years one has been obtainable for the sum of 1 ss. Until quite recently each 5s license had to be ' endorsed whenever the owner entered a county ia which he had not been before with the same license, which occasioned a little cost and some delay. The same appertained to boroughs. Now, however, it has generally been dbne away with, and a 59 license once obtained serves for a twelvemonth, subject of course, to some restrictions as to character and offences against the laws. This has given rise to considerable veiled begging, as a tramp who can scrape together 5s for the license and say le to purchase a few small articles with, eau, under the protection of his license, travel the country and carry on his begging to a cer • tam n extent with impunity. For a fact, the small hawker generally " mooch-es" all that he gets, and if in danger of detection he " gulls " the " methony" —constable—by the production of his certificate as a hawker. Of course, it occasionally happens that the constable is one too many for him, when the " hawker" runs the risk of imprisonment or the loss of his license. The tramps of to-day, unlike the old•fashioned "jolly beggarmeu," consist of men generally pre- tending to be artisans out of employ, men who have learned or know something of a trade, but are too indolent to follow it up, and who, if they obtain a situation, are too much given to drink to retain it. Such are dubbed by bona fide tramps "travelling tradesmen," and neither class very much loves the other. The genuine tramp as a rule gets a better living than the tradesman," and it is not uncommon for the latter to be assisted by the former. The " travelling tradesmen," after working a few days, will go on the spree with their earnings, brag audaciously until the money is spent, and then again "sing small" until once more in luck. The prac- tised tramp knows he can generally get sufficient " panem " (food) and money for a "shove over" (lodgings), and is consequently somewhat independ- ent; but that class is gradually dying out, and few now remain on the road. Therefore the former free- masonry of tramps is nearly broken up, and anyone visiting a common lodging-house—their usual meet- ing place—now, who had visited such houses twenty years ago, would be struck with the change. Im- provements, so-called, have been introduced. Model lodging-houses have been started; yet for my own part I would far rather have entered a lodging-house which pertained in the slightest degree to respect- I ability twenty years ago, that I would enter the average model of to-day, which are frequently occu- pied by " spongers " who take a mean advantage of a "chum," whereas in the old days the knowing ones would help the younger hand to learn to get his " dorough," that is, to make his living. Tramping is now no easy work, and if passable in summer when sleeping out is pleasant, the winter months try the strongest, and trudging from town to town, with nights passed in vagrant wards, is not a luxurious way of passing life. Yet many prefer it to work, and some are really forced to.it ; the latter will abandon the job as aeon as they are able, and the former will stick to it as long as a charitable (?) publics ,will help them.

TEA PARTY AND CONCERT AT STUBSHAW CROSS.—OR Monday the annual tea party and concert was held at St. Luke's Schools, Stubshaw Cross. An excellent tea was provided for about 300, but only half that number was present owing to the incessant rain. After tea the vicar returned thanks to the tray givers and to the ladies and gentlemen who had assisted in the preparation of the party. He also specially thanked Mrs. Croft, who had got up the concert entirely by securing the aid of many of her own relatives and friends from Liverpool and elsewhere. The programme was then gone through, and the whole of it was so well rendered that the audience became enthusiastic. All the lady singers received imperative encores, and Min Copley and Mr. Gilbey were each recalled a second time after obliging with an encore song, and with difficulty es- caped singing a third. The proceedings came to a close soon after ten o'clock, after perhaps the best concert ever given in these schools. MINERS' MEETING.— On Saturday the Park-lane check- weiglimen held their annual tea meeting at the Park Hotel, Park-lane, and was partaken cf by about 50 checkweighmen and their friends. Mr. Edmund Walkden was called upon to preside. Au excellent programme was arranged for the entertainment of the guests, consisting of speeches, songs, trios, &late, dancing, &c.—The first toast was "Success to the Park-lane Checkwelgh 'Fund," and was proposed by Mr. John Partington. Mr. Woods was called upon to reply. He said he believed he would be right when he said that at present things were working very smoothly between the employers' weighman and the men's checkweighman, and he hoped such a atate of things might long continued, for he was sure if they could work in harmony and peace it was far more comfortable and better for all concerned. The Secretary then read the accaunts for the year, which showed that the income was £364 103 up, expenditure £554 15s, balance 1883 £O, balance now £l5 Ms nid. Mr. James Mee presided at tbe piano, and waa assisted very ably by Mr. Henry Marshlew en the violin. Programme: —Sono', by Luke Gaskell, "The flowing bowl ;" trio, by J. Frodsham, J. Partington, and J. Prior, "Donney-hook Fair," the above caused much amusement; song, by E. Atherton, "Who's to fault ;" recitation, by T. Lomax, " Nature's gentleman," given in masterly style ; song, by H. Wright, "Green peas ;" reading, by E. Walkden, "Quality row," Lancashire dialect; song, by T. Jones, " Abyssiana war song, by J. Partington," Be kind to your dog, boys duett, by T. and L. Gaskell, "The Woodlands ;" song, by J. Gore, "In the deep ;" song, by J. Unswortb, Man with honest heart," and other songs by L. Gaskell, J. Gore, H. Wright, E. Atherton, and G. Hunter. The singing and dancing was kept up until 10-30 p.m. Votes of thanks to Mr. Wools, mrs. Cunliffe, and the Chairman, brought, a very interesting meeting to a close.

He did not think there was in Lancashire a society which stood more securely than that one did„ (Hear, hear.) He also mentioned that the expenses of the manigement of the society amounted to very little more than 2120' a year, which was little over a quarter per cent. (Hear, hear.)—Mr.. William Appleby, one of the auditor,, 111 the course of a few re- marks complimented the secretary on the creditable manner In which be had performed the duties of his office. He was convinced, be said that there was not another so- cietr in Lancashire that was in such a sound financial con- dition as that society. The report was then unanimously adopted, aud after a few remarks by Mr. Joseph Emmett, one otthe directors, the election of officers was proceeded with,. the whole of the officers being re-elected. Cordial votes of thanks were then passed to the Chairman and to the officers of the society.
