div.p: _ RUFFIANISM IN WARRINGTON. A, young man named Richard Jackson was charged before the borough naagistrates at Warrington, on Monday, with having committed various, offences on Saturday even- ing. The charges were (1) with being drunk and disorderly in Dial-street, (2) with assaulting P.C. Smith whilst in the execution of his duty, (3) with being drunk and disorderly on, and refusing to quit, the licensed premises of William Alexander, Dial-street, .(4) with doing wilful damage to the amount of 10s. by breaking a door, and (5) with assaulting William and Ellen Alexander. Prisoner went to the Hose Inn; Dial-street, and conducted himself so violently that the landlord endeavoured to eject him. Prisoner was so:rough that the assistance of the police was obtained, and P.C. Smith went to qdell the disturbance. When being taken into cus- tody Jackson kicked the officer on the mouth and about the legs, kicked the landlord, William Alexander, and struck the landlady a blew on the face. He also did damage to the extent of 10s. It was his eleventh appearance.—He was find £2 5s and costs, making £3 15s 6d, or a month's im- prisonment in default.--At the same sitting of the magis- trates, three young men named John Bowen, Wm. Bowen, and Thomas Duckworth. were brought up, in custody, on serious charges. ?John Bowen was charged with being drunk and 'disorderly in Market-street on Saturday night, with as- sawing P.C. Shaw, and with assaulting Samuel Ellison whilst assisting Shaw. William Bowen was charged with rescuing John Bowen, hie brother, and with assaulting P.C. Shaw) and Duckworth with assaulting Ellison.—Chief Con- stable Hunt, in stating the case, said that John Bowen was a wiredrawer, living in Stamford-street; William Bower, a hawker, living with and working for Mrs. Lockyer, Mill- street; and Duckworth, a blacksmith, living in Powys. street. On Saturday night, in the Market, John Bowen Was seen to assault without the least provocation a man named George Lynch, a foreman at Messrs. Jasper Brothers. Mr. Place, market inspector, who was also a constable, witnessed the assault, and seized Bowen. P.C. Shaw came up, and demanded the prisoner's name. 111) gave it as "William Jones, 127, Rodney-street," and as the officer knew there was no such number in that street he took him into custody. William Bowen then appeared on the scene, and made a desperate attempt to rescue his brother. As was usual in such cases Shaw then arrested William Bowen, letting the other prisoner go, and as William was being taken to the station John, going behind the constable, dealt him a vio- lent blow on the back of the head with some instrument, in consequence of which he had since been off duty. John Bowen was afterwards re-captured,. and Duckworth was also taken into custody on the charge of assaulting Shaw and Ellison, the latter of whom was called by Shaw to ten • der him assistance. The case was, Mr. Hunt added, one of the worst of the kind that had been brought before the magistrates during the present year.—After hearing the evidence, the Bench decided that the evidence was not strong enough to convict Duckworth, but sentenced the Bowen's to two months' hard labour each.

div.head: IfAYDOCK.
div.p: IfAYDOCK.

- -- CAPTURE OF A PICEFOCKET.—At Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, a young man named John Wilson, from Lon- don, was charged with frequenting Haydock Park coursing meeting on the 24th October, with intent to commit a felony. —On the day in question, about noon, Mr. Caulfield, of the Wheat Sheaf Inn, Wigan, was standing amongst other people, at Haydock Park, when he felt some one tugging at his watch chain. Looking round, he saw the prisoner had hold of the chain, and tried to seize him. Prisoner, how- ever, broke away. He was followed by prosecutor and others, and was finally taken into custody by a constable. When charged he admitted having attempted to steal the watcb.—Mr. Moore, solicitor, Warrington, who defended pleaded guilty, but said that the prisoner was unable to ac- count for having done such a thing.—Prisoner was a mar- ried man, and, as he stated that it was the first time he had been brought before a court of magistrates, he (Mr. Moore) asked the Bench to deal leniently with him.—Prisoner was committed to gaol for two months, with hard labour.

HAYDOCKTOCAL BOARD. The monthly meeting was held on Monday afternoon. Present—Messrs. W. italharre, J. Cunliffe, W. Alker, and T. Turnbull (clerk.) Mr. Bat harry was elected to preside. After accounts amounting to £s2s 8d had been examined and passed for payment, the minutes of the last meeting were read and confirmed.

GENERAL DISTRICT RATE.—The Clerk stated that with respect to the general district rate for the ensuing half-year, the estimate of expenditure had been approved at the last meeting. It appeared that the treasurer's balance on the general account up to the end of September was £3OO, and deducting that from the amount required, £477 las lid, left very little, for which a rate was to be levied. But it was always better to have a balance in hand at the close of the year instead of having the account overdrawn. At the last meetingit was suggested that they should have an 84 rate, but there would be no necessity for a rate of that amount. A rate of 81 in the £ would be quite sufficient. That would give them a balance of £l5O or £2OO in hand at the close of the year.—The Chairman remarked that it was very satis- factory, and they were evidently doing well.—Mr. Cue- life moved that a general district rate of 64 in the £ be laid, and Mr. Alker seconded the motion, which was adopted,_

TEE WATER SUPPLY.—In answer to the Chairman, Mr. Turnbull stated that the reservoir was partly empty, and Mr. Pilkington had suggested that it should be properly cleaned before any more water was put in.—Mr. Cunliffe : How much is there in it ?' It it half full P—Mr. Tufnbull : Oh, no.—Mr. Cawley (surveyor) was then called, and in re- ply to the Chairman he said there was no water in at present, but Messrs. Evans had promised to syphon a supply Dom their reservoir.—The Chairman : Is any part of the bottom of the reservoir dry yet 7—Mr. Cawley : There is a little at the top end.—The Chairman : 12 there any sediment in it? —Mr. Cawley : No, only the clay same as when the water was turned in. There is no dirt in worth speaking of.—Mr. Cunliffe thought it was quite necessary that the reservoir should be cleaned out when it was empty, and he would move a motion that it be cleaned.—Mr. Allier seconded the motion, which was passed.—The Clerk was afterwards in- structed to ascertain the price of a suitable filter bed for the reservoir.—The-Clerk then read a letter from a number of the inhabitants at Double Locks, which stated that they gave notice that unless.water was brought intotheir premises while the canal was " off " they would pay no more water rent. They had, 30(1 yards to carry their water at present, and it was not fit for domestic use after lying in the pipes. There was a population of over 70 persons with- out water, and they hoped the Board would comply with their request.—The Chairman asked where they got their water from at present.—The Clerk : There is a standpipe.— The Chairman: How is it that they did not take the water at first 7—Mr. Turnbull: I don't think it was agreed for the water to go across the canal.—Mr. Cunliffe: Not in Mr. G-oldsworth's report—The Chairman : Could a pipe not be taken across the canal ?—Mr. Turnbull : Yes, it could be easily put across. All we should have to do would be to get permission, from, the London and North-Western Railway Company, who own the canal.—The Chairman ultimately remarked that they could do nothing in the matter at present, and the-matter dropped. SPECIAL Mumma —The Clerk reported that he had.' received a letter from the Public Works Loan Commissioners stating that the next half year'S interest was due on the 20th November. It would be necessary to sign a cheque for the amount that day, and a special meeting of tbe Board was required for that purpose.—lt was decided to hold a special meeting of the Board on the date mentioned,. at ten o'Clock in the forenoon. NONFALTMENT OF RATES.—The Clerk submitted a list of persons who had not paid their rates, her the half year end- ing September, and stated that the totals were as follows: General district rate .L 23 5s 7d, waten rate £1 18s 10d. He asked the Board to pass a resolution to that effect, to enter in the. rate book—Mr. Cunliffe:• Are the rates irrecover- able P'--,The Clerk: Most of them are recoverable, but there should be a resolution for the necessary entries to be made in the rate book.—On the motion of Mr. Cunliffe, seconded by Mr. Alker, the motion was passed. A VACANCY.—The Clerk intimated that Mr. Greenall had been absent from the Board's n:teetings during the last :six months, and a vacancy was thus created. It was for the Board to fill up the vasancy.--Mr. Cunliffe moved the re- election of Mr. GreenalL—Mr. Alker seconded, and the motion was agreed to. This was all the business of interest.

At Maidstone Assizes, on Monday, Mr. Justice. Manisty condemned the Salvation Army processionsnbut deprecated the scandalous counter-proceedings. A FIGHTING Loam—Lord Marcus Beresferd appeared at the Bow-street Police Court, London, on Wednesday' in an- swer to an adjouzned summons charging him with having assaulted Mr. T. G. Bowles, proprietor of Vanity Fair. Mr. George Lewis, for the Complainant. said that on October 16th Mr. Bowles drove to his office, and, upon alighting, was met by the defendant, who demanded the name of the writer of a letter published in T'anity; Fair containing false statements about the defendant. On refusal, the defendant struck the complainant violently in. the face and used ob- jectionaliie language. Mr. Bowles having deposed to the circumstances of the assault, Lard Egmont admitted that he wrote the. letter, which referred to Mrs. Trevelyan's case, , solely to obtain assistance for the lady, who was a connec- tion of his family. Ile had no desire to wound Lord Beres- ford's feelings. Mr. Montagu Williams for the defence Called two witnesses as to the circumstances of the alleged assault. Mr. Vaughan, in view of the conflicting character of the evidence, decided to commit the defendant for trial, laccepting his own recognisances in £5OO,

div.p: GENERAL NEWS
The apppoiistreent of Lord Melinda to tin Viceroyalty of fudia is gazetted:

Ic According tondvices receiver/ at the Adnthalty, Commo-• lore Erskine was to have left Brisbane on Tuesday, for New ,Grainea. The secretary of an Oddfellowe ledge is irp custody at ;Middleton on a charge of embezding money belonging to 'the °tar.

The Duchess of Albany with her children leftßa?moral ott Tuesday afternoon and proceeded to•Lendon by the three o'clock train from 211 moral. Mr. Henry Somerville, the well-knomn dramatic reader, IS dead. He was creditedwith the wonderful power of reciting from memory the wbeittot Shakspere's plays. A valaable horse was found in a field near Nottingham, on Saturday, stabbed to death by a miner's pick. A large re- ward has been offered for the arrest of the offender. The expenditure incidental to the International Health Exhibition has been very, considerable but so far as can be ascertained at present the surplus will be about £30,000. I On the stage of one of the less successful London theatres is a large model of Jerusalem, prepared, it is said, with great accuracy, and an explanatory lecture is delivered by a clergyman.

MR. HIISKIN will very shortly close the publication of hit' Fors Clavigera, and set to work instead on a brfet auto- biography. He has not even seen the reputed Turner pie. tures bought by an Exeter hairdreeser. Two PERSONS KILLED BY A Errtm.—A farmer, near Mal-- lingar, named Mulvihill, was attacked and fatally gored by a bull. An alarm was given, and a young woman named Moran went with a shovel to her employer's assistance. The bull turned upon the woman, and killed her also. THE DUBLIN SCANDALS.—At the Dablin Commission, on Tuesday, Gustavus Cornwall and Martin Kirwan were charged with conspiracy to commit certain offences. Mal" coltu Johnson and George Taylor deposed to acts, princi- pally by Kirwan, substantiating the indictment. Mr. Moaroe having opened the defence, the Court adjourned. THE PREMIER ON THE•CRISFI.—Iti acknowledging the receipt of resolutions passed at a meeting of the City Liberal hosociation, Mr. Gladstone says he is sensible of the Impor- tance of that expression of opinion on the question of the • Franchise Bill, and expresses the assurance that his great desire is to avert dangers whick may be apprehended from persistence in a course equivalent to a ref aeal to pass the bill.

INCOME OF THE WORKING CLASSHS.—The inquiry initia- ted by the late Mr. Bass M.P., on the total income of the working classes of the United Kingdom, and carried oat suc- cessfully by Professor Leone Levi in 1867, is about to be renewed by desire of Sir Arthur Bass. M.P. The amount of income then ascertained, including money and money's equivalent, was £418,000,000. Professor Levi hopes to make known the result of the inquiry in January next. A CAPTAIN SENTENCED FOR TRAIN WRECHING.—A TO- remarkable case was tried before sheriff and jury at Stott-. haven, on Saturday. In September a determined attempt was made to wreck a passenger train on the Caledonian Rail- way, and inquiry led to the arrest of Charles Newton Biggs, late captain in the 09th Regiment. No motive could be shown, but the evidence against the accused was conclusive, and he was convicted. Sentence of twelve months' imprison- ment was passed.

ARRIVAI. OF -A PORTION OF THE NISERO Caw.—Tbe steamer Ajax, of Liverpool, arrived in the Thames on Sun— day, bringing 18 of the crew of the Nisero, of Sunderland. The names of the men, who were reported "all well" on landing, are not given in the ship's- papers. They were shipped at Penang September 21st, and the vessel called at Port Said October 12th, since which she had not called at any port. Some of the men landed at Gravesend, and the others went up to London docks directr ACCIDENT TO A WEDDING PARTY.—A, wedding party from I Minster met with an unfortunate adventure on Sunday. The " knot" having been tied, they drove to St. Nicholas, but on the return journey a spirited Irish cob attached te• the waggonette became unmanageable. Charging a hank, the restive animal overturned the vehicle and deposited bride and bridegroom, bridesmaids and friends, in one strug- gling mass upon the ground. Beyond a few cuts and bruises, none of the party were injured,' but the conveyance sustained considerable -damage. THE BISHOP' OF ST. ASAPII, in replying to a letter from the Rev. Leycestar Lvne (Father Ignatius) asking why be had been inhibited from preaching in Llangollen Parish Church, slates that he was exceedingly sorry to have to issue the inhibition, and that he had no wish to hurt Father Ignatius's feelings, but that under the circumstances he did not see how he could avoid it. His Lordship also expres- ses the hope that Father Ignatius might see his way to place himself in such a relation to-the Church of Eng- land that no bishop might deem it necessary to inhibit him.

THE SUNDAY POs.—Mr. John Bright, M.P., having re- ceived an invitation to attend a conference to promote the Sunday closing of all post offices, has declined. He predicts that if the Sun.lay Rest Association succeeds for a time in this object, failure must follow. lie says, "I think the closing of the post in London on Sundays is a great incon- venience, and, as to its effect on. family correspondence, a great evil. But lithe London system were extended to the whole kingdom it would cause an amount of confusion that would be intolerable. The Sabbath was made for man, and not man for the Sabbath."

_ A SUGGESTIVE LIST.—It is proposed to circulate for pub- lic information the list of peers voting in the division by which the Franchise Bill was thrown out last session. Lib- eral peers like Lord Granville, Lord Derby, and the Duke of Argyll will be paired off with the Marquis of Salisbury, Lord Cranbrook, and Lord Cairns. The better known Con- servative peers will be thus paired off as far as the numbers of the minority go, after which there will appear a residium of obscure or utterly unknown peers forming the majority which opposed itself to the overwhelming majority of the House of Commons.

MEETING .OF COUNTY COURT JUDGES. A meeting of the Judges of the County Courts in England and Wales - was held on Saturday, at the Birmingham County Court. to discuss matters relating to their jurisdiction and the ad- ministration of their office. The meeting was presided over by Sir Richard Harington, Judge of Nenhamptonshire, Ox. fordshire, and Warwickshire district, and the following among other judges were present :e-Jetdges Thompson and Collier, Liverpool ; Judge Bedwell, Yorkshire. North and East Riding; Judge Wynne.Ffoulkes,Lancashire and Che- shire ; Jedge J. J. Powell, Leeds and Bradford. The judges remained in deliberation for several hours. PRACTICAL PROTEST AGAINST REPUTED ATHEISM.-011 Saturday, at Northampton, St. Crispin's Church, built ex. pressly for shoe operatives of the town, was dedicated. Tbe arrangements had been carried out by a committee of 300 working shoemakers ; and the cost, £3,000, is defrayed by contributions from all classes. The church will acoommo- date 400,.and contiguous to it a building is erected mallet St. Crispin's Hall. The dedication service was performed by the Bishop of Peterborough, in the presence of a large gathering of clergy, as well as a crowded general congrega- tion. The project is regarded as a protest against the notion that infidelity is rampant among the local working classes,

A MAYORAL "AT HOME TO WORKING-MEN," The Mayor. of Liverpool (Mr. T. Holden) deserves credit for a new departure in the direction of municipal receptions. On Saturday evening he devoted about three hours to the recep- tion of representative working-men, including the presidents and secretaries of the different trade societies and men from the chief firms in the city. More than 500 tickets were issued, each admitting two to the reception, so that there could net have been fewer than 1,000 guests present. The principle OD which so many mayors have recognised only the wealthy ratepayers ignoring entirely those wha pay the bulk of the-rates has thus been spiritedly set at naught in Liverpool. RADICALS AND THE HOUSE Or LORDS.—A great demon- stration, under the auspices of the National Radical Feder- ation, and having for its object the abolition of the HOLM lof Lords, was held on Sunday in Hyde Park. Deputations from all parts of London representing most of the working- men's Liberal and Radical Associations in the metropolis came in procession to the park, where nine distinct meetings were addressed. An identical resolution in favour of the. abolition of the Hereditary Chamber was passed by all the meetings, and the proceedings throughout were most orderly and unanimous.—About 15,000 working-men, many of them. as yet non-electors, met in Newcastle-on-Tyne on Saturday, and passed resolutions supporting the Government and con- demning the House of Lords. _

_ ILDI2D RICHARD GROSVENOR AND THE REDISTRIBITTIOH. SCHEXE.—The Crewe Town Council having asked Lord Richard Grosvenor to receive a deputation and to be the- hearer of a petition to Sir Charles Dilke, setting forth the. claims of Crewe, Nantwich, and Sandbach, for a member under the proposed redistribution scheme, his lordship has- written expressing his willingness to receive a deputation on the subject, but he adds—" I can assure you that it is most unnecessary trouble that you are taking, as you may rest assured that the claims of Crewe will be fully considered and recognised, in the scheme of redistribution proposed by the Governixiont, All the tante as to population, &c., are fully known to those who have the preparation of the scheme, and it is only a needless loss of time both to those. gentlemen who propose to take the trouble to come to Lon- don and to. myself to go over those facts again. Under these circumstances, I wou'd suggest that the deputation be post- poned untfa at least the scheme is laid before the country.— I am, dear sir, yours faithfully, RICHARD GROSVENOR.—To Mr. T. Cooke, Town Clerk." INTMNATIONAL HEALTH., EXHIBITION. LANCASTLIRR AWARDS.—The awards of the international juries were gazerted on Monday, and among them are the following Manchester Corporation, diploma of honour for water and earth closets and exhibits.; Manchester Institution for the Deaf and Dumb, bronze medal in °Las 54 for apparatus for teaahing Oa, blind ; Manchester Technical School, silver medal in class 50 for apparatus for elementary trade teach- ing in school, in class 51 for apparatus for elementary science in school, and class 53 for apparatus for teaching , handicrafts in school; Oldham School of Science and Art, gold medals in clas3es 50, 51, and 53 as above ; Mayor and Corporation of St. Helens, diploma of honour in olass 23 for water and earth closets, ,&c.; Mr. W. Dickinson, bronze medal in class 31e and ale for transport or sick and wounded in I war and peace ; Mr. John Heywood, bronze medal in classes 50, 51, and 53 for school fittings, apparatus, fic. ; Mr. A. W. Kershaw, Lancaster, bronze medal in class 22 for house drains, dm. ; Lancaster Royal Albert Asylum for Idiots and Imbeciles of the Northern Counties, diploma of honour in class 55 for collective displays of school work and appb- ances ; Mr. J. B. M'Cullum, borough engineer, Blackburn, silver medal in class 21 for w.c. cisterns ; Mr. W. Roth well, Bolton, silver medal in class 19 for machinery, Jr.c., for the preparation of dress; Mr. W. 13. Stephenson, M.D., idLiCk• burn, silver medal in clasp 24 for grates, stoves, ,te,

div.head: WIT AND HUMOUR.
div.p: WIT AND HUMOUR.

To become an able man In any profession, there are three things necessary—nature, study, and practice. Young man from the country to Scotch policeman: " Whar's Oxford Street ? " Constable sternly : " Why, wbar it was yesterday! None o' yer larkin' wi' me!" CAUSE OF THE COMPLAINT.—Doctor to patient, "You mast first of all remove the cause of this nervousness, then the complaint will soon disappear." Patient : " It's no go; I should have to kill my wife then !" THE EFFECT OF "Hello, Smith, haven't seen you for a week. Been sick? You ought to take a vacation." Smith: "Just got back from one, and feel ex- hausted, of coarse. A few days' work in the office will set me all right again." A L'ITALIENNE.—A gang of Italian labourers near Sara- toga were recently cat down ten cents a day. Instead of striking, they cut an inch off their shovel-blades at night. The " boss " asked what it meant. One of the men replied, "Not so mach pay, not so much dirt lift ; all right —job' last the more long. Italian no fool, like Irishman ; he no strike." Moaz Tzuswifss —'Twas ever thus from childhood's hours I've seen my fondest hopes decay; I never tried to 03°1 tl Mqr b wlat rye wastti hal! 4 day- never Look girl to church, the longest way back horde to plan, but that she left me in the larch and walked back with another man. I never had a fond gazelle to glad me with its dark blue eye, but had a goat which knocked me out ;," My life is marred with buts," said I. HE INSULTED PAPA.—" Emma, I hear you have broken off with George." "Yes. I am sorry, but it had to be." "Why, what did he do?" "Well, you know, last Sunday night, papa kinder kicked him off the steps, and when he came round Monday he brought a pair of slippers, with the toes padded, and asked me if I wouldn't get the old man to put them on." Mentz HE DID.—" Can you refer me to your last em- ployer?" Inquired a Detroiter of a man who had applied for the position of a coachman. " Yes, sir." "Very well: you can call to-morrow." The man took his leave but returned in a moment to observe: "I forgot to say that I left because we kicked each other. As he kicked twice as fast and twice as hard as I did, he ought to be willing to give me a good recommend." TAKING TIME BY THE FORELOCK.—" I wish to look at some mourning goods," said a lady as she entered a dry goods store. "Yes, madam," replied the clerk; "this way, please." After looking through the entire stock she re- marked that she would come in again in the course of a day or two. "May I ask," said the clerk, in a sympathetic tone of voice, "if the death occurred in your immediate family?" "There has been no death, yet," she replied, sadly, "but my husband is very low." SUNDRY PLACES.—The place for babies—Baby-lon. The place for scholars—School-craft. The place for lovers— Court-land. The place for soap-makers—Ash-land. The place for temperance societies—Cold-water. The place for sleepy-heads—Bed-ford. The place for laundrymen— Washing-ton. The place for cooks—Pots-ville. The place for farmers—Rich-land. The place for anglers --Fish-kilt The place for hungry men—Sandwich. The place f..n. reporters. Pencil-yanks- The place for carpenters—Plane- well. The place for butchers—New Market. The place for Chinamen—Que-bec. The place for vocalists—Sing Sing. THE OLD, OLD bTORY.—" You are going with us to our pic-nic, ain't you ?" asked little Tom. "Yes, my dear child," replied young &pips, "Your sister honoured me with an invitation, and I would not miss such an opportu- nity for anything in the world. By-the-way, Tom, here is a new silver sixpence. Now I wast you to tell me some- thing I want to know. Mr. Gayfellow isn't going, is he ?" "Oh, yes !" "Hang him! I thought I should have your sister all to myself to-day." "But you shouldn't want to hang Mr. Gayfellow. He was the one who told sister to Invite you." "He ! Why, what did he want me for ?"1 "To carry the baskets !" Hz WAS " CONSINED."—They walked a half-drunken, seedy-looking chap into the Central Station the other night, and among the personal property found in his pockets was a greasy old note-book, in which was written under the current date: "I can't stand this misery enny longer, and have decided to consine my body to the daps of the Ripper. Goad-by, coald world." "Why didn't you 'consine' accord- ing to written agreement ?" queried the captain. "Just goin' to when 'rested." "Humph! You'd better live until you learn how to spell." "spell !" echoed the prisoner, as he stepped back and raised his bands. "Why, I was a Town Clerk for seven years! Spell! Why, I was the first man in Wisconsin to drop the 'h' out of sugar and leave half a dozen useless syllables out of sops! Consine me to a sell if you will, but don't abuse me !" A TOO-PENITENT THIEF.—A stray horse which had been running for several months within a short distance of Weiser County, Idaho, was claimed and sold by a saloon- keeper named C. A stranger who had just arrived in the locality, hearing the circumstances, procured a description of the animal, called on Mr. C., and asked him if he had sold such a horse. "I did," Mr. C. replied. "Sy what 'authority ?" was the next query. "I claimed him," said C. Well," said the stranger, "there is no use disputing about the matter. You claimed him and I claim him. We'll just let a jury decide whom he belongs to. "Stop, stop," ex- claimed C.—" there is no use of that! If I made a mis- take, I am very sorry, and am perfectly willing to make amends." "Now, Mr. C.," the stranger replied, "don't aggravate the offence by denying it. You would stand far -higher in my estimatios if you acknowledged that you stole the horse.", "Well," said C.," we won't quarrel. Say what you value the animal at and I'll pay you?" "Fifty dollars," was the answer. Five minutes afterwards the stranger de- parted with that amount in his pocket, having received pay- ment for a horse he never saw.

Snocrrixo A FATHER.—John William Rose, 22, indicted on Monday at the Oxford Assixes for the murder Of his father at Witney, was acquitted, the jury believing that when he shot his father he had good grounds for supposing that the life of his mother was in peril. SOMETHING LIRE AN " ALIEI."—SeYeU men who were charged at the Limerick Quarter Sessions with maliciously wounding a labourer, have experienced the full benefit of the legal axiom that there is no defence like an alibi. In this case the accused were successful in spite of them- selves. They assaulted the prosecutor, destroyed one of his eyes, eyes and grievously wounded him on the head. Shortly ; afterwards they proffered compensation, but it was not ac- cepted. Then the happy thought occurred to them of "proving" an dibi, and they succeeded in making a sympa- thetic jury believe, or pretend to believe, that they had not been present at the outrage. The jurymen acquitted them, and they left the court with flying colours. ALARMING FIRE IN EDINBURGEL—A two-storey tene- ment in Hawthornbank, Edinburgh, was early on Tuesday destroyed by fire. The working-class occupants, 21 in all, escaped by the windows, and one old woman was severely burned. Nearly all suffered from the cold, some of them being almost destitute of clothing. The Rev. Canon Mere- dith, of St. Mary'a Cathedral, has received the homeless into his mission rooms. SUPPOSED SILOCKLNG MURDER IN LONDON.—A dis- covery was made on Wednesday in London of human re- mains, which are supposed to be part of a female's body, portions of which were found in Alfred Mews and Bedford- square. As a constable was passing No. 33, Fitzroy-square, which is used as a drill hall and armoury for a company of Middlesex volunteers,he observed a large brown paper parcel on the area floor. He went down, and ascertained that it contained a portion of the trunk ef a human body and some pieces, all in an advanced stage of decomposition. With assistance he conveyed it to the Tottenham Court-road Police Station, where it was examined by the divisional sur- geon, who confirmed the accuracy of the constable's antici- pations of the nature of his discovery. This further dis- covery leads to the supposition that a terrible murder has been committed, and that the perpetrator is endeavouring to escape detection by dropping portionsof the body in various parts of the metropolis, having previously cut it into pieces 'small enough to be ef easy carriage, and unlikely to arouse suspicion. It will be remembered that there have now been found a human skull, an arm, and a portion of a leg. The right arm is tattooed about two inches above the wrist in black and red, the latter colour being very bright. The hair on the skull is dark brown, and the skull is that of a woman aged between 25 to 40 years. The police hope from the tattooed marks on the arm to gain some information that will lead to the remains being identified. div.head: FOR A POLL.
div.p: FOR A POLL.

Sir,—When at the town's meeting last Thursday week, which was called for the purpose of asking the ratepayers to allow a twopsnny rats to be levied to assist the promo- tion of another scheme for the Manchester Ship Canal, it Is very probable that, if one had heard less abuse and more argamsnt as to whether the Town Council had the right or power to levy a rate for this purpose, or whether it would lot be wiser and more in keeping with equity to try the woiantary principle, instead of the compulsory one, I might have been converted to the various speakers' ways of think- ing. Bat it was the lack of disaussion of the question the meeting was called to discuss; the knowledge that many as well as myself would rather give a !shilling voluntarily than have a penny taken from them by force; and the un- fairness that real opponent carriers should be compelled to pay towards the promotion of an opposition carrying com- pany, that caused me to demand a poll. It is out of defer- ence to the wishes of the horny-handed working-man, and the solicitations of a few sterling friends, that I withdraw the demand for a poll before any expense is incurred.— Yocrs faithfully, T. MORRIS. THE S ANKEY-STRE hT PILLAR LE TT ER BOX. Sir,—The Pillar Letter Box having been removed from Trinity Church to the front of Messrs. Tunstall's office, op- posite Goloorne-street, may I ask through your columns if the office now opened at Messrs. Holmes and Harrison's, Market-gate' is intended to be kept open until 9-30 p.m., same as the box referred to? If not, I feel that a great mistake has been made by those who have ordered its re- moval. The extra time allowed at that box has been a great boon to the residents of North and South-East Wards, especially on wet nights. By its removal so much nearer to the General Office it seems to me that the convenience of the public has been overloelted.—Yours truly, A RESIDENT OF SOUTH-EAST WAttD.

div.p: ASSISTINO TEIE POLICE.

Sir,—Curiosity I;ime to attend Ciejia—rringten Borough Court, on Monday, when amongst other cases that were tried was one in which three roughs were charged with as- saulting a constable and a man who came to the assistance of the constable. The roughs were, very properly, sen- tenced to a term of imprisonment, but I could not help con- sidering it " passing strange " that the man who wis as- s tulted whilst assisting the police was allowed io leave the Court not only without any offer of a reward for his ser- vices, but without even a word of commendation for his conduct. Possibly anyone rendering assistance to the police in their time of need is not entitled to reward, and should not expect any, but I think our magistrates might mark their sense of the conduct of anyone giving assistance by a few remarks of a commendatory nature. Of course, it is forgetfulness that accounts for the omission. Ido not for a moment think that our chief magistrate and his fellow- justices would depreciate anyone's assistance, but what I think is that they should try and not forget, and should render honour where it is due. FAIR PLAY. Warrington, October, 1834.

div.head: STRIKE OF THE PARISH CHURCH CHOIR.
div.p: THE STRIKE OF THE PARISH CHURCH CHOIR.

Sir,—The report now in circulation in reference to the attitude of the Rector to his voluntaty choir must have given a rude shock to the susceptibilities of many who have been accustomed to associate that rev, gentleman's name with the late Charles Dickens's "Model Curate." A respect- able and respected body of parishioners—connected for many years with the church choir—desiring to make known their wishes in regard to an important change then about to take place in the direction of the musical portion of the ser- vices, send a deputation to the Rectory to solicit an inter- view. The Rector declines to sea or to hold any communi- cation with them on the subject, reserving to himself the right to make whatever change he thinks necessary. Now in the names of all the gods at once, 13p mi.what meat does this our Cw4ar feed,

That he hath grown so great We meet with curious developments occasionally, and this is one of them. From the "Model Curate "—by a process of evolution which it would puzzle Professor Tyndall him. self to explain—has developed tke "Arrogant Rector."

The kind of character which grows up -under the domina- tion of such a man may be imagined. There are individuals who have been connected with the Parish Church for a quarter of a century, and who have never dreamed of oppos- ing the will of the Rector. They have grown accustomed to the yoke, and bear it meekly and with patience. Bat even warms can turn upon occasion, for it appears that several of the poor oppressed ones, led on by the bold assur- ance of the more daring spirits in the choir, have actually ventured to "strike" against the tyranny of this "proud priest." But they repented early and have returned to their allegiance, no doubt more highly esteemed I?) than ever by their "dear pastor." No arguments of the Liberationists can appeal with greater force to the minds of thinking people thin do these simple facts. Mr. Gladstone undoubtedly saw farther then he cared to acknowledge when he referred to tha danger to the Church from dissensions in her midst as more likely to bring about her fall than any attacks from'svithout.—Ymrs respectf ally, PARISHIONER.

Sir,—Referring to the very excellent accounts given by you of the above affair, I mast (and I believe I am in a pasiticn to do so) take exception to a portion of the one you gave last Saturday. The " defence" of " one who went "is not absolutely correct. Lot me explain. That par- ticular individual must not forget the fact tint on the Sat- urday night referred to N e., the day he says he returned from Wales), he distinctly told the new organist, amongst expressions of sympathy from others also, and in the pre- sence of at least a dozen members of the late choir, that e' he regretted under the circumstances he was afraid no further action could be taken," or some words to that effect. This took place outside the church gates, and as the night wan rather a cold one the organist invited them into the church. In response to that invitation some five or six (certainly not more) went inside, including one scheduled member. The remainder refused to go inside, thinking (as all bad apparently made up their minds) it would simply be a waste of time to discuss the matter further. It was then and there (iaeide the church) that the rest of the mem- bers were thrown overboard, for they had gone away having •ovary faith in their colleagues. So much for the member's statement that " after consultation with many of the mem- bers he expressed himself satisfied, and declared to them 'his intention to take his place in the choir on Sunday." La regard to another part et your statement you say that '" if the Rector refused to meet the choir, they should de- cline to take pert in the service on the following Sunday." This, sir, is a very important point, for this " gentleman " makes it one of his miserable excuses far resuming his posi- tion in the choir stalls. That statement also is not correct, and in proof of what I assert, I need only refer to the origi- nal resolution, the latter part of which reads " taking into consideration existing circumstances, they reluctantly feel compelled to decline taking part in the services of the church ' until such times' as the Rector and wardens meet the choir with a view to coming to a mutual understand- ing." This was agreed to unanimously, as the very fact that every member absented himself on the Sunday showed. As for the individual in question saying that "he proposed and framed the resolution in his capacity as chairman," tha la all moonshine. Tree, he put it to the meeting in the way he says, but at the same time he expresed his opinion that it was the only course left open, and also said that he felt very much aggrieved at the insult offered. I contend then that he did actually propose it and WAS a consenting party to it. You refer also to a meeting at the house of one of the members last week. I am in a position to say that this meeting did take place on the Tuesday evening, and was of a very stormy character indeed. Nothing definite was arrived at, and as it was stated that the Rector and wardens were consulting together that very evening, it was suggested by the old member who resumed duty last Sunday,, and at whose instigation the meeting was called, that an adjourn- ment should take place until the Friday evening, in order (es he put it) to see what came of the meeting at the Rec- ta rev. After some discussien this was put by another mem- ber: in the form of a resolution, duly seconded, and carried; and with that understanding the meeting separated. Ac- cordingly on the Friday evening some oi the members pre- sented themselves at the appointed time, and were very much astonished to be informed in a contemptuous manner that no such adjournment had ever taken place If that was sot should like ti know how it was that a certain sec- tion were apprised that no meeting would be held, and it is passing strange that some six or eight (whom no doubt they wished to shake of) heard not a single word in any Shape or form. This is only one amongst many tricks these worthies who ressmed duty last Sunday have played—as neat a bit of trickery as ever was planned, you can truly call it; and indeed was well carried out.

They cannot, however, be congratulated, for they have -forfeited their own self-respect, have entirely lost the confi- dence of the majority of the congregation ; and in the face of tbese plain facts how they can enjoy their present position is a mar—el to yours truly, Warringtom, 29th Oct., 1884. GRONNY SLOPER. THE WARRINGTON CORPORATION AND THE SHIP CANAL.

Sir,—ln the colon-in; of your issue of Saturday last, there was a letter anonymously signed "Libra. This is I the none de plume of the gentleman, an employe of the I Pearson, Knowles, Limited, who attempted to second Mr. Morris's proposition at the ratepayers' meeting, but to whom the ratepayers refused to listen ; they refused to be charmed by the voice of either the proposer or the seconder. That the seconder was " Libra " I know for a certainty ; for he obtained the information contained in the letter rela- tive to the rateable values of the premises occupied by those who addressed the meeting; besides, he speaks so profes- sionally of 'felts and credits. He has attempted to ridicule me in the estimation of my fellow-townsmen. I take no exception to this, but the means he has adopted are not fair. Ile informed your readers that I am k poor man, because I live in a house rated at only £l9 per annum, and the amount that I should be called upon to pay, supposing the rate of 2d in the pound be ilevied, would be 39 2d. Now his inference is clear, which s this: that because I live in a cottage and not in a mansion my opinions upon the Ship Canal are not worthy the attention of my fellow-townsmen. Surely this is a ridiculous mode ot argument to adopt, to disprove the validity of my arguments in favour of the rate of 2cl in the pound towards the Ship Canal. For what are the facts

of the case as far as regards " Libra " and the Canal? Why not very long ago," Libra" was my neighbour; and had he occupied the same house still, he would have been called upon to pay 43 23 as against my 33 2d. But now he 'lives in the country and won't be called upon to pay any- thing! For a man who will pay nothing, to ridicule one I who will pay something towards the Ship Canal,out of the rates, is a breach of good taste, and A gross error of judg- ment. The other personal references in the letter, are only On a par with thcse of myself. My reason for actively supporting the Ship Canal is, that I am one of two responsible managers of a manufactory that makes from 100 to 120 toes of wire per week, 90 tons of which are ex- ported. Considering " Libra " is a man who does not neglect Sunday duties, I marvelled at the blood-thirety termination of his epistle, " The opponents to the rate I hope mean war to the knife and knife to the hilt," "Libra " be advised; that twaddle and personalities do not constitute sound argu- ments ; and when next you write upon this subject, have the courage to subscribe your name and give the public the reasons of your opposition, of which at present they are ignorant. —Yours respectfully, GEORGE WOODS. Bewsey-terrace, Warrington, October 28, 1884.

Sir, —I have read all that has appeared in your "spicy paper" about the Ship Canal, and as now the question of eompulsory contribution is to the fore, there is one view of the subject I should like to bring before my fellow work- men, that I have never seen advanced yet, and I hope that one of your many readers may dispose of it satisfac- torily. The cause of the construction of the Canal is said to be the heavy charges incurred by shipping at Liverpool, and the heavy rates of carriage between that place and Man. chester. As a working-man very much interested in the subject, I asked myself the question—How are these char- ges and rates expended, as according to railway reports. only a small share is paid to shareholders, being at best but 7 per cent of the whole? I have also seen it stated that the Canal is to pay more than this ; so that any reduction in the rates will not come out of the returns for capital. If not out of capital, it must come out of labour in some form or other. I suppose it will be that where the present system employs 20 men, the Canal will employ two, throwing the other 18 upon an already overstocked labour market. There is to be a very great saving in shipping goods. Instead Of paying men to unship and reload into waggons at Liver- pool; instead of paying railway companies to employ a lar- rger number of men, goods are to be taken right up to Man- chester, throwing a great number of men out of employ. tient, and upon the market which is said to be ruled by the law of supply and demand, and placing working. men more than ever at the mercy of the capitalists. • I have beard men talk of the amount of work it will bring into the district. So it will no doubt whilst being constructed, and a large number of men also, but when it Is finished all these men will toe waiting for work, the same as it is in our works at the present time—three men for one man's work—with the result that "if you don't like it you may go." What is it that has made it 53? Not altogether the law of demand, but in a great measure these great labour saving schemes, of which this is one. What has the employment of machinery by agriculturists done? For every skilled artizan it may have found labour, it has seat a dozen off the land into the shops to reduce the value of that labour. What has that great steel invention by Bessemer done? Found one man work and thrown 20 men upon the mar- ket; shut up entirely a great number of iron works through the country, thrown thousands of ironworkers out of em- ployment, and reduced the wages of those at work to the last degree. In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread all thy days "; the man who doesn't work, shouldn't eat, is the modern rendering, and, say the rich, we will do without manual labour as much as possible, and we can't pay men to do nothing, so what mast he do? Why starve ! Strange, that the working•men of Lancashire should help them to do it ! With my poor education, and very small knowledge of great economic principles. I don't see why working-men should rush so madly into these things. Now as to levying the ratepayers of Warrington in in support of it. I consider this to be most unwise and improper. Where has the enormous sum already subscri- bed gone to, and not a shovel or spade bought yet ? And are we to find money to go the earns way? Let the people of Warrington set the value of the men to the town who oppose this, against the value of the men who support it. T. whom does the town owe its prosperity more than to Messrs. Bleckly, Rvlands, and Crosfield ? What would the town have been to-day but for their energy? As working- men we ought to support theca, knowing that every penny expanded in or upon a work comes out of a fund of which our wages are the residue.—Yours, Jrc., T. T.

Sir,—Were it possible to calm the troubled waters of the Ship Canal question by a liberal use of oil, I would willingly make the effort, but I am afraid that, as some of us are now called upon to pony out "that would be impossi- ble. There has beed an impression abroad that the people of Warrington to a man were in favour of the scheme. I suppose that with the exception of one large property owner —Mr. Diggle—the impression would be a pretty correct one at the present time. When one looks through the corm- pondem in your last issue, it is found that certain fortunate individuals, owners of property, object to paying anything towards the scheme, or snail I say object to hav- ing a rate of 2d. in the £ levied, because, say these lucky ones, "it will fall unequally upon the people." The sbop• keeping class, property owners, direct ratepayers, and last, but not by any means the least, the mill owners, are the parties who will have to pay. The compound householders, lo•lgers, and certain unclassified individuals who helped to swell the Public Hall meeting will get off scot free. . . . . . . . . •

Objection is also taken to the application of the borough funds for prernoting private schemes. Well, now it seems to me that just here I find the opportunity for pouring a little oil out, in the shape of confessing at once, that there is an apparent injustice. But I ask the sufferers to consider a moment what the question is at issue. I must candidly confess that not one of the speakers at the recent meeting touched the sore point, yet at the same time each speaker was a ratepayer. Well, what is the chief and most important point at issue? Why this, that we, the people of Warrington, must be up and doing, or our town will become like the town of Drou- field, in Derbyshire, a deserted one. And then what will become of mill owners, property owners, and indeed all of us? Certainly there is ne immediate fear of this, but then, as our forefathers worked and thought for us, so mist we make wise provision for those who, will follow ue. May I give one example as to benefits to be derived from having a navigable canal ? A barque recently arrived at Garston with 2,500 bales of cotton on board for Oldham; 50 representatives from that town went to view the ship. The vessel was chartered to Garston in order to escape the Liverpool ctrarges and dues. The saving is nearly £3 per 100 bales, or on the whole cargo nearly £200; I should think no more argument is needed to prove the great necessity for improved means of transit. Our friends will, lam sure, all allow this, but, ear they, why should we be called upon to pay sums of meter,' towards promoting a private scheme? I deny that the scheme is a private one. It is national in ie importance, and it is a necessity for tie future welfare of this part of England. If the scheme should by any mischance become a private one it will be to the everlasting disgrace of the towns immediately interested. Should it be se, what is to hinder the railway companies from absorbing it in their voracious maws as they have done the canals? "dreads the socialistic tendencies of the scheme, and thinks it may lead to "business being done by the com- munity for the community." I think this quoits possible myself, and if it should prove to be one of the means lead- ing towards a more equable distribution of the werld's wealth, we must all hail it as a blessing. A " ileavily-tesed Cottage Owner" looks upon the scheme es being good because it will lead to laree sums of money being expanded in our neighbourhood. If this be so his property will rise in value. By the way, I wonder how many cottage owners there are who will be called upon to pay more than LI towards the scheme? lam bound to pull up at this point. " Libra " steps in and says "Prin- ciples are at stake," and I should guess that for this prin- ciple he is willing to pay, and make others pay, another Id in the .£ or else why talk of "War to the knife, and the knife to the hilt." I hope he has reflected since seeing his letter in print, or lam afraid he will come under the same heading as Mr Diegle of being not worthy of his country. " Libra " is hardly gentlemanly in his references to in- dividuals. Ido not admire Dr. Mackie in scarcely any of , hi doings, but I held that on the Ship Canal question he deserves well of Warrineton, and I cannot see how advertis-1 ing with hie paper is likely to reimburse him his contribu- tion of £l,OOO. Cannot " Libra " see the fallacy in his re- marks? Four gentlemen are named who in. the whole will contribute .£3 as 21. I take his figures without question— as householders I take it. Against these we have ten firms assessed at £14,083, and four of them on £10,941. Now, I ask " Libra " to be fair and give us the individual assess- ment of the active masagers of the four firms. Is it not a fact that the gentlemen reside miles away from Warrington? But I hold " Libra " makes a serious departure from his own beloved "principle." As we appoint members of Par- liament to arrange our Imperial taxes, so we appoint local gentlemen to arrange our local taxes; and if the Mayor and other public spirited gentlemen are to be pulled up short, and tileir personal expenditure to be paraded as a reason why they should not take part in such public mat- ters as will benefit the town, we shall soon have cabala cry- ing out— this, cries one side of the council hall, Do just the reverse the minority bawl; The result of all is, Ulm' this terrible tongue war, There's nothing done for the town until the town's done for. "Look before von Leap " in his letter makes one think that the uniformity of thought in the four letters contribu- ted could only result from pre-arrangement. There is a slight relief from this in the advice given at the close of his letter. It is 80 good I will repeat it. "At any rate we should make onselves as safe as possible by following the example of the Manchester Corporation, and before we part with our money we should obtain from the Provisional Committee of the Ship Canal a guarantee which will in- demnify us against any liability whatever beyond the pay- ment of the levy referred to." I quite agree with this; at the same time it is a contingency scarcely likely to arise. A few more words, and I have done. Two printed sheets were circulated at the meeting, one of which was signed by Mr. Bleckly. I think we remember him as a guardian of the poor, and being interested in stone-breaking. What we shall remember him fcr in the future will be that he, in our Council Chamber, made the grandest speech in favour of the Ship Canal that has yet been delivered in Warrington ; websthat i;ntbbiast a titr speecellualal l°bgtacles were swept away like cob- round was found whereon he and Alderman Joseph Davies could stand and pose as true War- rington patriots; that out of the enthusiastic Council meet.

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 1, 1884.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 1, 1884.

ing grew a Ship Canal scheme propaganda that caused Mr. Davies to have a Ship Canal office in the Market-place, and ultimately took the owner of the "Old Warps "on a lectur- ing course through the town. Who of the Workingmen's Committee that remembers the graphic and most interesting speeches made in the Chamber of Commerce by Mr. Alder- man Davies or Mr. Thomas Morris, in favour of the scheme, but what must feel somewhat dumbfounded at their present attitudes? What mighty State secret is there behind it all ? Mr. Bleckly, I am afraid, holds the secret of it all,and could a tale usfold. With Mr. Davies Lain most astonished. I , remember the meeting in the National School, when with pointer in band he so eloquently urged upon the people the necessity that existed for giving their support to the scheme. Could it be that he saw a possibility of weaving in with his Old Warp some new weft, and so coming out with a piece that would grgify even his self-interest? A smaller document, bearing voar own imprint, was cir- culated at the meeting. This was signed by representatives of fifteen firms, who were kind enough to tell us that 'trade is bad in every department." We working-men know this, and we also know that our employers give as a reason for this that the railway charges run away with all the profits. With what little logic we possess, we argue thus: Thit were it not fcr exhorbitant railway charges our employers could successfully compete with foreign manu- facturers ; that inasmuch as the railway interest is so powerful, so wide in its ramifications, employers do not care to wage war with it, preferring rather to reduce their work- men's wages, it being so much easier, and resulting to the capitalists benefit in a double sense, viz., as investor and as employer. In conclusion, I must say that I think very few ' compund householders would refuse to pay this extraprdin- -1 ary rate if asked by his landlord.
CLIFFORD DIX.

as strong before.—By Mr. Bellamy: When he first com- plained to Jones, Jones was at the still about a hundred yards from the chamber. He (witness) did not know that the chamber door was open then.—By Mr. Handley : Five minutes would elapse before he went to the chamber door after first smelling the gas. There wee only one man in charge of the bleaching powder chambere, and that was Jones. There were several men to help him. John Faraworte, of 31, Shaw street, and bleaching Pow- der maker at the works, said he had been employed there five years. His duties were to work the stills and the pow- der chambers. he and Jones worked alternate shifts. There were no printed directions for him to work by. He had four chambers to attend to, and one of them was the one where the accident happened. He had full control over the making of the powder. He described the process of manu- facturing chloride of lime, and stated that when the lime had absorbed all the chlorine gas it could do the chamber having previously been disconnected from the still, the re- mainder of the gas was drauelited up the chimney by a flee, Iso that there would be no gas in the chamber when the door was opened. When the chamber was connected with the chimney, they eased the door farthest from the con- nection, by slacking the wedges, and opening the door with a bar, from half an inch to an inch wide. The cross bars he always left in. He had had no instruction, but worked accor- ding 0 his experience. He thought Jones had been at the , works three months. .He could not tell whether the mana- ger gave him any instructions. When he (witness) went to ' the works, there was a foreman over the chambers who in- structed him, but he learnt mostly from his own experience. ' Before the accident happened he did not thick it would be , . so dangerous to open the door of the chamber.—By Mr. Handley : It was the usual practice to ease the door at midnight, when they could not see whether the , lime had absorbed the gas or not. The gas could not Is seen in the night. Occasionally be had seen chambers opened without the connection being made with the chimney, when there had been DO gas on.— '1 he Coroner: Then you would not do that at night.—Wit- nem : Only in the day time. The connection is always pat ; on at night, and especially in winter time.—By Mr. , Handley : Jones and he were responsible for the emission of 3 gas.—By the Coroner: Be did not know whether Jones • would have the necessary experience to know how much ) gas was unabsorbed.—Mr. Linaker asked whether in the • plant there was at the works, there would be any chance of - an accident of this kind, if a man used ordinary care.— ) IVitness repliea in the negative.—Mr. Linaker: Using , ordinary care in easing the door is there an appreciable emis- sion of gas P—No; because there is a suction of air.—Mr. I King: Then was it owing to timelessness that gas escaped this time P—Very likely it was owing to the door opening I too far.—By Mr. Linaker: He had three men under him in I the night time, and he considered them quite sufficient.—By ' the Coroner: There was only himself and Junes to look after ' the chambers. The other three mee were engaged at the ' plant for generating the chlorine gas, but when he required ; them they must aid him. They were within call. • Dr. McDougall deposed that about two o'clock on Satur- day morning last he went to the works and in the time- keeper's office he saw one of the children. It me dead. In ; the foreman's house he saw the other child, which was also • dead. He had made a post mutual examination of both • bodies. He was of opinion that the cause ot death was suf- L focation, most probably produced by a gaseous poison. . -. Charles Jones, of Nelson-street, said he was stelman and I fereman at the works, and had been there about three I months. About a quarter past one on Saturday morning I he went to put a draught on the chamber to draw the gas I off. He opened the bottom of the door to give it vent. . He jerked the bar and the door flew away too far. He l tried to get the door back again, but he had to run away • because he found himself smothering. He ran to get a I drink of tea. Atherton told him something would have • to be done, and he (witness) went back again and tried • to close the door, but could not. Atherton then aided him. ' He removed both bars before he opened the door. He 1 , always had removed them, but at ether times the door bad been at the command of the bar. A man named Findlay i showed him how to work the chambers when he first went I there. He was paid Sc per shift, and He made six shifts a i week. So far as he was aware the manager had never seen i him open a chamber. He had been engaged in the same • kind of work for the last eleven or twelve years at Widnes, IVestor, and Runcorn. He had never been warned not to . take the bars from the door. At the works where he was • employed, Widnes, there was no bars. The door was I knocked opened and the gas allowed to escape into the air. i He considered the arrangement for letting the gas off at the [ Alkali Company's works a very good one. Findlay told him I that the bars were removed, and then the door eased. He (witness) generally opened the chamber four hours after he eased the door. He had no instructions when to do this. 1 The inquest, which had lasted about four hours, was then I adjourned. ADJOURNED INQUEST: THE VERDICT. The adjourned inquiry was resumed before Mr. J. E. Woreley on Thursday afternoon. The fi-st witness called was Mr. George B. Anderson, of Palm Cottage, Greenway- road, Runcorn, who said he had been manager of the Run- corn works of the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Company for 15 months. He engaged Jones on tbe 17th August to take charge of the bleaching powder plant, and manage the still. Prior to his taking entire charge, he had him for two days with Findlow, whose duties were to take down the doors in the presence of a foreman. Findlow thoroughly understood draughting, and he presumed be gave Jones instructions: During the time Jones was with Findlow there was no drauglating done, but Jones was sent to Runcorn from Wes- ton as a practical man. He did not know as a matter of fact whether Jones knew how to draught a chamber or not. In Findlow's time there was a foreman who had charge of this department. Jones took his plate. It would not be right for Jones to take the bars from the chamber door before he draughted the chamber ; nor for the doors to be knocked dowse and allow the gas to escape into the air. He should not consider it a very good arrangement for the bars to be taken out and the doors then closed. ft is quite- possible for the dmughting to be done efficiently with the-bars off, but he should not allow it to be done if he were aware of it. —By Foreman : He hod been accustomed tee have charge of bleaching pewder pilot previous to corning to Runcorn. He considered the plant at the Runcorn works' to be better than usual. To each chamber there were atmospheric exhaust pipes, and they were connected either in another chamber, or the chimney, never with the aie.—The Foreman asked if it would not be possebie to have a pipe to let in air, so that the chlorine gas, when the chamber was furnished, might be expelled without opening the door.—Witness said it was quite possible, and was cross-examined at length on other points. At the request of Mr. Linaker, John Findlow, of Halton-roaJ, labourer at the company's work', was called, and said he remembered Jones- coming to the works. Mr. Anderson ordered him to show Jones round, and he did so. He did not tell him anything about closing the doors. He supposed he had had experience, as he knew he had been engaged in a similar work before. The Coroner said there were about six witnesses present who would tell how they suffered from the effects of the gas, but that fact was patent to thereeall, and he thought there was no necessity to call them. The jury concurred, and the Deputy Coroner then summed up the evideuee. The jury retired, and after an hour's absence they returned into court; and Mr. W. Hendley, the foreman, read the verdict as follows :—Oar verdict is that the two children, Thomas Spencer and Grace Spencer, were suffocated by an emission of cialbrine gas from nurneer four chamber of the bleaching powder plant of the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Cempanre 'Works, at Runcorn, such emission of chlorine gas being due to an error of judgment and by misadventure on the part of the man in charge of the chamber, by name- Charles' Josses, ,in opening the door of the said chamber while the- chamber :was strongly charged with chlorine gas. The jury, being assured by the evidence that the appliances in use at the bleaching powder plant at the said works are equal to and in ,many eases superior to those in use at many other works of a like character, strongly recommend that as daylight is 'absolutely necessary to a certain knowledge of the absorp- tion or expulsion of chlorine gas from bleaching powder ohambers, that such chambers should miles be opened in the daylight, and after carefod. inspection by the manager. They ,further recommend that each chamber should be provided with an arrangement for the admission of-atmospheric air, so as to render the partial opening of the door, for the pur- pose of drafting, unnecessary. They also suggest that prince-4 regulations, eauctioned by the Ewa' Government Board, should be placed' in the hand e of every bleaching ,powder man, stating the danger and duties of his employ- ment, and that no man should be employed in such dan- gerous, work without his capability having been tested by the manager- -I.' The Deputy Coroner said be concurred irethe verdict. He hoped that the recommiindations of the fury would receive that attention they most decidedly deserved. ' Mr. Linaker said he had been instructed by the general manager of the works to say how keenly he felt the result of the accident. No human aid could restore the children; )but the manager had given instructions that the motber was to be taken away and attended to. The only thing they could do was to give a substantial sum to the father, to repay him for the great anxiety oe mind which be had suffered. The proceedings, which had lasted four boors and a half then terminated.
