The members of the Fire Brigade, with the hose and reely proceeded to the spot, and the outbreak wee put down with very little difficulty. In the Chancery Division; on Wednesday, Mr. Justice Pearson made an order that some children of a deceised naval captain should be brought up in the Protestant faith. The mother of the children was a Roman Catholic, and be- fore marrying her the c sptain promised in writing that bile children should be educated in that faith, but he after• wards changed his mind. SHOCKING CHARGE AGAINST A. GIIARDIAN.—A coroner'el jury on Monday returned a verdict of "manslaughter" against William Lea, a farmer near Whitchurch, and his wife, who had, wh:lst driving home in a trap, knocked down and fatally injured an old woman named Davies. Lea, who is a guardian for the Whitchurch Union, La charged with having beep drunk at the time. Div Wiaarr Faro:se—The frauds on the Wigan Cor- poration by its late treasurer, Holt, appear from a report just presented by the burgesses' auditors to be much more serious than hitherto disclosed. The auditors now put Holt's defalcations to over £13,000, exclusive of whatever frauds nuy be discovered in the collection of the funds now ap- pearing as owing for private improvements,
THE WARRINGTON CHIEF CON- STABLE'S REPORT.

The Chief Constable of Warrington has just issued his annual report on the police establishment and the state of ; crime for the year ended Septeraber 29th, from which we , give the following copious extracts :—The number of per- I sons taken into custody, and summoned, and dealt with summarily, is 2,379; last year, 2,280; being an increase of 99 for this year. Of these 344 males and 166 females were discharged, and I 465 males and 404 females were convicted; 1,339 males and 471 females were resident ; 420 males and 99 females were non-resident; 1.032 males and 220 females were English ; 755 males and 345 females were Irish ; 13 males and 5 females were Scotch; and 9 naales were foreign- ers, 639 males and 320 females could neither read nor write; 1.068 males and 249 fern ales could do one or the other, or both, imperfectly; 41 males and 2 females could read and write well ; the remaining 39 males being well educated. Thirty-seven persons were proceeded against for assaults on the police, of whom 3 were discharged and 34 convicted ; 233 for common assaults, of whom 115 Were dis- charged and 108 convicted ; 151 for breaches of the peace, of whom 31 were discharged and 120 convicted; 24 for cruelty to animals, of whom 3 were dissbarged and 21 con- victed; 366 parents who neglected to send their children to school were proceeded against, 46 being discharged and 320 convicted; 149 persons were proceeded against for breaches of Employers and Workmen's Act, 1875, 66 being discharged and 83 convicted; 634 persons were had up for drunkennees 90 being discharged and 574 convicted. For offences against Local Acts and Borough Bye Laws 193 persons were proceeded against, 31 being discharged and 162 convicted; 70 persons were had up for neglect of family, 10 being discharged and 60 convicted; 115 persons were taken into custody, dm., for larceny, 14 being discharged and 101 convicted. For offences against the Vagrant Act, 86 were taken into custody. Other minor offences not specified in this report make up the total of 2,370 persons proceeded against summarily. The indictable offences are 59, for which 29 persons were proceeded against, viz :—Three for "shooting at, wounding, stabbing, dim ," 2 miles discharged and 1 male committed for trial; burglary and housebreak- ing, 2 males and 2 females committed for trial; robbery on highway, 4 males and 1 female committed for trial; horse- stealing, I discharged; larceny fro,n person, 5 males and 1 female cammitted for trial ; simple larceny, 1 female dis- charged and 2 males and 1 female committed for trial ; lar- ceny by servant at Post Office, 1 male committed for trial ; frauds and attempts, 2 males discharged and 2 males com- mitted for trial; attempted suicide, 1 female bound over to appear if called upon. The only appreciable differences existing between the figures of this and last year are : Corn. moo assaults, 31 more this year; Elementary Education Act, 17 less; drunkenness, 40 lees; Local Acts, ate., 52 more; neglect of fainily, 7 less; larceny, 13 more; vagrancy, 47 less. The number of persons brought in and convicted of drunkenness on Sundays is 43, 26 being residents and 17 non-residents. Time offence book shows that 162 petty larcenies and indictable offences have been reported during the year; property to the amount of £392 8s 31 having been stolen, of which £2lO 10s 61 was re- covered, whilst £173 17s 9d remains still to be accqunted for. The chief of these robberies consisted of three of cash, £5O, £2l, and £2O, unrecovered; one of furniture, £47 101, recovered ; three of goods, furniture, and tools, about £2O in each case, all recovered ; a gold watch, £l7, unrecovered; and a number of watches, £l6 103, partly recovered. 107 warrants have been issued and 147 executed. The value of the property stolen during 1883 was £214 12s 10d; re- covered. £57 Os 94; and unrecovered, £1573s Id. War- rants issued in 1883 171, executed 152. The reparts of sudden, violent, and unnatural deaths number 71, of which 21 were referred to the Registrar, or were certified by doctors after inquiry by the police; 50 were inquired Into by the coroner, and the following verdicts given : 19 persons died from natural Causes ; 17 from accidents;. 4 committed suickle ; 3 misadventure ; 2 found drowned, 1 found dead on the railway; these three open verdicts; 1 hydrophobia,' rupture, I excessive drink- ing, and 1 fatty degeneration of the heart. There are with- in the borough 87 licensed victuallers, 48 beerhouse keepers, and 71 off-license holders, including grocers and liquor dealers, and a refreshment house keeper. Two licensed vic- tuallers, 2 beerhouse keepers, and 3 off-license holders were summoned ; the cases against the licensed victuallers being dismissed; 1 beerhouse keeper was *fined ss, and the other paid costs, 4s 64; 1 off-license holder was fined £5 and costs; 1 fined in costs, 19s 63 : and I dismissed. Thirty- nine transfers have been made. 124 pedlars' certificates have been issued, for which £3l was received; and 12 chim- ney sweepers' ditto, for which £1 IN was received, and these amounts have been duly paid over to the county tree. starers of Lancaster and Chester. The sum of £llO 15s has been collected from the parents of children detained in re- formatory and industrial schools during the year ended September 29th last, and duly remitted to the Rome Offica. There are 33 children detained in these schools at the pre- sent time. Ten convicts on ticket-of-leave, and 15 persons under police supervision, have reported themselves during the year. Three of th• former and three of the latter con- tinue to reside in the borough. The tramps booked this year are 5,223, as against 5, 763 last year. The acreage of the borough is 1,442; population in 1831, 41,456; estima- ted population now, 44,500. The police establishment con- sists of 42 members, viz,, 1 chief constable, 1 chief inspector and clerk, 2 uniform inspectors, 4. sergeants, and 31 con- stables, the salaries and pay of which amounted to £3,248, 6s fdd clothing, , £267 12e 7d; station-house, books, and stationery, £193 17s 11d; miscellaneous charges, £39 17s sd; total cost, £3,749 14s 7d. The changes in the force have been eight constables dismissed and 1 resigned. The number a depredators, offenders, and suspected persons at I large in the borough is 125; number of houses of bad char- acter, 20: The whole force has had 255 days leave of ab- sence, and those absent through sickness have had 408 days amongst deem. including men hart whilst upon duty. The sum of £lO3l 6cl has been received for extra service of the police at theatre, concerts, balls, sports, etc., during the past•year. In aadition to the numbes of borough prisoners , already mentioned, there have been brought in 29 persons charged witheaffences in other towns and acceunted for in our foreign charge-book, 63 persons brought in by, and for the Lancashire County Police, 1 taw Cheshire County Police, and 16, by the County Court officers. One hundred and sixty-nine persons have been surnmioned for non-pay- ment of rates. With regard to the mil tray on the march I through Wan ington, 18 officers, 391 non-commissioned offi- cers and men,and 465 horses have been provided with bil- let accommodatioi for one or two nights, as the CA3O re- quired during the year.

div.head: TERRIBLE ACCIDENT AT A RUNCOHN
div.p: TERRIBLE ACCIDENT AT A RUNCOHN
CHEMICAL WORKS. TWO CHILDREN SUFFOCATED.

lAn accident attended with shocking results, occurred at the Runcorn works of the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Co., early on Saturday morning. About one o'clock, Charles ' Jones, foreman of the bleaching powder department, procee- ded to one of the chambers in order to clear it of chlorine gas ready for the " packers " in the morning. He connec- ted the chamber with the chimney by means of an earthen- ware pipe, and he had then to slightly open the door to allow of the admission of air. The door, a ponderous affair, is held in its position by a crane erected upon the top of the chambey, and is closed by two bars, fixed into staples lin the wall, and by a screw at the top and the bottom. It is the usual practice to unfasten the screws, take the wedges . from the bars, and then by means of a crowbar to open the door from half an inch to an inch wide. The bars are left : in and prevent any wider aperture being made. Jones, how- ever, cast oft both bars, inserted his lever, and gave a "jerk." Immediately the door swung open to a much wider extent than was necessary, and chlorine gas escaped in large quan- tities. Jones attempted to close the door again, but feeling himself being overcome by the noxious gas, he ran away to a place of safety. For five minutes the gas was rushing forth in de se volumes, poisoning the atmosphere for a con- ! siderable distance around. Lying in the canal, and moored 1 near to the works, was the flat "Ant," in the cabin of which ; was the captain, Charles Spencer, his wife, and two children. Swpaesntee7r feelingterrified to afl find thatokin sensation, own; s got r r ounpnte dd le) crka, and which " took his breath away." He quickly descended into the cabin, seized his two children named Thomas and I Grace, and ran along the canal bank followed by his wife, all the family being nearly naked. At length they arrived at another flat, and took refuge in the cabin. But the last- , dious gas still pursued them, and the children died there, while Mrs. Spencer became insensible Aid arrived, how- ever, and the whole family was removed. Brown, the cap- tain of the flat, and his wife and child alsa made goad their escape. The deadly gas penetrated as far as Bridge-street, 1 and many people came under its deleterious influence, and it is stated that one man was so affected with the fumes that he fell down in the street. Many of the labourers on the works fled from the place, but not before they had been partially "gassed." Mrs. Spencer, who was in a very dangerous state on Saturday, is DOW in a fair way towards convalescence, under the care of Dr. MacDougall. She was visited at the earlier part of the week by Mr. , Charles Wigg, the managing director of the Alkali Com- pany, who promissd to defray the expenses attendant upon the funeral of the unfortunate children, and to pay the costs of her complete restoration to health. The bereaved parents expressed themselves very grateful for Mr. IVigg's kindness.

THE INQUEST. The inquest on the bodies of the children was held at the Court Room, Bridge-street, on Monday afternoon, before Mr. J. E. Worsley, the deputy coroner. Mr. W. Handley was the foreman of the jury. Mr. J. Burton appeared for the father of the deceased, and Mr. W. H. Linaker repre- sented the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Works There were also present Mr. A. E. Fletcher, chief inspector under the Alkali Acts, Mr. Ballard, the district inspector, Mr. Charles Wigg, managing director of the Alkali Company, Mr. Anderson manager of the works, and Mr. P. Speakman. Supt. Leah watched the proceedings on behalf of the police. The jury spent about half an hour inspecting the scene of the accident, and, on re-assembling, the Deputy Coroner said he thought the vetclict the jury would give would resolve itself into this. If they found that Jones was properly supplied with everything to conduce to the public safety at the works where he was employed, and that be was not doing his duty, and neglecting the uses of the safeguards provided, the jury would have no alternative but to corns to the conclusion that be was guilty of manslaughter, and they would 30 commit him. If, on the other hand, they found that he was obeying instructions from others, or that he was within the limits of his employment, or tat he was not supplied with those precautions which rendered hie employment safe, they would not than destare that verdict. The Deputy Coroner informed the jury that a very grave respensibility rested upon them, and a very important question noon their verdict. The safety of people in their beds, whether in houses or in Mats, depended spon the man- agement and control of the powerful gases which. were manufactured in such works- as the Runcorn Alkali CO'M• pany's works, and he boped the jury would chs their duty fearlessly, and without any regard to what the ultimate re- sults of their verdict might be.

Charles spencer, father of the deceased, said he- lived at Welsh row, Gilbert street, Runcorn. He was eraplbyedi aa 'captain of the flat "Antrowned by Mr. Philip Speakman. On Friday night the flat eras lying in the canal opposite 'the bleaching powder loading place of the Runcorn•Soao and Alkali Company's works. He and hie wife and two children were in bed in the cabin. About one o'clock on Saturday morning he was lying awake and eceelled gas coming in ;the cabin. Ina short time the smell became stronger, and he weiat on deck. He then returned into the cabin and took the children out, telling his wife to make the best of' her way out, as there was something wrong. The gas "took his breath awayr When they had got a hundred yards- away from the dat they were quite "spent," and they went into the cabin of a boat, of which.a man named Browzrwas the captain. He wakened Brown, who went for assistance. iHe did not remember anything further. He did not re- member whether the children were, alive or dead vvherr he. I arrived at the boat. When he regained consciousness he wag in the timekeeper's lodge with one of the children by his side. He and his wife were then taken into the house of Mr. Anderson, the manager, and treated very kindly. After the children had been seen by the doctor, they were removed to his own house in Gilbert street. All the time he and his- wife were almost naked, as they had no time to dress. By Mr. Handley: There was gas in Brawn's boat. The gam "followed them along." Brown's wife and child were on, board,.but they got oat.—By Mr. King : Brown's boat was- a hundred yards (ruin his, and was further from the works.— By the Coroner :—His boat was moored where it was ready for him, to discharge his cargo in tbs. morning.—By Mr. Follett He had never stayed there at night time before. Jbseph Brown, of Welsh-row, Runcorn, datman, said he was captain of the fiat Beetle, owned by Mr. Clarke, of Weston Point. He described being awakened, and Mrs. Spencer asking to be allowed to go into the cabin with her two children. Ile told her to go in andssleep with his wife, and he would dress himself and sleep on the locker. He took a•ixtrikl from her and placed it on a form, but it fell off. and then Mrs. Spencer fell to the cabin door. He picked the child up, and putting his head through the "scuttle hole," he saw Spencer standing on the bank gasping for breath. Spencer went down into the cabin, and he (wit- ness) and his wife than began tie cough. Spencer, his wife, and children were lying on the floor insensible, and be, sus- pecting that gas was the cause, got upon deck, but the gas was so 9troog that he fell to the groundi He tried for help, and two men from the works came along. He told them there was a man and his wife and two-children dying in the cabin. He then saw them walking away, each carrying a child,.and Spencer and his wife following. He asked where his wife and child were, and the man told him in the cabin. He then saw his wife with the child in her arms. He took the child from her and covered it with his shirt, but be did • no% know which way to go, as he was unable to tell whether he was walking into the gas or not At length he heard, some one calling "This way," and went is the direction of the voices. In passing the works on previous occasions he bad smelled something strongly, but be could not tell what It was.—By Mr. Fairhurst: He had emelt it strongest most In the early morning. He added that sometimes when he had been passing he had had to get hold of the horse's head in order to get it past. It seemed to be staggering. The flatmen had complained frequently of the gas.—By Linaker: He never smelled the gas so strong as he did on Saturday morning —By Mr. Burton: He had never been told not to tie up his flat up where it was. John Atherton, of 2, Wilson's-row, Runcorn, foreman over the salt cake, department at the Runcorn Soap and Al- kali Company's works, deposed that about one o'clock he smelled gas rather strongly, and be went to Charles Sones, who was in charge of the stills, and asked if he could check the gas a little. He replied that "it would all be over in a minute or two." He went back towards the shed, and met Spencer and his wife gasping for breath. He placed them on board the Beetle, and then went again to Jones and told him he must try to stop the gas. He went to No. 4 chamber and found the door open. Jones closed it, and he (witness) placed a bar across. There were two bars to each chamber deor. The were fixed into staples in the wall. Both bars. when be arrived, were on the grcund.—Mr. King: Could you have gone through the gas P—Witness No.—By Mr. Linaker : The place where he worked was between the chlorine stills and the canal. If chlorine gas came out in any quantity it would interfere with him in his working, and he always complained when there was any undue quan- tity. He had not to complain once a month. He had been at the works three years, and he had newr smelled any gas

THE Garownsur SCHOOL—Thera will be an examination to elect two free scholars to the Grammar School on Wed- nesday, December 17th. Particulars, as to qualitication for the examination, will be found in our advertising colutnns. THE THEATHE.ROYAL—The handsome new theatre will be opened under the patronage of the Mayor and numerous other local gentlemen on Tuesday, The wee de resistance will b 3 the successful drama " Grelly's Money," and the re- ceipts will be given to the Warrington Infirmary. A WIFE BEATER Putostizo.—John Jackson, a young man, was sent to prison for twe months by the Warrington maaistrates on Wednesday for assaulting his wife on the 23rd of October, and he was also ordered to Day 10s. a week towards her support, under a maintenance order, on his release. The evidence showed that he had systematic- ally assaulted his•wife.

THE NEW THEATRE-. ROYAL Briasley Sheridan on Monday applied to the Warrington borough magistrates for a dramatic licence to perform stage plays at the new Theatre erected by him in Scotland-road.—Alderman Davies remarked that he had that morning been to see the theatre, and he thought that it would prove a successful one.—The Mayor, who presided, said that the Bench would grant the license under the Same rules as the one previoesly held by Mr. Sheridan. They wished Mr. Sheridan success in his undertaking. SUDDEN DEATH, AT SAISKEY BRIDGES —On Sunday morn- ing. about seven. o'clock, as a person named Frank Beddall, of Dial-street, Sankey Bridges, was going into the yard of his house he there found a man lying. in a dying condition, groaning, and with one of his hands held out. The man died before medical assistance could be procured. The body was afterwards identified as being that of Robert Slater, 50. years of age. a single man, residing in Lythgoes-lane, War- rington. Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, held an in- quest on the body at the Black Horse nn, Sankey Bridge, on Tuesday afternoon, when the jury returned a verdict of death from natural causes, probably epilepsy accelerated by exposure.

R)w IN SIAVER-SCRERT.—At the. Warrington Borough, Police Court, on Monday, seven boys,,named James Bryer, Martin Brennan, John Brennan. James Lee, Joseph Peel, Thomas, Knockton, and Richard Fairhurst, were summoned for stone-throwing on the night of the 20th inst.—lt appeared that a woman named Lee, residing in Silver-street. was drunk in company with a soldier, and a crowd followed her home. Stones were thrown in consider- able quantities, and serimat damage was done to the house. The boys summoned, with the exception of Lee, were iden- tified as having been concerned in the row. Their defence was that they saw others " heaving " stones and bricks, and did the same.—Lee was consequently discharged, and the others. were fined Is 6d each, including costs —The leniency of the sentence caused the Chief Constable (Mr. Hutt) to express surprise, as the row had been of such a serious nature and at a time when the absence of the police, who were on duty on the mete taken by the torchlight pro- Session, held the same evening, was taken advantageof. SOCTRIVOLITH WITH CROFT SCEIOOL BOARD. The first ,meeting of the newly-elected School _Board for the above place was held on Tuesday. when there were present Messrs R. Owen, N. Taylor, and E. W. Sankey. It was resolved that Joshua Ball, of Southworth Hall, and Mr. Jamee Hunt, of Turret Hall be elected to fill the two vaeant seats to be filled on the Board. It was also resolved that Mr. Hunt be elected chairman for the ensuing three years; that Mr. Ball be elected vice-chairman for the same period: and that Mr. Ball be appointed treasurer to the Board. The Rev. T. P. K.irkinan having resigned the office of clerk to the Board, it was agreed that_Mr. Owen be appointed clerk in his place. It was further agreed that Mrs Peat should be appointed school cleaner on the same terms as her predecessor, and that a school attendance officer be advertised for.—We may men- tion in connection with this Board, that in reply to an °lain- tion made by the Rev. Mr. Kirkrnan, against the validity of certain nomination papers at the recent election on the ground that some of the signatures were not genuine, the Education Department writes that according to the order it was for the returning officer to determine the validity of the nomination, and they had no power to interfere with his , dedsien.

WARRINGT3N CHA3fB ER OF COMMERCE.—A meeting of the Council of the Warrington Charaber of Commerce was held on Monday, when the question of high rates for railway carriages between Warrington and London and other large markets was discussed. It was considered that , the high rates acted adversely against the Warrington i manufacturers, and it was resolved to bring the matter be- fore the different railway companies. At the request of the promoters of the National Inventors' Exhibition of 1885, it was decided to bring that matter before the inventors and manufacturers of the district. The Council nominated Mr. Charles Broadbent, the president, to join the Council of welcome to the exhibitors of the American Exhibition, London, 1836. This was all the business of interest. WYCLIFFE WTI:TAM IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY. A paper on "'be present aspect of commerce in England" was read by Mr. J. W. Botrchier at a meeting of this society, OR Monday evening. Ile referred to the general depression in trade, and the variety of causes by which it had been brought about, expressing his conviction that the trade of England, and especially the iron trade, would never again assume the position of prosperity which obtained about a dozen years ago, except in the event of a Franco-German, or other great war abroad, and as a present remedy he ad- vocated smaller profits for employers, a better state of feel, ing between employers and employed, greater contentment on the part of all classes, and especially a greater practice of temperance and thrift amongst the working-classes. ' Hader such conditions, he was inclined to take a sanguine • view of the aspect of commerce in this country.—Mr. S. Kenyon took a melancholy view of the situation, from I I which he concluded that England as a commercial country was "going to the dogs ;" while Mr. H. Roberts combated this opinien, and stated that instead of the inffated condi- tion of affairs in years gone by the commerce of England . was slowly but surely making progress, and in fair corope- ) tition would hold its own anywhere.—r. Clay also ex- pressed himself in like terms, and the discussion was soon afterwards brought to a close. • ROBBERY IN A Tram.—William Noon, labourer, was on Wednesday charged bdore the borough magistrates with I committing a robbery under singular circumstances. The • charge was that of stealing from the person of Annie Mien- roe, of Liverpool, in a train on the Cheshire Lines-Railway, bltween Manchester and Warrington, a purse containing 12s. I. 10d. in mon-T. Chief Constable Hunt said that the com- plainant was Ann Munroe (22), of Gerard-street, Liverpool. - The prisoner was well known in Warrington. Annie Mien- roe went to Mancnester to meet her sister Marv, who had • served twelve months in Strangeways, and was being re- leased. Mary Munroe got 9s. from the Prisoners' Aid 1 Society, and the two went to the Ceetral Station and booked for Liverpool. They got into a third•class carriage, which the defendant, who was smoking also entered. As they did ! not like his conduct the girls left the compartment, and at ; the time Annie had a parse in her hand, which she after- ! wards missed, and went back to the compartment. As the train was leaving at the time, the case could net be investi gated then, and the two girls rode in the same carriage with the prisoner to Warrington, and they stated that they saw ! him throw the purse out of the window. At Wartington he was given into custody, and subsequent search resulted 1 in the purse being found on a line near the spot where the girls had said he threw it out of the train. As the theft tap- , peered to have been committed blore the train left Man- i chester, the prisoner was•remanded to be handed over to ; the Manchester police, and provision was made for sending ' the girls, who were left penniless, forward to Liverpool. ' CAMBRIDGE UNIVERSITY EX TENSION LECTURES.—The fifth lecture on " Literary Masterpieces." in connection with this movement was delivered in the Lecture-room, at the ' Museum, on Monday evening, by Mr. R. G. Moulton. The lecture was the first of three Which Mr. Moulton intends to give on Goathe's Faust, its subject being "Faust on Easter Eve." Goethe'a Faust, the lecturer said, plight be described as a masterpiece amongst masterpieces, and in approaching that subject he would ask them to remember that they were seeing a specimen of the romantic drama, one of the notable features of which was its perfect freedom and breadth. It ranged over every possible shade of feeling—grave and gay, with the most rapid alternation between; every variety and kind of scene; no limitation of the subjects that may be touched, and no limitation of the number of persons and details which may be crowded into the same piece. These were the features of the romantic drama, and Goethe had carried them to their farthest conceivable limits. Again, the subject with which this drama dealt was the supreme of all human interest, the great contest between good and evil in which man felt himself involved. In the previous lec- ture they had seen that subject treated by Marlow. But Marlow wrote what might be called the childhood of modern life; his was a perfectly simple theoloey, and his magic amounted to no more than spectacular marvels. But in Goethe they had a man whom those who were foremost to- day in all countries delighted to look ipon as their master. In Goethe they were seeing the most universal of all minds , applying itself in the most elastic of all forms of art to the treatment of the most deep-reaching of all possible themes of human interest. In Mephistopheles they had portrayed that most wonderful conception of the spirit of disparagement and depreciation; he was a spirit who evermore denied—the very antithesis of worship. Throughout the whole drama he was continually disparaging and belittling all with whom hiwas brought into centact. Faust's rapturous worship of nature he damped with reminders of the rain and damp of the physical discomforts and reaction that was sure to come. Ile admits that he has no belief even in scepticism itself. In the first part of the drama Mephistopheles nowhere ap- peared, but he was still bihy in the work of temptation, for they saw his hand in all that happened. The temptation was as yet internal and subjective. He took advantage of his spirit nature to work upon the thoughts of Faust. Cho lecturer then treated in detail, in a most interesting manner, the earlier portion of the drama, and in doing se recited various passages with great effect. At the close of the lec- ture the usual comments were made on the papers.

A Warteeitent.TO SHOPICIMPRafft —We requested to caution tradesmen of the town against the practice of ex" posiug their goods outside their shop windows and doors. thus offering an actual temptation to those who are prone to steal and also to those who may not be prone, but being in urgent want, may not be able to resist the temptation placed•directiv in their way. There has been several shop robberies within the last few days. end it is feared' there will be more, if tradesmen are net more-prude:.WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT:—A sitting of this court was held before the judge, Mr. W. Wynne Flaulkes, on Thursday. The only case of interest was one in which a 'Manchester draper, Francis Young, sued William Wells, of I Crewe, for the sum of £2 7,1 6d, as balance of an account for a suit of clothes supplied in 1817.—Mr. A. Browne, solicitor, Warrington, represented the plaintiff, andtthe, de- fendant conducted his own case. He did not dispute tile debt, but pleaded that he was- an infant at the time tbe transaction was made, being under the age of 21'years. I also pleaded the statute of limitation' the debt having been I standing more-than six yeare.—His Honour- saicitdelendanS could not plead infancy as the clothes were necessary., but the statute of limitation really sheltered him. Technically he was not obliged to pay the debt. but as a man of honour he ought to do. Judgment would be given, for defendan't, without costs. The defendant had joined the army soon after the transaction, and went to India, being discharged in June last. MEETING OF BAKERS.—A meeting of the Warrington Branch of the Amalgamated Union of B +kers waa held in a room at the British Workman Coffee-house, liorsemarket- street, Warrington, on Saturday afternoon, when a discus' sion took place OR the trade in- general and the remunera- tion paid to operative bakers. Mr.Davieso master baker of - the town, wag present, and received a cordial welcome, and there were also present rensesentatives from Manchester and Runcorn and a considerable number of operative bakers-Mt. Davies-addressed the meeting, and urged upon all operative bakers the advisability of joining the Union —MT. Jenkins, gen. sec. (Manchester),, mentioned that the Amalgamated Union. had paid £5,000 in funeral claims, and the variooS branches had paid in sick and out-of-place pay WO £90,000 to £lOO,OOO since the year 1861; when the iTniOn was formed. The Warrington Branch, which consiete or 50 or GO members, had in-that period paid £B4Goirr sick sac! out-of-place money. FOurteen new members were initiate,' into the Union.

Lord Roscbery will preside over a great Liberal demon- stration to be held at Epsom on Novembor 20. h. Mr. Campbell Bannerman has been soffering from a cold, but is considerably better.

The Tichborne 'claimant arrived in Leeds on Friday after- noon, and met with an enthusiastic reception from a large crowd which had assembled at the Railway Station. In the evening he addressed a meeting in the Albert Hall..

FRANC- E AND MADAGASCAR7—A volume containing 70 despatches respecting the affairs of Madagascar was issued from the Foreign Office, on Friday evening. Under date Tamatave, July 16th, Consul Graves forwards Lord Gran- ville an interesting account ot his visit to the Malagasy ,capital, where he was received with every attention grid courtesy. Nearly everyone with whom Mr. Graves con- versed expressed a desire for the termination of war. No 'inconvenience on account of the vier is felt by the govern- ing class or the people of the interior. AN. OLD MAN BURNED TO DEATH IN LIVERPOOL.-011 Friday morning a tire broke out in a court in Markham- etreet, in Liverpool, and before the flames could be extin- guished an old nun named Tyskoe was burned to death. The deceased was in the habit of taking a candle with him te-bbd, and to this is ascribed the origic of the fire.—On Friday morning. Messrs. Joseph Heap and Son's rice and stvgar warehouses, in Beckwith:street, Liverpool, were dis- covered to be on fire. The 'upper storeys were greatly in- jured,.the top storey and roof being gutted. Suwon's RAILWAY Comsois.—A collie= between two mineral trains occurred on Friday morning just outside Newport (Mom) on the Great Western Railway. A train from Gloucester was travelling over the loop from the main line to. Pontypool when a heavily laden traiu from Newport Docks bound for Ebbw Vale dashed into it, cat it into halves, and sasashed 15 waggons. Two of the waggons rolled over a high embankment. The permanent way was much. destroyed. The driver and stoker of the Newport train had narrow escapes. The line was blockerl for nine hours.

CANADIAN WHISKY RIOTS.—TWO CONSTABLES KILLED. A. Central News telegram, dated New York, Friday, states :—Ntirs has been received at Toronto that the whisky rioters at Michipicoten have fought the constables, killing two and wounding an inspector. The roughs are in posses- sion of the town.

KIANCE AND CHINA. SHANGHAI, FRIDAY.—The Chinese authorities have COM- menced operations for blocking the Moosung river. Tha con- 'centratiou of Chinese troops in the neighbourhood of Shan- ghai and Pekin still continues. THE CHOLERA. NAPLES, FRIDAY AFTERNODN.—ORIy four fresh cases and one death from cholera have occurred here during the past 24 hours.

IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—FBIDAY. The House met at four o'clock. DYNAMITE STORES.-Sir W. ILATICOURT, replying to Sir E. Watkin, said the unguarded condition of stores of dyna- mite had attracted attention, but there were doubts as to who were responsible for their safety. As there were float- ing stores in Thames Creek, he had induced the Admiralty to take charge of them, although that department was not responsible.

THE BIIISSINGHLM SQUABBLE.— Lord R. CHURCHILL asked Mr. Chamberlain if he had other documents of the same nature as those be quoted from last night, and whether he would have any objection to give him legally attested copies of all the documents, so that legal proceed- ings might be instituted.—Mr. CHAMBERLAIN said he had 'other documents, but he woald readily give copies of those he had quoted ; and further, that he would throw no diffi- culty in the way of further investigation. DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS.—The adjourned debate On the addrese was resumed. Mr. Med TER rose to. move an amendment relative to the present depressed condition of agriculture and commerce. He insisted that Free Trade, as it was called, had the effect of keeping away every pri- vilege from the traders of England, giving them nothing In return, and by this means and a system of bounties the property of this country was being utterly destroyed. He moved the following addition to the address :—But humbly to direct Her Majesty's attention to the depressed condition of commerce and agricMture, and regret that Her Majesty's speech contains no reference to a subject of such paramount importance. Mr. ECROYD seconded the amendment. He hoped the Government would take into consideration the desirability of appointing a Royal Commission or Joint Committe of both Houses te investigate the matter in all its bearings.—sir M. Lone blamed the Government for not putting into force any of the recommendations of the Richttond Commimions.

TO THE ELECTORS OF WEST SUTTON WARD.— LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,—The term of three years, for which you did me the honour of electing me as one of your representatives in the Council for the West Sutton Ward, will expire on the let November, and I therefore beg again to offer you my services. Should you again honour me with this mark of your confidence, my best efforts shall be exerted in the in- terest of your ward, and of the borough generally.—' remain. Ladies and Gentlemen, your obedient servant, ED WARD JOHNSON. Elephant-lane, Button, October 17th 1884. TO THE BURGESSES OF PARR WARD. As the period for which you re elected one to represent you in the Council has almost expired. I hasten ts inform you that Ido not intend seeking reelection. The claims on my time are such that of late I have nct been able to devote that time and attention to your interests I should like to have done, and which you have a right to demand from your representa- tive. As a member of the Council, it has always been my aim to merit the confidence you had so unreservedly placed in me, and to discharge my duties faithfully to all. I thank you most sincerely for the honour so long o mferred upon me. Your obedient servant. THO NI AB WALKER. Merton Bank Alkali Works, St. Helens. Lancashire, 14th October, 1884. -• 1N PARLIAMENT. SESSION 1885. THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL BILL. WHEREAS a Meeting of the Owners and Ratepayers of the Borough of Warrington-. in the counties of Lancaster and Chester, was held on Thursday, the Twenty-third day of October. 1884, in the Public Hall. Rylands-street. in the said Borough, in pursuance of the Act of the 35th and 36th Vic., cap. 91, intituled ". an Act to authorize the application of Funds of Municipal Corporations and othtr governing bodies in certain cases " And whereas at the said meeting, held at the time and place aforesaid, I, as Chairman of such Meeting, and in compliance with the statute, proposed the following resolution "That this meeting consents to the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses of the Borough of Warrington promoting, in con- iutction with others, a local and personal Bill in Parliament for the purpose of incorporating a Company and empowering such Company to construct a canal from the river Mersey to the City of Manchester, navigable for Ocean Steamers and Ships of large burthen, and to the contribution out of the Borough Bate to the cost of such promotion of a sum not ex- ceeding twopence in the pound upon the annual rateable value , of the Borough for one year." And whereas the said resolution on being put to the meet- trig was carried, whereupon demand was made that such I question should be decided by a Poll of the Owners and Rate- payers. NOTICE IS THEREFORE HEREBY GIVEN, that such POLL will be held, in manner provided by the Public Health' Act' 1875, and the Schedules thereto. 1. That such poll will be taken by Voting Papers in manner provided by the Public Health Act, 1875. 2. That such Voting Papers will be delivered on Monday, the , 24th day of November. 1884. and any person qualified to ' vote, who shall not have received a Voting Paper on that day, may apply personally to me. at the Town's Clerk's office, for a Voting Pap.r. on any day before Friday, the 28th day of November, 1881. between the hours of Two and Four p m. 3. That such Voting Papers will be collected on the said Friday, the 28th day of November, 1884. by the persons appointed by me for that purpose between the hours of Nine o'clock in the Morning and Six o'clock in the Evening. 4. That I shall attend to examine and cast up the votes thereat, at the Town Hal,, in Warrington atoresaid, on • Saturday, the 29th day of November, 1884, and on as many days immediately succeedi g, as may be necessary, be- tween the hours of Ten oic,ock in the F.,renoon. and Four o'clock in the afternoon, of each day, and that in case any Voting Paper duly delivered shall not have been collected through my default or that of the person appointed to re- ceive the same. the Voter, in person, may deliver the same to me. before Twelve o'clock on the said 29th day of Nov- ember, 1884. And I hereby further give notice that any owner or proxy will be entitled to leave a voting paper delivered to him, if. on or before Saturday, the B'h day of November, 1884, he serAis a claim in writing to me, at the Town Clerk's Office, containing the particulars required by the second schedule to the Pubic Health Act, 1875. to be contained in claims. And further, that forms of claim may be obtained on personal application tO the Town Clerk's office. Dated this 31st day of October. 1884. JOSE PFL HARRISON, Mayor and Returning Officer.

Herbert Eidson, Esq., chartered accountant, 5, St. James's Square. Manchester. SECRETARY. Mr. Joseph Starkey, 21, !South Crustle-street, Liverpool. -- PROSPECTUS. This Company has been formed for the purpose of acquiring the lease agreed to be granted by George Fortercue Wilbra- ham, Esq , to Mr. Thomas Barrow, of Plots of Land at Over and Weaver, near Winsf ,rd, in Cheshire, the heart of the salt district, for a term of 40 years from the 19th day of July. 1882, and Pumping Brine, Manufacturing White Salt, and Mining Rock Salt on such premises. The land available is about one mile and a inalf in length, situate in the valley of the river Weaver, and has by borings already made been proved to contain one of the richest, if not the principal. of the Brine runs in the Winsford salt district. A most valuable feature in this undertaking is the having the sole right of pumping the Brine; which will be utilised before it can reaca the district where the existing salt works are situated. The land it is further believed contains valuable and exten- sive beds of Rock Salt, which will ultimately prove to be a source of great profit to the Company. as lirck Salt of good quality in the Northwich district is being rapidly exhausted. _ It is proposed to erect extensive winks for the manufacture of Bait on the most imptssved pluriples, and it is believed that a considerable saving will be effected by the adoption of improved furnaces, svhicn will more effectually consume the smoke than those generally used at the existing works. As the demand for Salt in the Winsford district is increasing yearly, it is confidently anticipated that the position of the land secured will enable the Company to intercept the flow of the brine from those lands to the existing works, which are situate at a lower level, and by sinking a shaft or shafts enable this Company to supply Brine to such existing Salt Works, for wh'ch it Is belie red there will be a good demand. This can be done before the works for making salt are erected. The greet extent of land along the Weaver valley, commenc- ing at the Lower Flashes, in the direct line of the Brine Row which will be under the immediate control of this Company, will give unequalled facilities for obtaining a continuous sup- ply of Brine at all times, thereby avoiding that prolific source of inconvenience and difficulty with existing works—an inter- mittent and diminished supp,y, which has, in some instances, compelled proprietors to carry Brine in barges along the river, so as to continue manufacture. The anticipated cost of erecting salt works capable of produc- ing 1,500 tons of salt per week would be about .212,000. In this sum is included the cost of sinking a shaft, which will not only produce the brine necessary fur enabling the Company to manufacture this quantity of salt, but would also enable them to supply brine to other manufacturers. It is abundantly clear from the facilities and concessions obtained by this Company that from the manufacture of the before-mentioned quantity of salt a profit of £B,OOO would be realised. The plan of the site secured will readily coevey an idea of the advantageous position in which the Company's works are placed. and the facilities afforded for supp ying bike to other proprietors. The only agreement entered into is one dated the 9th day of June, 1884. between Thomas Barrow, of the first part, and Joseph Starkey, on t ehalf of the Company, of the other part, whereby the said Company agrees to pay the vendor £B,OOO, In 1,600 fully paid up shares, for his interest in the lease, one. half available at the end of twelve months, the other at the end of two years, which raid agreement was adopted and con- firmed by this Conopany by an agreement dated the 24th day of June, 1884. Under the agreement above referred to it is provided that a royalty of 4d per 1,000 gallons shall be paid on the Brine, except when it is conveyed for manufacture elsewhere than on the estate, when the royalty will be 5d per 1,000 gallons. The royalty on Rtek Salt is agreed to be 40 per ton, with a minimum pit rent of £5O per annum, if worked. Without holding out any extragavant hopes of excessive dividends, the Directors have confidence in recommending this as a safe investment, and one that will yield fair and remunerative returns. Particular attention is called to the following reports, and application for shares may be made to the Secretary of the Company, where the above agreements can be seen, arid copies of the Memorandum of Association obtained. -- Northwich, July 24tb, 1883. Messrs. Herbert Eidson and Co„ Manchester. Dear Birs,—l have your letter ot July 19tb, respecting Mr. Wilbraham's concession to Mr. Barrow, af Rock Ferry, of the right to sink for and use brine and erect salt works, arc., on hls estate on the banks of the river Weaver, in the neighbourhood of Weaver Hall. Having on more than one occasion made an examination of the property referred to, I am of opinion that Ihere are exten- sive beds of rock salt underlying it, and that there is a copious supply of brine of the best quality. I am also of opinion from the configuration of the surface and the subsidences which have gone on persistently for the last 50 years, that a very considerable pottion of the brine used in the Winsford Salt Works is drawn from this district, and that soy works for the manufacture of salt erected on this property would abstract a portion of the brine which would otherwise go to Winsford. I know of nothing that would lead me to think that any works erected further up the Weaver than the neighbourhood of Weaver Hall would be likely to interfere in any way with works erected between Weaver Hall and Winsford. The supply or brine I believe to be practically inexhaustible (though it may ductuat eat times), the estate being the very centre of the brine-producing area. lam strongly ef opinion that for a long period no complete failure of brine need be an- ticipated, and that works erected in this neighbourhood would be able to manufacture salt on as cheap a scale as any works In Cheshire. Brine may be pumped at a cost of 21-d. per ton of salt con- tained in it, and the average price of such brine to the pur- chaser is ed. per ton, showing a very large profit. The effect of extensive pumping in this district would be to cause a smaller supply to the Winsf.Td works, and there is every probability that a good demand for brine to supply those works would be the result of aI ch pumping. Yours very truly, (Signed) THOMAS WARD. Northwich, September 25th. 1884. Joseph Starkey, Esq. Dear eir,—l was pleased to learn that you had found brine in considerable quantity on the estate of Mr. Wilbraham, at Over. In the present state of the trade this find is most valuable. The concessions you have secured for boring and searching for brine on Mr. Wilbraliam's estates, on both sides of the Weaver, are very valuable, and will enable you, in my opinion to have the control of one of the finest supplies of brine in the Cheshire salt district, and put you In the position of supplying any of the works below Winstord, either on the Over or Wharton side of the river if necessary.—Yours very truly, THOMAS WARD. Bridgewater Foundry, Runcorn, Oct. 2nd, 1884. Dear Sir,—Having made trial borings at Dairy House and Ways Green, on Mr. Wilbraham's eitate, between Weaver Hall and Winsford, I found plenty of brine, and of good strength, and which rose about 130 feet in the bore hole at the last boring at Ways Green, and I am of opinion rock salt is in abundance to produce such a large yield of brine.—Yours very respectfully, E. Out of the 31 entries, no less than seven were M"Sold everywhere in simply packed in common table salt, which, in some in. Tablets is. each. OOD COMPLEXION stances, had been previously, thoroughly dried. , The ur Larger sizes, Is. 6d. & Is. 6d. exhibitors who chose this mode of preparation were Mrs. Dent (810), Mrs. Lawder (912), Miss Dolber (915), Mrs. Cuming (924), Mr. L. Woods (928), Mr. Pierce (937), and Miss Rose Hubbard (932). The eggs when broken were 'alike in quality; the salt had absorbed a rather large " portion of the waters of the albumen, or white, conse- quently there was a considerable air cavity at the larger end, the presence of which was evident by the sound produced when the eggs were shaken. The white was thickened by the loss of the water, but otherwise very little changed, and the eggs were perfectly good for pastry or cooking purposes, being superior to the com- mon shop eggs obtained in London during the winter season, being free from any objectionable odour or taste. I do not suggest that such eggs would answer for sale, as the shaking of the contents would be objectionable. In one exhibit the eggs had been wrapped in thin paper before being placed in the dried salt, but they were found on testing not different from the others. Mr. Swallow sent eggs packed in sand and salt, but the result, as might have been expected, was similar to that produced when pure salt was used. Miss Fryer (911) employed a mixture of slaked lime and salt, with a similar result, nor could I detect any appreciable difference in those of Mr. H. Johnson (939)', that had been previously rubbed With gum water; like the other salted eggs, they were quite good for kitchen use, and had the same large amount of air-space. "There was one example of the gum process, that of Miss Rose Hubbard (931). It is given thus by the ex-• hibitor :—‘Eggs dipped into a strong saturated solution of pure gum arabic. Operation twice repeated. Eggs thoroughly dried, then wrapped in paper and packed in bran. Eggs three days old.' These eggs had been very carefully prepared; a thread had been tied round each, by which it was suspended after being dipped in the gum. On being tested, they were found to be equally good with tho best of the other processes, the loss of water being checked by the thick coating of gum. But the process itself necessarily entails some trouble. "Taking into' account the success of the processes in which oil and grease are employed to close the pores, it is difficult to account for the failures of those in which the eggs are dipped into melted wax or paraffin. Three examples of the former medium were exhibited. Miss Rose Hubbard (929) showed those preserved by the Henwife' process :—Take each egg and envelope in fine tissue paper, leaving a screw of paper to hold by. Heat a mixture of sperm and wax, or suet and wax, to 100 deg. Dip the egg in once, and leave to cooL Repeat the process when the first coat is dry. Each egg should be perfectly clean and dry. A little starch may be rubbed over it before wrapping in paper. Packed in fine dry flour. Eggs laid the same day as preserved, namely, June 26th, and also a second set (930 packed in fine Sawdust in place of flour, the eggs being days old when preserved, June 26th; and Miss H. Belgrove (926) showed a collection preserved with white wax, and then packed in sand. On removing the wax from the -eggs of these three collections, the shells were seen to be more or less disceloured, and on opening the air space was found to be mildewed, and the contents quite unfit for use—even the yolks being changed. Some years since I tried a somewhat similar experiment with pure white solid paraffin, placing the eggs separately in glass vessels, and pouring some melted paraffin at 108 degrees over them when quite fresh. I expected that, as the air was perfectly excluded, the eggs would be admirably preserved, and confess to have been very disappointed at finding in three months they had become unfit for use. The eggs shown by Mr. L. Fade (912), wrapped in oiled paper and dipped in boiling resin,' proved, on being opened, which was done with some difculty, owing to the adhesion of the resined paper, to be quit unfit for use; in fact, the heating of the boiling resin had caused them to become offensive. "There were four collections in which the preservation depended on the closure of the pores of the shell by rub- bing in fat or oil. Those of Mr. P. Marigold (918) were stated to have been Preserved in beef and mutton dripping, melted together, a little painted over each egg, and then wiped with a cloth.' Mr. A. Brooke's (934) were Rubbed in well with butter.' Miss Neal's (927) Painted with salad oil and packed in sand.' Those of Miss Belgrove Taken fresh from the nest, painted with salad oil, and wrapped in paper, packed inlflour.' The whole of these were fit for kitchen purposes, being equal to ordinary shop eggs; but as there had been no absorption of water, as in the case of those packed in salt, and the evaporation had been checked by closing the pores of the shell, the white was thin and watery. Those of Miss Neal, packed in sand, were very clean, as were those of Miss Belgrove ; but the extra trouble and expense of packing in paper and flour did not appear to produce any corresponding advantage. "Three collections, those of Dr. Benson (920)4 Miss Monk (933), and Mr. Browne (938), showed a combina- tion of the last two methods, theeggs.being first but- tered or oiled, and then placed in Salt. The result in the three cases was satisfactory, but the white was more watery than in those cases where salt alone was used, as the transmission of water through the shell was checked by the oil or grease. • The results of three liquid preservatives were shown. Mrs. Buchan (916) forwarded eggs in limewater only; Miss Dalrymple (923) sent specimens preserved in lime- water with a very small quantity of salt;' and Mrs. Terrot (914) employed the following receipt:—' Twenty quarts of water loz. saltpetre, 3.1 b. salt, six tablespoon- fuLs quicklime; 'boil the water and saltpetre and salt twenty minutes and pour that hot upon the quicklime; the next day rfilt in the eggs, keep the pot covered in a cool place.' All of these were perfectly sound, and quite good for the cook's use; from being kept in fluid, all evaporation of the watery portion of the contents was prevented, and the shells were consequently quite full. There was so little alteration of the appearance of the eggs when wiped dry that they might have passed current as ordinary shop eggs. The white was some- what thinner than usual, but perfectly free from any musty odours. Those in the more compound solution did not differ perceptibly from the others out of pure limewater. . "Two sets remain to be considered. Mrs. Ellis (917) showed eggs coated with moist lime, which formed a friable cement round them, and they were then packed in bran; on testing they were found as good as many of the other processes, but there was no superiority to compensate for the extra trouble, Mr. Thomas J. Syer (922) showed dry air process, with smallest possible amount of surface of shell allowed to be touched. No artificial coating of shell. The eggs placed small end downwards, in a tightly-closed cabinet with sliding shelves perforated with holes, no preparation being em- ployed... The eggs had kept fairly well, but the size and expense of the cabinet would prove objectionable if em- ployed on a large scale, one for 112 'eggs costing 245. and measuring 20in. by 18in. by 10in. deep. Three exhibits do not require notice, as preparations were used, the composition of which was not given, and one had no particulars whatever." SEASONA.BLE HINTS. We are now fast approaching the end of October, and in spite of the splendid autumn grass is getting very scarce, and what there is of it is poor and without much nourishment For fowls, some substitute must be found, and this can be done without much difficulty. There are plenty of winter greens to be obtained at a reasonable price, of which cabbage is the chief, and a good sized cabbage to every half-dozen fowls will be found a great boon. Failing this, or as an alternative, turnips, potatoes, or any roots may be given. They are better if boiled first, and then 'mixed with the soft food. On a large farm, or where there is a good kitchen gar- den, very little difficulty will be found in supplying the needs of the birds; and if in other places where they have to be bought, it is quite worth buying them.
